DIFFUSION AND EFFUSION The spontaneous intermixing of molecules of one gas with another at a given temperature and pressure is called Diffusion. Diffusion is the random movement of a gas from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Examples: Fragrance of rose. Intermixing of NH3 and HCl gases gives dense white fumes of NH4Cl. Reddish brown bromine Br2 gas taken in a test tube will combine with air taken in another test tube. Red vapours of Br2 gas will spread in the test tube containing air. When a drop of liquid ink is left into bottom of test tube containing water, it will spread evenly throughout the water. Effusion is the escape of gaseous molecules through extremely small pores in a region of low pressure. This escaping of molecules is not due to collisions but due to their motion one by one. GRAHAM'S LAW OF DIFFUSION AND EFFUSION A Scottish scientist Thomas Graham in 1831 (1805-1869), measured the rates at which different gases effuse from an apparatus at the same temperature and pressure. He found that the lighter the gas (the lighter its particles), the faster the gas escaped from the apparatus. Mathematical form of Graham's Law of diffusion of gases: The rate of diffusion or effusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density at constant temperature and pressure. r 1/d, where r rate of diffusion, d density of the gas. But density is directly proportional to molar mass M. So r 1/M or r k/M, where k is constant of proportionality. Consider two gases with r1 and r2 as their rates of diffusion and d1, d2 be their densities and molar masses M1, M2 respectively. For two different gases, equation can be written as r1 k/M1 and r2 k/M2. Dividing equation, r1/r2 (M2/M1). It may also be written as r1/r2 (d2/d1). Example: Equal volumes of HCl and SO2 are confined in a porous container. What would be the comparative rates of diffusion of these gases through the porous walls? The molecular masses of HCl and SO2 are 36.5 and 64 respectively. Solution: Molecular mass of HCl (M1) 36.5 amu.

Molecular mass of SO2 (M2) 64 amu. Rate of diffusion of HCl (r1) ? Rate of diffusion of SO2 (r2) ? According to the Graham's Law of Diffusion: r1/r2 (M2/M1) (64/36.5) 1.753 1.324. So r1 1.324 r2. The rate of HCl will be 1.324 times the rate of diffusion of SO2. LIQUEFACTION OF GASES Gases can be liquefied by Joule-Thomson's effect. The liquefaction of gases can be achieved by cooling them to low temperature. When a highly compressed gas is allowed to escape through a throttle (small hole), the temperature falls to such an extent that it liquefies. At low temperature, the gaseous molecules come close to each other with the result that intermolecular attractions increase. When it is allowed to escape through a nozzle (small hole) from high pressure to low pressure, the molecules move apart. In doing so, energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular attractions. This energy is taken from the molecules themselves, so the gas is cooled. This process is repeated for many times until the gas completely changes into the liquid form. Linde's Method (1895) According to Joule-Thomson's effect "When a highly compressed gas is allowed to escape out through a throttle, the temperature of the gas falls to such an extent, that it changes into the liquid form". This is the basic principle of adiabatic expansion which is thermally isolated from its surroundings. Steps: Air is compressed to 200 atm approx. Most of the water in the air condenses and is removed. Then the heat generated as a result of compression is removed by passing the gas through cooling pipes. The dry gas is then passed through a copper spiral coil. It is then expanded to almost atmospheric pressure through a controlled valve. When the air comes out the valve the expansion takes place from 200 atm to 1 atm. In this, a fall of temperature occurs. This cold air goes up and cools the incoming compressed air. This cycle is repeated several times. Ultimately the expanding gas finally drops and the remaining air is liquefied. The condensed air collects in the chamber and can be drawn off. Claude's Method The principle of appliances such as refrigerators, heat pumps and air conditioners all work on the principle of Joule-Thomson's effect. A compressor compresses a gas such as Freon. The hot Freon gas passes through coils on the outside of the refrigerator. Air at room temperature cools down the hot Freon and as a result condenses it. The liquid Freon then passes through an expansion valve into low pressure tubes which are inside the refrigerator. As the liquid Freon evaporates rapidly, the heat of vaporisation needed to do this is drawn from the refrigerator and its contents, thereby cooling. Then the Freon gas is once again drawn into the compressor and the cycle starts over again. Example: Cooling pop can (container). A small container holding liquid CO2 is built right into the can.

When the can is opened, the liquid CO2 vaporises and escapes out of the top of the can. The heat absorbed by the vaporising CO2 can lower the temperature of the POP by about 16C in a few seconds. Thus the temperature is lowered considerably. Applications of Kinetic Molecular Theory The Velocity of molecules: The equation for the root mean square velocity deduced from kinetic equation is: Crms (3RT/M). Where Crms root mean square velocity, M molecular mass of the gas, T absolute temperature. This equation gives a quantitative relationship between the absolute temperature and the velocities of gas molecules. Higher the temperature of a gas, greater would be the velocities of the molecules. Graham's Law of diffusion of gases: According to the postulates of Kinetic Molecular Theory, the Kinetic Energy of the particles is proportional to the Absolute Temperature. (1/2) m v2 (3/2) k T. So v (3kT/m). At constant temperature, K.E will remain constant so (3kT) Constant. Therefore v 1/m. Thus the kinetic molecular theory predicts that the average speed depends upon molecular mass (m). Further the average speed of the particles is inversely proportional to the square root of their molecular mass. PLASMA (THE FOURTH STATE OF MATTER) Plasma is the fourth state of matter. It was identified by William Crooks in 1879. It is molecular gas changing into atomic form and then to ionic form at high temperature. Molecular gas Atomic gas Ions. At a temperature of 10000K to 100000K (10eV to 100eV) electrons are removed from atoms. Plasma is composed of a mixture of un-ionized gas, free electrons and charged particles. Most of the universe contains matter in the Plasma state e.g., shining stars and interstellar space is filled with plasma. On our planet plasma does not exist. Plasma is fourth state of matter. Properties of plasma: It is a substance in which many of the atoms or molecules are ionised effectively making it easy for electrical charges to flow freely. It takes place at very high temperature. Plasma has the following properties: Plasma consists of neutral particles, positive ions and free electrons. Plasma is strongly influenced by both magnetic and electric force. Plasma shows a characteristic glow depending upon the gas present in the discharge tube e.g., Oxygen gives a red glow, hydrogen green and Nitrogen purple or pink glow.

INTRODUCTION A simple definition of a liquid is that "it is a material that assumes the shape of a container without filling it completely". A gas on the other hand takes the shape of the vessel and expands to fill it completely. A solid neither takes the shape of the vessel nor expands to fill the container completely. The definition of a liquid is satisfactory on the whole with the following exceptions. Some materials, polymers (e.g. PVC etc); they appear in the solid but at higher temperature they behave like liquid even before they melt. The cohesive force i.e. force among the molecules of substance in a liquid are stronger than those in a gas even though less than in a solid. MOLECULAR INTERPRETATION OF LIQUIDS: The kinetic molecular theory also applies to liquids. Postulates of kinetic molecular theory for liquids are: The molecules of a liquid are relatively close together. The intermolecular forces among the molecules of a liquid are stronger than those among gas molecules but not sufficient to hold molecules in fixed positions. The molecules of a liquid can slide past each other. The Kinetic Energy of liquid molecules is directly proportional to the Absolute Temperature. At a particular temperature, the average K.E of the molecules is equal to the K.E of the molecules of liquids. Simple Properties of Liquids There are some simple properties of liquid e.g. diffusion, compression, expansion, motion of molecules, spaces between them, intermolecular forces, and Kinetic Energy based on Kinetic Molecular Theory. We can use the Kinetic Molecular Theory to account for the simple properties of liquids. Diffusion: The diffusion in liquids takes place because the molecules move from one place to another due to K.E. The restricted movement of the molecule reduces the rate of diffusion e.g. a drop of ink when added to water diffuses slowly due to relatively small empty spaces between the molecules. The diffusion between closely packed molecules of liquids is slow due to less collision between them. Compression (effect of pressure): A liquid cannot be compressed significantly by increasing the pressure because the molecules are already in close contact with one another e.g. an increase of pressure from 1 atm to two atmospheres reduces the volume of water to 0.0045 percent which is negligible. However the same pressure reduces the volume of a gas up to 50 percent. Expansion (effect of temperature): The liquids expand on heating because the intermolecular forces between them decrease. Moreover the increase of temperature increases the effective collisions between the molecules. If the temperature is decreased, contraction of volume takes place. This property is useful for making thermometers, e.g. mercury thermometer. In it, if the temperature rises, the mercury expands in the capillary tube. As the volume of capillary tube is much less than the volume of the bulb containing mercury, a small expansion gives a large movement of mercury thread. Motion of Molecules: The molecules of liquids have low speed due to larger forces of attraction among them.

They have low kinetic energy. However the kinetic energy is moderate. Spaces between Molecules: The spaces between molecules are small due to close packing. However the molecules in a liquid have empty spaces. INTERMOLECULAR FORCES The forces of attractions among the molecules of a substance are called inter-molecular forces. For example, the molecules in a liquid are held together due to inter-molecular attractions besides bonds. The forces of attraction existing among the molecules of a substance are also known as Vander Waal's forces. The physical properties of liquids can be explained in terms of their intermolecular forces. Types of intermolecular forces are of five types: Dipole-Dipole forces Ion-Dipole forces Dipole-Induced dipole forces London Dispersion forces Hydrogen bonding Dipole-Dipole Forces: Polar molecules have charges at different parts of a molecule. Due to these charges they attract each other. The interaction between the positive ends of one molecule with the negative end of another molecule is called dipole - dipole forces. This means dipole - dipole interactions are forces between permanent dipoles in molecules. Examples of polar molecules are hydrogen chloride (HCl) chloroform (CHCl3) etc. For polar substances, greater would be the value of thermodynamic properties such as boiling point, heat of vaporization, heat of sublimation etc. London Dispersion Forces: The atoms of noble gases and non-polar molecules become liquefied and solidified under appropriate conditions of temperature and pressure. The forces that attract non-polar molecules to one another in the liquid phase are called London dispersion forces. On the average, the electron charge density is evenly distributed in a sphere. However, at any given instant, the actual location of the electrons around the nucleus can produce an instantaneous dipole. This temporary dipole in one atom can influence the distribution of electrons in neighbouring helium atoms, producing induced dipoles in those atoms. The forces of attraction between an instantaneous dipole and an induced dipole are known as dispersion force. It is also called as London dispersion force, named for Fritz London who offered a theoretical explanation for these forces in 1928. Factors Affecting London Dispersion Forces: Factors affecting the London dispersion force are: Atomic or molecular size Polarizability Number of atoms in molecules Atomic or Molecular Size: The strength of these forces depends upon the size of the electronic cloud of the atom or molecule. With the increase in size of atom or molecule, the dispersion becomes easy and these forces become prominent. Inert gases are all monoatomic gases. They do not make bonds with other atoms because their valence shells are complete. Their boiling point increases down the group from He to Rn. This is because of increase in molecular size. Polarizability: Polarizability refers to the ease with which the electron cloud is distorted. The more tightly bonded electrons in small atoms are not as easily polarized as the more loosely held electrons in larger atoms. For example fluorine is a gas at room temperature, the second member, Cl2 is also gas but more easily condensed than F2.

Bromine is a liquid and Iodine is solid at room temperature. These molecules are easily polarizable, the intermolecular forces are strong enough to form liquids or solids. Number of atoms in a molecule: Large molecules make contact with neighbouring molecules over a greater surface area than small molecules. Greater the number of atoms in a molecule, greater is the contact between the molecules. Table shows boiling points and physical states of some hydrocarbons. Notice that C2H6 and C6H14 have the boiling points as -88.6C and 68.7C respectively. It shows that the molecule with a large chain length experiences stronger attractive forces. Hydrogen Bonding: A hydrogen bond is the attraction between the lone pair of an electronegative atom and a hydrogen atom that is bonded to either N, O or F. This limits hydrogen bonding to the participation of nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine atoms. Hydrogen bonds are weaker than covalent bonds but stronger than dipole-dipole interactions, which are stronger than dispersion forces. The boiling point and heat of vaporization of water are higher than those of H2S. Water molecules attract each other through H-bonding. H2S molecules attract each other by dipole-dipole forces. The boiling points of hydrides of group IVA, VA, and VI-A show a regular increase down the group except NH3, H2O and HF show abnormally high values in the respective series. This is due to hydrogen bonding in their molecules. The boiling point of H2O seems to be more affected than that of HF. As F is more electronegative than O, we should expect H-bonding to be stronger in HF than H2O. But boiling point of H2O is higher than that of HF. The reason is that fluorine can make only one hydrogen bond with the hydrogen of the neighbouring molecule. On the other hand oxygen atom can form two hydrogen bonds with the neighbouring molecules. NH3 can also form only one hydrogen bond as it has only one lone pair. Solubility of Hydrogen Bonded Molecules: The compounds that have hydrogen bonds are soluble in water. Ethyl alcohol can dissolve in water because both can form hydrogen bonds with each other. Similarly carboxylic acids are also soluble in water, if their molecular sizes are small. Cleaning Action: Soaps and detergents perform the cleaning action. Their molecules contain both polar and non-polar ends. Their polar parts are water soluble due to hydrogen bonding and non-polar part dissolve oil or grease. Attraction between water and polar end of soap molecule pulls the oil or grease droplet into the water. Hydrogen Bonding in Paints and Dyes: Paints and dyes have adhesive action due to hydrogen bonding. Similarly hydrogen bonding also makes glue and honey sticky substances. Clothing: We use cotton, silk or synthetic fibres for clothing. Hydrogen bonding is of great importance in thread making fibres. This hydrogen bonding is responsible in their rigidity and tensile strength. Food Materials: Food materials like carbohydrates consist of glucose, fructose, sucrose, each of them contains OH groups which is responsible for H-bonding in them.

Hydrogen Bonding in Biological Molecules: The shape of proteins, substances essential to life, is determined partly by hydrogen bonding. The activity of enzymes, the protein molecules that catalyze the reactions that keep us alive, depends upon the forming and breaking of hydrogen bonds. The hereditary information passed from one generation to the next is carried in nucleic acid molecules which have helical structure. PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF LIQUIDS The physical properties depend upon intermolecular forces. The properties may be classified as under: Additive properties: These depend upon the number and kind of atoms present in the molecule e.g. molecular weight. Constitutive properties: These depend upon the arrangement of atoms in the molecules and not on the number of atoms e.g. optical activity. Colligative properties: These properties depend on the number of ions and molecules present but do not depend upon the structure of molecules. e.g. Osmotic pressure etc. Vapour Pressure and Boiling Point: When a liquid is heated, its V.P. increases due to the decrease of intermolecular forces with rise in temperature. As a result more and more vapours escape in the air. A stage reaches when the liquid begins to boil. So the temperature at which the vapour pressure of the liquid becomes equal to atmospheric pressure or some external pressure is called boiling point of that liquid. E.g. Boiling Point of water at 760 mm Hg 100 C. Boiling Point of water at 23.7 mm Hg 25 C. Effect of Pressure on boiling point of a liquid: There are two practical applications regarding the effect of pressure. Effect of Increase of Pressure: Food can be cooked easily in pressure cookers, which is a closed container. The vapours are not allowed to escape out and, therefore, develop more pressure. This increases the boiling point of water. Pressure cookers help us in cooking the food quickly even at high altitude. B.P of water at 2 atm pressure is 130C. Effect of decrease of pressure: Substances which decompose at their B.P can be obtained in the pure form under low pressure by vacuum distillation e.g. Glycerine has a B.P of 290C at 760 mm of Hg at its B.P. it decomposes. Now in order to get it in the pure form, the V.P is decreased with the help of vacuum pump. The B.P decreases to 210C at 50 mm of Hg, so it can be easily distilled. In this way the liquids can be purified. Evaporation: The process by which liquid molecules escape from the surface and change into vapours at a temperature below the boiling point is called evaporation. The molecules with sufficient kinetic energy can escape from the surface of the liquid. Evaporation is the change of state of a substance from liquid to gaseous phase. Evaporation takes place at all temperatures. The factors which can affect the rate of evaporation are as follow: Surface Area: The rate of evaporation increases with increasing surface area. This is because large surface area allows more molecules to evaporate.

Intermolecular Forces: The escaping tendency of molecules depends upon attractive forces between the molecules. The liquids with strong intermolecular forces have less evaporation. Thus water has less evaporation rate than petrol. This is because water has stronger intermolecular forces (H-bonding) than petrol which has weak dispersion forces between the molecules. A liquid which can rapidly change into vapors is called volatile e.g. petrol is more volatile than water. Temperature: Evaporation takes place at all temperature. Rate of evaporation however is affected by the change in temperature. Increase in temperature increases the number of molecules having kinetic energy sufficient to overcome intermolecular forces and escape more readily from the surface of the liquid. Thus the rate of evaporation increases with increasing temperature. This is why clothes dry more readily in summer. Vapour Pressure (V.P): In open containers, evaporation continues until all of the liquid disappear. But when a liquid is placed into a closed container, amount of liquid decreases for a period of time and then does not change. In closed containers, the vapours cannot escape. Therefore, as the vapour concentration increases, some of the vapour molecules lose energy and return to the liquid state. This process is called condensation. Evaporation involves molecules leaving the liquid and condensation occurs when a vapour changes back to a liquid. When the liquid is placed in a closed container, it begins to evaporate at a constant rate, very little condensation takes place. But as the concentration of vapour increases above the liquid, the rate of condensation increases. After some time the rate of condensation equals the rate of evaporation. At this stage, the number of molecules being formed in vapour phase equals the number returning to the liquid phase, the system is said to be at equilibrium. "The pressure exerted by vapours in equilibrium with its liquid is called the liquid's vapour pressure at the given temperature". Vapour pressure can be expressed in the same units used for gas pressure. Vapour pressure depends upon temperature and intermolecular forces. Vapour pressure of a liquid depends upon intermolecular forces. Liquids having strong intermolecular forces possess low vapour pressure and vice versa. For example, water having hydrogen bonding between molecules has low vapour pressure. On the other hand, non-polar substances like ether have high vapour pressure due to weak dispersion forces. As temperature increases, the vapour pressure increases. This is because increase in temperature increases the average kinetic energies of the molecules which in turn decreases the intermolecular forces. For example, vapour pressure of water at 0 C is 4.6 mm of Hg but at 100C it is 760 mm of Hg. The relationship of vapour pressure and temperature is shown by the graph. It shows that the vapour pressure of diethyl ether (185 mm Hg) at 0 C is much greater than that of ethanol (12 mm Hg) or water (4.6 mm Hg). Ether is non-polar in nature. Therefore, its vapour pressure is due to its weak intermolecular forces (dispersion forces).

Thus at the same temperature, ether molecules require less energy to break free and change into vapour. Similarly, the intermolecular forces (H-bonding) in ethanol are not as strong as those of water. Consequently the vapour pressure of ethanol is greater than that of water at all temperatures. It is observed that each of the three vapour pressure curves cross the line corresponding to one atmosphere at different temperatures. Therefore they boil at different temperatures. Ether boils at 35 C, ethanol at 78C and water at 100C. Viscosity: It is a common observation that water can be poured very quickly from one container compared to honey and glycerine. The resistance of a liquid to flow is called viscosity. The larger the viscosity, the more slowly the liquid flows. Viscosity measures how difficult it is for molecules of a liquid to slide by one another. To understand viscosity, consider a liquid flowing through a pipe. It consists of a series of concentric circular layers. The resistance to flow is due to the friction between the layers of the molecules. The layers adjacent to the walls have minimum velocity and drag on one another and thus causes resistance. The viscosity depends upon the following factors: Molecular shape and size: Molecular size and shape strongly influence viscosity. Liquids such as water, acetone, benzene and ether, whose molecules are small and compact have low viscosity. Whereas liquids having large and chain like molecular shaped molecules like honey, glycerine and lubricating oil have strong forces of attraction that tend to tangle up with each other. This inhibits the flow of molecules and leads to high viscosity. So the large chain like molecules exhibit high viscosity. Intermolecular Forces: Stronger the intermolecular force among the molecules, higher is the viscosity. Liquids whose molecules form hydrogen bonds are more viscous than other without hydrogen bonding. For example water is more viscous than methanol mainly due to extensive hydrogen bonding. Temperature: Molecules move faster as temperature increases. This is because an increase in temperature decreases the intermolecular forces. This dependence is quite noticeable for highly viscous liquids such as honey and syrup. It is easier to pour these liquids when hot than when cold. Surface Tension: Have you ever seen effects such as the water strider to walk on water? What allows it? Surface tension is a tendency of the surface of the liquids to act as if there is a membrane stretched across it. We can understand that the level of liquids exhibit surface tensions. All molecules below the surface of the liquid are surrounded in all directions by other molecules. The force exhibited by such molecules is balanced in all directions whereas a molecule at the surface has molecules beside it and beneath it but no one above it. This results in an unbalanced force pulling the surface molecules inward. The molecules at the surface therefore, feel a net attraction inwards, which creates surface tension.

"The force in dynes acting at right angle on a unit length of surface is called surface tension". For a molecule to come to the surface, it must overcome the attractive force downwards. This means work has to be done to pull it to the surface. In other words creating new areas of a fluid requires an input energy. Surface tension is a measure of the amount of energy required to expand the surface of a liquid. Surface tension of a liquid depends upon the following factors. Intermolecular Forces: The surface tension of a liquid depends directly on the strength of intermolecular forces among molecules. Greater the intermolecular forces among the molecules of liquid, greater is the surface tension and vice versa. For example the surface tension of water is higher than many organic liquids like alcohols, ethers, benzene etc. this is due to strong hydrogen bonding among water molecules. Temperature: Surface tension of a liquid decreases with the increase of temperature. This is because increase in kinetic energy of the molecules decreases strength of intermolecular forces. Units of Surface Tension: Surface tension is different for different liquids due to the presence of different types of intermolecular forces. Unit of surface tension is joule per square meter, or Newton per meter, Nm-1. Anomalous Behaviour of Water Normally, water does not expand like many substances. In ice hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in a rigid but open hexagonal stage. As ice melts, some of the hydrogen bonds break, and water molecules move into the holes that were present in ice structure. As a result water molecules are closer together in liquid water than in ice. When ice melts, there is about 9 decrease in volume and a corresponding increase in density. So, water is anomalous in this regard, because the liquid state is less dense than the solid for most other substances. If we continue to heat water just above the melting point, more hydrogen bonds break. The molecules become still more closely packed and the density of liquid water increases until it reaches a maximum density at 3.98C. Below 3.98C the density of water decreases with decreasing temperature, as we would expect for a liquid. These density phenomena explain why a freshwater lake freezes from the top down in winter. When temperature falls below 4C, the more dense water at 4C sinks to the bottom of the lake. The colder surface water freezes first. Since ice is less dense than liquid water, the ice that freezes remain at the top to cover the lake with a layer of ice, which insulates the water underneath. Thus under this thick blanket of ice, fish and other aquatic life can survive. Application of Hydrogen Bonding to Explain the Properties of Water Hydrogen bonding contributes to its unique properties, which are as follows: High Surface Tension of Water. The force on the surface of water is high due to hydrogen bonding between water molecules. Therefore a high surface tension is developed.

This is proved by the following data. Which liquid has lowest surface tension? Water has the highest surface tension (7.29 x 10-2 N/m) as compared to other liquids. High specific heat: Specific heat is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of 1g of the substance by 1C (or by 1K). For example specific heat of water is 4.180 J/gC. It is much higher than those of metals. It takes almost ten times as much heat to raise the temperature of 1g of water 1C as to raise the temperature of 1g of iron by 1C. Conversely, much heat is given off by water even a small drop in temperature. The vast amounts of water on the surface of Earth thus acts as a giant heat reservoir to moderate daily temperature variations. That is why the climate near large bodies of water such as lakes, ponds, oceans etc, is more moderate than interior of the land. High heat of Vaporization: Water has a high heat of vaporization due to extensive hydrogen bonding. A large amount of heat is required to evaporate a small amount of water. This is of enormous importance to us because large amounts of body heat can be dissipated by the evaporation of small amounts of water (perspiration) from the skin. This effect also accounts for the climate-modifying property of lakes and oceans. High boiling point: Water has a high B.P. due to strong H-bonding. It is practically observed that the B.P. of water is 100C at one atmospheric pressure (760 mm) at sea level, however, the organic molecules like benzene (B.P 80C), ether (35C) etc. have lower B.P. due to poor interactions between the molecules. ENERGETICS OF PHASE CHANGES All physical changes are accompanied by energy change in the form of heat. A quantitative measurement of the energy is the measure of the strength of intermolecular forces. Heat of Fusion (ΔHf): The amount of heat required to convert one mole of a solid into liquid at its melting point is called molar heat of fusion (ΔHf). The heat of fusion for ice is 6.02 kJ mole-1. H2O(s) H2O(l), ΔHf 6.02 kJ mole-1. Heat of Vaporization (ΔHv): The amount of heat required to convert one mole of a liquid into its vapours at its boiling point is called molar heat of vaporization. H2O(l) H2O(g), ΔHv 40.7 kJ mole-1. Heat of Sublimation (ΔHs): The amount of heat absorbed when one mole of a solid sublimes to give vapour at a particular temperature at one atmospheric pressure is called molar heat of sublimation. I2(s) I2(g), ΔHs 62.42 kJ mole-1. Energy Changes and Intermolecular Forces: As a result of melting of a solid, a small change in intermolecular distance and potential energy takes place in atoms, molecules or ions. On the other hand on evaporation, the atoms, molecules or ions undergo large changes in their intermolecular distance and potential energy. Therefore, heat of vaporization is much greater than that heat of fusion.

Examples: ΔHv (heat of vaporization) for H2O (40.6 kJ mole-1 at 373.15K), for NH3 (23.35 kJ mole-1 at 239K) and for CO2 (25.23 kJ mole-1 at 194.5K) are high due to their polar nature and strong intermolecular forces. ΔHf (Heat of fusion) will be as under: H2O(s) H2O(l) ΔHf 6.02 kJ mole-1 at 273.15K. I2(s) I2(l) ΔHf 15.65 kJ mole-1 at 386.7K. Iodine solid has the highest value of Heat of sublimation i.e. 62.42 kJ mole-1. The values for other halogens are F2 6.54 kJ mole-1 at 53.5K, Cl2 6.41 kJ mole-1 at 172.2K, Br2 15.5 kJ mole-1 at 265.9K. Dynamic Equilibrium between two Physical States: Dynamic equilibrium is a reversible process where the two opposite changes occur at equal rates. For example solid to liquid or liquid to gas and vice versa takes place. Many systems tend towards the condition of dynamic equilibrium. At 0 C, ice exists in dynamic equilibrium with liquid water. Ice(s) Water(l). LIQUID CRYSTALS AND THEIR USE IN DAILY LIFE History: In 1888 an Austrian Botanist, Frederick Reinitzer discovered that when crystals of cholesteryl benzoate are heated, it forms a milky liquid at 145C. On further heating, the milky liquid suddenly becomes clear. When the clear liquid is cooled, the reverse process occurs. This milky or turbid liquid is called liquid crystal. The liquid crystal state exists between two temperatures i.e. melting temperature and clear temperature. It is a form of matter intermediate in characteristics between a liquid and solid crystal. They have properties of liquids and show fluidity, viscosity, surface tension etc. Definition: (i) The substance which can flow like a liquid and also have some of the properties of solids within a certain temperature range are called liquid crystals. (ii) The intermediate phase lying between the solid phase and the normal liquid phase is called liquid crystal. Uses in daily life: Liquid crystals are used as temperature sensors. This is because the liquid crystals change their colour with change in temperature. They are used to monitor temperature changes where conventional methods are not feasible, e.g. they are used in thermometer for measuring skin temperature of infants. Some of the modern room thermometers contain liquid crystals with a suitable temperature range. With temperature changes, the liquid crystal show up the figure in different colours. They are used to find the point of potential failure in micro-electronic circuits. They are used to locate the veins, arteries and tumours, e.g. when a layer of liquid crystal is painted on the surface of the breast, a tumour shows up as a hot area which is coloured blue. Thus this technique helps in early diagnosis of breast tumours. Hence, plants import carbon dioxide from the environment primarily. The oxygen released from photosynthesis is much more than the need of respiration; hence, it is exported out of the plant body. At night, plants begin to perform exchange of gases just like animals i.e., they absorb oxygen and release carbon dioxide to the environment as no photosynthesis takes place. text: The term osmosis is defined as the movement of water from the region of its higher concentration to the region of its lower concentration through semipermeable membrane. The movement of water into the cell is called endosmosis while the movement of water out of the cell is called exosmosis. The movement of water into or out of the cell exhibits three kinds of water potentials: water potential, solute potential and pressure potential. Water potential is a measure of the potential energy in water that enables it to move from one region to another. Potential is denoted by the Greek letter ψ (psi) and is measured in units of pressure called Mega Pascal (MPa). In plants, water potential is represented by Ψ. Water potential of a medium is directly proportional to the concentration of water in that medium; therefore, pure water has highest water potential. Water potential of pure water is designated a value of zero. Water potential of solutions or the cells must be less than zero i.e., in negative range. The water potential of solutions is mainly influenced by solute concentration and atmospheric pressure. Water potential can be broken down into its components using the following equation: Ψ Ψs Ψp. As individual components change, they raise or lower the total water potential of a system. When this happens, water moves to equilibrate, moving from the system or compartment with a higher water potential to the system or compartment with a lower water potential. Therefore, for water to move through the plant from the soil to the air (a process called transpiration), the conditions must exist as such: Ψ of soil Ψ of root Ψ of stem Ψ of leaf Ψ of atmosphere. Solute potential (Ψs): Solutes reduce water potential by consuming some of the potential energy available in water. This measure of decrease in water potential of a medium due to the addition of solutes is called solute potential. Solute potential is negative in a plant cell and zero in distilled water. In other words, the amount of available potential energy is reduced when solutes are added to an aqueous system. Thus, Ψs decreases with increasing solute. The internal water potential of a plant cell is more negative than pure water because of cytoplasm's high solute content. Because of this difference in water potential, water will move from the soil into a plant's root cells via the process of osmosis. This is why solute potential is sometimes called osmotic potential. Pressure potential (Ψp): When pressure in addition to atmospheric pressure is applied to pure water or a solution, its water potential increases. It is equivalent to pumping water from one place to another. In a living system, when water enters the plant cells by osmosis, pressure increases inside the cell making the cell turgid and increasing the water potential. This increase in water potential of a medium due to the addition of water or due to the increase in atmospheric pressure is called pressure potential.

text: Pathways of Water Uptake by Roots The root epidermal cells are freely permeable to water and other minerals while cortical cells are differentially permeable. From root hairs water enters the epidermal cells. Then water moves along the concentration gradient. It passes through cortex, endodermis, pericycle and reaches the xylem vessels. There are three pathways taken by water to reach the xylem tissues: (a) The apoplast pathway, (b) The symplast pathway, (c) The vacuolar pathway. Apoplast pathway: The apoplast is the system of adjacent cell walls, which is continuous throughout the plant. When water moving through spaces in the cell walls reaches the endodermis, its passage is stopped by casparian strips (a band of suberin and lignin bordering four sides of the endodermal cells). This is called apoplast pathway. Symplast pathway: Movement of cell sap that involves cytoplasmic connection of adjacent cells is termed symplast pathway. The symplast is the system of interconnected protoplast in the plant. The cytoplasm of neighbouring protoplast is linked by the plasmodesmata. Once water and any solutes it contains is taken into the cytoplasm of one cell it can move through the symplast without having to cross further membranes. Movement might be aided by cytoplasmic streaming. The symplast is an important pathway of water movement. Vacuolar pathway: In the vacuolar pathway water moves from vacuole to vacuole through neighbouring cells, crossing the symplast and apoplast in the process and moving through membranes and tonoplast by osmosis. It moves down a water potential gradient. Structure and Function of Xylem and Phloem There are two types of conducting tissues in plants, namely xylem and phloem. Xylem conducts water and minerals from the roots to the upper parts of the plants. Phloem conducts organic food from the leaves to the other parts. Types of xylem and their functions: Xylem is a complex and permanent tissue that consists of four cell types: the tracheids, vessel elements, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma. Tracheids are dead, elongated cells with tapering ends and lignified walls. They have mechanical strength and give support and help in conduction of water and minerals. These cells are universally present in xylem of all vascular plants, which are therefore, called tracheophytes. Xylem vessels are dead, very long, highly thick walled tubular structures formed by the fusion of several vessel elements end to end in a row. Vessel elements are shorter than tracheids but work as a pipeline in plant body as they are placed one above the other. Xylem vessels are found in angiosperms where they are involved in conduction of water and minerals and also provide mechanical support to the body. Xylem fibres are also dead but narrow, highly elongated, highly thick walled cells with tapering ends. They are mainly responsible for mechanical support to the plant body. The only living cells of xylem are xylem parenchyma, which are thin walled, broad cells and are involved in the storage of water and minerals temporarily during conduction.

text: Types of phloem and their functions: Phloem is a complex and permanent tissue that consists of four cell types: the sieve tube elements, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres (bast fibres). Sieve tubes are the long tube like structures, which translocate solution of organic solutes (sucrose) from leaves to other parts of body. These are formed by the end-to-end fusion of cells called sieve tube elements. Sieve tube elements are thin walled living cells but do not have nuclei; actually, their nuclei are lost as they mature. These cells are narrow at the centre and wide at the ends. A transverse or oblique pore bearing partition, the sieve plate, separates two successive sieve tube elements. Due to the absence of nuclei, the functions of sieve tube elements are controlled by adjacent companion cells. The sieve elements and companion cells, together form a functional unit that act as conducting channels and are involved in transport of organic solutes. Companion cells provide energy to sieve tube elements for their activities. Like xylem tissue, phloem also possesses parenchyma and fibre cells. Phloem parenchyma are storage cells and phloem fibres are very much thick walled supporting cells. Ascent of Sap Water and minerals are absorbed by the root epidermal cells from soil from where these substances are first moved to the root xylem cells and then to the leaves. This upward movement of water and dissolved mineral from root to the leaves through xylem tissue is called ascent of sap. Since this movement occurs against the gravity therefore, a considerable force is required to conduct water and minerals in tall heighted plants. The most acceptable theory that explains this movement is generally called TACT theory. According to this theory, four factors such as Transpiration pull, Adhesion, Cohesion and Tension (TACT) are combined to form a collective force that is mainly responsible for ascent of sap. Transpiration pull: When stomata are open, the water molecules move from the region of high potential (surface of leaves) to a region of low potential (in the air). This evaporation in the same way pulls the water column from the xylem tissue. This force is called transpiration pull. Adhesion is the attractive force between water molecules and other substances. Since both water and xylem cells are polar molecules so there is a strong attractive force for water within the narrow capillaries of the xylem. Adhesion of water molecule to the wall of xylem cells assists upward movement of the xylem sap counteracting the downward gravity. Adhesion also helps to hold water in the xylem when transpiration is not occurring. Water molecules attract one another, forming weak hydrogen bonds. This attraction among water molecules is called cohesion and the hydrogen bonds formed between them are termed as cohesion bonds. Mechanism of TACT force: The column of water molecule within the xylem is at least as strong and unbreakable as a steel wire of the same diameter.

Opening and Closing of Stomata We have studied the structure and distribution of stomata. Stomata are open in day and close at night. The opening and closing of stomata is regulated by the turgidity of guard cells. When guard cells are turgid, stomata are open and when they are flaccid, the stomata are closed. There are two theories for opening and closing of stomata: (i) Photosynthesis theory, (ii) K ions influx/efflux theory. Photosynthesis theory: When guard cells are exposed to light, the process of photosynthesis is started. As the concentration of glucose is increased, the solute potential and water potential of guard cells become more negative. Since, the surrounding epidermal cells have high water potential, the water begins to move from surrounding epidermal cells to the guard cells. The entry of water into the guard cells makes them turgid and thus, stomata are opened. In the evening when the process of photosynthesis is stopped, the concentration of glucose is decreased because some glucose has been consumed in respiratory activities of guard cells, some of it is transformed into sucrose so that it can be transported to other parts, and the remaining glucose is converted into insoluble starch and is stored for later use. The decrease in glucose concentration causes an increase in water potential of the guard cells. In this way, water begins to move from guard cells to surrounding epidermal cells. Due to loss of water guard cells become flaccid, thus stomata are closed. K ions Influx/efflux theory: According to this theory, the start of photosynthetic activity in the morning when plant is exposed to light, causes a decrease in level of CO2 in the guard cells. Low level of CO2 favours or stimulates the influx (inward movement) of K ions into the guard cells from the surrounding epidermal cells by active transport. At the same time, malic acid is ionized into malate ions and H ions due to the exposure of blue light (a part of visible light). The accumulation of H ions causes decrease in pH of guard cells, which are then pumped to surrounding epidermal cells in order to maintain the pH of guard cells. The incoming K ions are combined with malate ions to form potassium malate which is highly soluble in water thus decreases the water potential of the guard cells. In this way water begins to move from surrounding epidermal cells to guard cells. The entry of water into the guard cells makes them turgid and thus, stomata are opened. In the evening, the photosynthetic activity is stopped and level of CO2 rises in guard cells.

Translocation of Organic Solutes The movement of prepared food (organic solutes) to different parts of the plant body through phloem tissue is called translocation of organic solutes. Source and sink or direction of translocation: Unlike ascent of sap, this movement cannot be characterized as upward or downward because prepared food is to move to different directions. Therefore, in order to describe direction of this movement it is usually said that translocation always occurs from a source to a sink. The term source is applied to the area of supply of food such as food preparing organ or storage organ (when it supplies the food). The term sink is used for area of utilization of food such as metabolizing organ or storage organ (when it stores the food). A leaf is purely a source while fruit is particularly a sink; on the other hand root and stem act as both source and sink. Composition of translocating fluid (Phloem sap): Analysis of phloem sap have revealed that it consists of 10-25 dry matter out of which 90 is sucrose (cane sugar), while remaining are other organic and inorganic substances. Mechanism of translocation: Pressure flow or mass flow theory explains the mechanism of translocation of organic solutes. According to this theory, the sugars produced at a source, such as photosynthesizing leaves or storage organ are actively loaded by the companion cells. The increase in concentration of sugars in the phloem, lowers its water potential, thus water will enter by osmosis from the xylem cells. This increases the hydrostatic pressure in the phloem cells, which pushes forcibly the sugary solution away from the leaf (source). The pressure gradient from source to sink causes translocation from the area of higher hydrostatic pressure (the source) to the area of lower hydrostatic pressure (the sink). When this solution is reached to the sink such as roots, the root cells running actively absorb the organic solutes from this solution. The loss of solutes in the phloem sap causes an increase in water potential so the water from the phloem flows back to the xylem tubes. Osmotic Adjustment (Osmoregulation) The maintenance of water and solute level in the body is called osmotic adjustment or osmoregulation. Water and solute relations establish three types of osmotic situations: isotonic, hypotonic and hypertonic. Different osmotic conditions cause different effects upon net movement of water in and out of the cells. If a cell is kept in a medium which has higher water potential and lower solute concentration than cell sap, the water begin to move from medium to the cell (endosmosis) and the cell becomes turgid. Such medium is called hypotonic medium. On the other hand, if a cell is kept in a medium which has lower water potential and higher solute concentration than cell sap, the water begin to move from cell to the medium (exosmosis) and cell becomes plasmolysed. Such medium is called hypertonic medium. Both hypotonic and hypertonic type of conditions compel for osmotic adjustment. The ideal situation for a cell is isotonic in which water potential of the cell and outer environment is equal, therefore, there is no net movement of water in or out of the cell. However, this situation is rarely available to the plants. Osmotic Adjustments in Plants of Different Environment On the basis of availability of water, plants are classified into hydrophytes, mesophytes and xerophytes. Each group is exposed to different osmotic conditions therefore, show different osmotic adjustments. Hydrophytes: The plants that are found in the area where abundant water is available, are called hydrophytes. Such plants are adapted to deal with flooding (excess of water). Such plants show very high rate of transpiration due to broad leaves with distribution of stomata on both sides of leaf, which are generally open in day and close at night. These plants store a very small amount of water, have thin cuticle or almost none, on their surface. Mesophytes: The plants that are found in the area where moderate supply of water is available are called mesophytes. Common crop plants such as wheat, rice corn are example of such plants. These plants are exposed in nearly isotonic conditions so face no drastic problem of flooding (excess of water) or dehydration (deficiency of water). Such plants show moderate rate of transpiration due to medium sized leaves with distribution of stomata on lower surface, which are generally open in day and close at night. However, these plants can close their stomata even in day. These plants store a small amount of water, have very thin cuticle on their surface. In tropical climates, many tall plants shut stomata during the hot days and open at night. Xerophytes: The plants that are found in the area where very little amount of water is available are called xerophytes. Desert plants such as cactus, opuntia are example of such plants. These plants are exposed to severely hypertonic conditions so face extreme degree of dehydration.

text: The growth is part of development process and defined as an irreversible increase in the size and mass of an organism. In plants growth involves four phases: cell division (production of new cells), cell enlargement (increase in size of cells), cell differentiation (modification of cells for particular functions). Plants add new organs like, branches, leaves, flowers and fruits continuously. This unique pattern is called continuous growth. Meristematic Tissues (Meristems) In higher plants, entire plant body is capable of growing, but in higher plants, growth is confined to the meristematic tissues or growing points that possess specialized tissues for growth. Such tissues are called meristematic tissues or meristems. The cells remain forever young and divide continuously. The new cells replace the old cells of the plant in these tissues. When a meristematic cell divides in two, one cell remains in the meristem is called an initial, and the other is called the derivative. By repeated mitotic divisions of the initial cells add new cells, the derivatives are pushed further and further away from the zone of active division. They stretch, enlarge and differentiate into other types of tissues as they mature. Meristematic cells are generally small and cuboidal with large nuclei, small vacuoles, and thin walls. A plant has two major kinds of meristems: the apical meristem and lateral meristem. Apical meristems: These are located at the tips of roots and shoots. Cell divisions and subsequent cellular enlargement in these areas lengthen the above and below ground parts of the plant. Since, these meristems are present in plants right from embryonic life, therefore, they are also known as primary meristems. Similarly, many other properties such as bond energy, relative strengths of bonds, and paramagnetism cannot be explained on the basis of this concept. SHAPES OF MOLECULES The shapes of molecules can be predicted by Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion Theory (VSEPR). This theory was suggested by Sidgwick and Powell (1940). According to this theory; the shape of a molecule or ion depends on the number of shared pairs as well as the unshared electrons around the central atom of the molecule or ion. Gillespie and Nyholm in 1957 proposed that the arrangement of atoms in a molecule is determined by the repulsive interactions among all electron pairs in the valence shell of central atom. Basic postulates of VSEPR theory are as follows: The electron pairs present around the central polyvalent atom are arranged in space as far apart as possible so that, there is minimum repulsion between them. A non-bonding pair or lone pair of electron occupies more space on the surface of an atom than a bonding pair. Both the lone pairs as well as bond pairs determine the geometry of the molecules. The magnitude of repulsion between the electron pairs in a given molecule decreases in the following order: Lone pair - Lone pair Lone pair - Bond pair Bond pair - Bond pair Lone pair causes deviation from ideal bond angles, which in turn change regular geometry. The two electron pairs of a double and three electron pairs of a triple bond contain a higher electron charge density. Therefore, they occupy more space than one electron pair of a single bond. However they behave like a single electron pair in determining the geometry of the molecules. Applications of VSEPR Theory The molecules and ions are classified according to the number of electron pairs present around central atom, irrespective of the fact whether they are of bonding or nonbonding type. In order to describe this theory, consider hypothetical molecules having central atom "A" with more than one terminal atoms bonded with it. Lone pair if present in the molecules is represented by "E".

The first bond formed between any two atoms is the sigma bond. All single covalent bonds are sigma bonds, and the electrons occupying a sigma bond are called σ electrons. A sigma bond is formed by the overlapping of the following types as shown: s-s, s-p, p-p. In pi bond formation, the two overlapping atomic orbitals do not lie on the bond axis. The overlap of p-orbitals in pi bond formation is not as good as that in a sigma bond. One or two pi bonds can form between two atoms. A pi bond is formed by side wise or lateral overlap between two p-orbitals which have their axes parallel to the molecular axis. Drawbacks of Valence Bond Theory It fails to explain: (a) The formation of coordinate covalent bond. (b) The formation of odd electron molecules or ions. (c) The paramagnetic behaviour of oxygen molecule. Molecular Orbital Theory The method of molecular orbital theory was developed in 1927-1928 by Hund and Mulliken and in 1929 by Lennard-Jones. It is assumed that linear combination of atomic orbitals form new orbitals called molecular orbitals which are characteristics of the whole molecule. The molecular orbitals extend over more nuclei of the bonded atoms. Two atomic orbitals after combining give two molecular orbitals which differ in energy. One of them, having lower energy is called bonding molecular orbital (BMO) while the other having high energy is called anti-bonding molecular orbital (ABMO). The bonding molecular orbital is formed by the linear combination (addition) of atomic orbitals while the anti-bonding molecular orbital is formed by the subtractive combination of atomic orbitals. Electrons occupy molecular orbitals according to Aufbau principle and Hund's rule. The electrons from each atom fill the bonding molecular orbital or π orbital while the anti-bonding σ orbital or π orbital may have zero, one or two electrons. The following diagram illustrates the formation of the molecular orbitals (lower energy and higher energy) and also the order of filling of electrons according to rules mentioned above. In this type of diagram, the combining atomic orbitals are shown on two extremes and the resulting molecular orbitals (MO) are represented in the middle column. Atomic orbitals of same energy are shown at the same level. The difference between the energies of atomic orbitals and the bonding MOs depend upon the extent of overlap of atomic orbitals. A large overlap results in greater lowering of the energy of bonding MO (and a corresponding large rise in energy in the anti-bonding MO). Larger the overlap, stronger will be the resulting bond. According to the above diagram, the sequence of energy levels in which electrons are filled up is: σ1s σ1s σ2s σ2s σ2pz π2py π2pz π2py π2pz σ2pz. There are two types of overlapping in molecular orbital theory: Head on approach (linear overlapping) or linear combination and Sideways approach (parallel overlapping). Head on approach can take place between s-s, s-p and p-p atomic orbitals. When two s atomic orbitals overlap, they form two molecular orbitals.

text: Molecular orbital which has low energy than an atomic orbital is called σ orbital. Molecular orbital which has high energy than an atomic orbital is called σ orbital as shown in the figure. Sideways approach or parallel overlapping: When axes of two p orbitals (i.e py or pz orbitals) are parallel to each other, they overlap sidewise. This results in formation of two molecular orbitals. The bonding molecular orbital π(2py) or π(2pz) has zero electron density on the nuclei. The electron density is uniformly distributed above and below the molecular axis. On the other hand, π(2py) or π(2pz) anti-bonding molecular orbital has node region. Since the 2py and 2pz atomic orbitals are of equal energy, the molecular orbitals arising from them are also of equal energy i.e., degenerate orbitals. Bond Order Bond order between two atoms after the atomic orbitals overlap is taken as half of the difference between the number of bonding and anti-bonding electrons. Bond order (No. of electrons in BMOs - No. of electrons in ABMOs)/2. For example, bond order formed in hydrogen molecule may be calculated as follows. Number of electrons in the bonding orbitals 2. Number of electrons in the anti-bonding orbitals 0. Bond order (2-0)/2 1. It is a common practice that only MOs formed from valence orbital are considered in bond order calculations. It should be noted that a bond between two atoms can be formed only when the number of electrons in the bonding orbital must be greater than the number of electrons in the anti-bonding molecular orbitals. As seen in the energy order of lighter molecules like B2, C2, N2, σ2px is higher in energy than π2py π2pz group orbitals. This reversal is due to mixing of 2s and 2px atomic orbitals. When the energy difference of 2s and 2p atomic orbitals is small; there is a possibility of mixing of s and p orbitals (hybridization of A.O.). text: BOND ENERGY (BOND ENTHALPY) When a bond is formed between two atoms, energy is released (exothermic process), the same amount of energy is absorbed (endothermic process) when the bond is broken to form neutral atoms. So the bond energy is the amount of energy required to break all bonds of a particular type in one mole of the substance. The strength of a bond is measured by its bond energy. The higher the bond energy, the stronger is the bond. It is determined experimentally by measuring the heat involved in a chemical reaction. It is also called bond enthalpy, as it is measure of enthalpy change at 298K. The enthalpy change in splitting a substance into its component atoms is called enthalpy of atomization. It is expressed in kilojoules per mole (kJmol1). It is the energy required to break up an Avogadros number (6.02x1023) of bonds i.e., one mole of bond. It is found that energies of multiple bonds are greater than those of single bonds. But a double bond is not twice as strong as a single bond and a triple bond is not thrice as strong as a single bond. It means that a σ bond is stronger than a π bond. Also, a polar covalent bond is stronger than a non-polar covalent bond. Bond energy of H-H in H2 molecule at 25C (298K) is 436 kJ/mole. The bond energy of Cl-Cl bond in Cl2 molecule at 25C is 242 kJ/mole. Bond energy of H-Cl bond in HCl molecule at 25C is 431 kJ/mole. Bond energy is a measure of bond strength. Higher the bond energy, the stronger is the bond. It depends upon the following factors: The greater the difference of electronegativity between the bonded atoms, the greater is the bond energy and stronger is the bond. For example, in H-F, the electronegativity difference is 1.9 and bond energy is 567 kJ/mol. In H-Cl, the electronegativity difference is 0.9 and bond energy is 431 kJ/mol. In H-Br, the electronegativity difference is 0.7 and bond energy is 366 kJ/mol. In H-I, the electronegativity difference is 0.4 and bond energy is 299 kJ/mol. From the above data it is observed that HF molecule has higher bond energy (567 kJmol-1) due to greater electronegativity difference i.e., 1.9. The smaller the size of the bonded atoms, the greater is the bond energy and stronger is the bond. The bond energy of H-H bond is 436 kJmol-1 and that Cl-Cl is 242 kJmol-1. This is due to the shorter bond length in H2 molecule and greater bond length in Cl2 molecule (larger size of Cl atom than H atom). Multiple bonds also affect the bond energy, greater the no. of bonds greater will be the bond energy. Table: Average Bond energies (kJmol-1) of single bonds.

text: EFFECT OF BONDING ON THE PROPERTIES OF COMPOUNDS Solubility of Ionic Compounds: Ionic compounds are soluble in water but insoluble in non-aqueous solvents. When a crystal of ionic compound is placed in water, the polar water molecules surround each cation and anion from the crystal lattice by their electrostatic attraction. The ions are detached from the crystal lattice by hydration. This happens when the hydration energy is equal to or greater than lattice energy. The energy released in hydration is used to overcome the repulsion between the ions are freed from their positions in the crystal. Ionic compounds do not dissolve in water because the attraction of water molecules is not enough to overcome the attraction between the ions. Their lattice energy dominates over hydration energy. For the same reasons, the non-polar solvents benzene and carbon tetrachloride cannot dissolve in ionic compounds. Solubility of Covalent Compounds: Covalent compounds dissolve in non-polar organic solvents such as benzene, ether, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. Covalent compounds are insoluble in water. However, some of them dissolve in water. The attractive forces of solvent molecules in non-polar solvents are enough for separating the intermolecular forces of attraction in covalent compounds. Hence covalent compounds dissolve easily in non-polar organic solvents. Solubility of covalent compounds in water depends on their ability to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Many organic compounds containing oxygen or nitrogen like carboxylic acids, alcohols and amines are soluble in water due to hydrogen bonding. Directional nature of Ionic Bonds: Ionic bonds are non-directional and rigid in nature. They do not show the phenomenon of isomerism. Directional Nature of Covalent Bonds: Covalent bonds are of directional nature. They show the phenomenon of isomerism. Due to non-rigid and directional nature of the covalent bond, covalent compounds have different arrangements of atoms in space. Hence many covalent compounds show the phenomenon of isomerism. For example C2H6O show structural isomerism: CH3-O-CH3 (Dimethyl Ether) and CH3-CH2-OH (Ethyl alcohol). Electrical Conductivity: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the form of ions in an aqueous solution. The ionic compounds have already separated ions which act as carriers of charge, so the reaction is so rapid because no bond formation or bond breaking is involved. Electrical Conductivity of Covalent Compounds: Covalent compounds do not conduct electricity because they do not have free ions in solution. They are neutral molecules. The bonds are generally much slower to react as they involve both bond breaking and bond making. The molecules undergo a chemical change as a whole. It is necessary to break the covalent bonds. Covalent compounds react in a variety of ways. The reactivity of covalent compounds depends upon the way a reaction proceeds and the product obtained at the end of a reaction. Density: The strong electrostatic force of attraction existing between the cations and anions in an ionic compound packs these ions very close to one another. This decreases the volume of the crystal and consequently the ionic crystals have high density.

text: Types of Solids: A Solid is a structural unit of atoms, molecules or ions, which are held together strongly enough to give a rigid structure. Four types of solids exist namely Molecular solids: Consists of atoms or molecules held together by inter-molecular forces. Solid water (ice) and solid CO2 (dry ice) are common examples. Metallic Solids: Consists of atoms held together by metallic bonding, examples silver, copper and gold. Ionic Solids: Consists of cations and anions held together by virtue of electrostatic attraction of the opposite charges. Examples are NaCl and CaCl2. Covalent Network Solids: Consists of atoms held together in large network or chains by covalent bonds. Diamond, graphite are typical examples. Difference between Covalent Network Solids and Molecular Network Solids (Metallic Solids) In Metallic Solids: Metallic solids consist of infinite arrays of bonded atoms; each cation in a metal has a coordination number sometimes four or six, but more often eight or twelve they are good conductor of heat and electricity. In Covalent Network Solids: Consist of infinite arrays of bonded atoms; no individual molecules can be distinguished (each piece of network solid may be considered a giant, covalently bonded molecule). They are non conductor of heat and electricity. Strong covalent bonds throughout these solids, give them great strength and high melting points.

INTRODUCTION When we presented stoichiometry in Chapter 1, we described that reactions proceed virtually to completion when the limiting reactant is completely consumed. This is true for reactions that virtually go to completion i.e., reactants are completely consumed and converted into the products. Such reactions are called irreversible reactions. Such reactions stop when the limiting reactant is consumed. However in many reactions the net formation of products comes to an end before all the limiting reactant has been consumed. Such reactions actually proceed in both the directions i.e. forward and backward and are called reversible reactions. These reactions reach at a stage called chemical equilibrium. At this stage the concentration of reactants and products become constant. But the reaction continues to proceed in both the directions without any change in concentration of reactants and products under existing conditions. Such reactions never go to completion and are called reversible reactions. In this chapter we will discuss how and why a chemical reaction comes to equilibrium. We will discuss the principles and applications of chemical equilibrium. REVERSIBLE REACTIONS AND DYNAMIC EQUILIBRIUM A reversible reaction is one in which the products once formed can react to form reactants. Such reactions do not go to completion even if stoichiometric amounts of the reactants are taken. These reactions take place both in the forward and backward directions under the existing conditions. Some examples of reversible reactions are given below: N₂(g) 3H₂(g) 2NH₃(g) 2NO₂(g) N₂O₄(g) PCl₅(g) PCl₃(g) Cl₂(g) The double arrow tells that the reaction is reversible. Consider the reaction between steam and carbon monoxide under appropriate conditions. On mixing macroscopic changes are observed (e.g., changes in concentration). Suppose that the reaction is started with same number of moles of both the reactants. When steam and carbon monoxide are mixed, a maximum number of collisions per second between them will occur. Therefore the forward reaction has its maximum speed at the beginning. This leads to a decrease in the concentration of the reactants. H₂O(g) CO(g) H₂(g) CO₂(g) As H₂O and CO are gradually used up, the forward reaction gradually slows down. As molecules of H₂ and CO₂ accumulate with time, more and more collisions per second between these molecules occur. Therefore reverse reaction proceeds with increasing speed. This means that forward reaction starts with maximum speed and gradually slows down, whereas the reverse reaction starts at zero speed and gradually increases its speed. H₂O(g) CO(g) H₂(g) CO₂(g) Eventually a time comes when both reactions proceed at the same speed. The reaction attains a stage said to be in chemical equilibrium. The concentration of reactants and products become constant. H₂O(g) CO(g) H₂(g) CO₂(g) Unless the system is somehow disturbed no further change in concentration will occur. The state of a reversible reaction at which composition of the reaction mixture does not change is called the state of chemical equilibrium. The plots of concentrations of reactants and products versus time are shown in Figure 7.1. What do these plots show? Why have they become parallel?

Since the concentration of reactants and products become constant it may appear that the reaction has stopped. But this is not true. On the microscopic level there is excited activity. Individual molecules of reactants continue to combine. Individual molecules of products also continue to combine. But the rate of one process is exactly balanced by the rate of the other. Therefore, this is a dynamic equilibrium. The system is dynamic because individual molecules react continuously, but the rate of the forward and reverse reactions are equal. It is at equilibrium because no net change occurs. The Law of Mass Action Two chemists C.M Guldberg and P. Waage in 1864 proposed the law of mass action as a general description of the equilibrium state. This Law you have learnt in grade X. It states that the rate at which a substance reacts is proportional to its active mass and the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the product of the active masses of the reacting substances. It can also be defined as the rate of a chemical reaction is proportional to the product of molar concentration of each reacting substance each raised to a power equal to its stoichiometric coefficient in the balanced chemical equation. The active mass means, the concentration of the reactants and products in moles dm³ for an aqueous solution. Consider the following general reversible reaction. aA(g) bB(g) cC(g) dD(g) Where A, B, C and D represent chemical species and a, b, c and d are their coefficients in the balanced equation. According to the law of mass action. Rate of forward reaction, Rf Aᵃ Bᵇ Rf kf Aᵃ Bᵇ (1) Where kf is the rate constant for forward reaction. Rate of reverse reaction, Rr Cᶜ Dᵈ Rr kr Cᶜ Dᵈ (2) Where kr is the rate constant for the reverse reaction. At equilibrium state: Rate of forward reaction Rate of reverse reaction Thus kf Aᵃ Bᵇ kr Cᶜ Dᵈ On rearranging: kf / kr Cᶜ Dᵈ / Aᵃ Bᵇ Where Kc kf / kr and is known as equilibrium constant, and the equation (3) is known as equilibrium constant expression. The square brackets indicate the concentration of the chemical species at equilibrium. Thus, the equilibrium constant expression for any reaction can be written from its balanced equation. Concentration of products are taken in the numerator and concentration of reactants in the denominator. Important Features of Equilibrium Constant Important features of equilibrium constant expression are as follows: Kc applies only at equilibrium. The subscript c indicates the concentration of reactants and products in moles per dm³ at equilibrium state. Kc is independent of initial concentration of reactants and products but depends upon temperature. At a given temperature, it has only one value. Whether we start reaction with pure reactants or pure products or any composition in between, the value of Kc remains unchanged. Kc is related to the coefficients of the balanced chemical equation.

The concentration of the products is placed in the numerator and those of reactants in the denominator. Each concentration is raised to a power equal to its coefficient in the balanced chemical equation. The magnitude of Kc indicates the position of equilibrium. When Kc is less than 1, the denominator is greater in magnitude than the numerator. This means the concentration of reactants are greater than those of products when the equilibrium is established. Whereas, when Kc is greater than 1, the numerator is greater in magnitude than the denominator. This means the concentration of the products are greater than those of the reactants at equilibrium. Examples of Equilibrium Constant Expression Write products in the numerator and reactants in the denominator in square brackets. Raise each concentration to the power that corresponds to the coefficient of each species in the balanced chemical equation. Example 7.1: N₂(g) 3H₂(g) 2NH₃(g) Kc NH₃² / (N₂H₂³) Example 7.2: 2CO(g) O₂(g) 2CO₂(g) Kc CO₂² / (CO²O₂) Exercise 7.1 The following reactions represent various industrial reactions at equilibrium. Write Kc expression for each of these reactions. Do not forget to balance the equations: S₈(s) O₂(g) SO₂(g) 2SO₂(g) O₂(g) 2SO₃(g) CH₄(g) H₂O(g) CO(g) 3H₂(g) Write the balanced equations that correspond to following equilibrium expressions. Kc CH₃OH / (COH₂²) Units of Equilibrium Constant Problem solving strategy: Write equilibrium constant expression. Write mol dm³ as units of concentration of each species within square brackets. Simplify the expression. Equilibrium constant may or may not have units. Equilibrium constant has no units if the number of moles of the reactants are equal to the number of moles of the products. For instance Kc for the following reaction has no units. H₂O(g) CO(g) H₂(g) CO₂(g) Kc (H₂CO₂) / (H₂OCO) Kc (mol dm³ mol dm³) / (mol dm³ mol dm³) No units On the other hand if the number of moles of products and reactants are not equal, Kc has units. For example: N₂O₄(g) 2NO₂(g) Kc NO₂² / N₂O₄ Kc mol dm³ In this way we can determine the units for Kc, however units of equilibrium constant is not usually written. Self Check Exercise 7.2 Determine the units for Kc for the following reactions: PCl₅(g) PCl₃(g) Cl₂(g) 2SO₂(g) O₂(g) 2SO₃(g) H₂(g) I₂(g) 2HI(g) The value of Kc at a given temperature can be calculated if we know the equilibrium concentration of the reaction components. Example 7.3 The following equilibrium concentrations were observed for the reaction at 500C. A₂(g) B₂(g) 2AB(g) A₂ 0.399M, B₂ 1.197M, AB 0.203M. Calculate Kc. Solution: Here A₂ 0.399 mol dm³, B₂ 1.197 mol dm³, AB 0.203 mol dm³ Kc AB² / (A₂B₂) Kc (0.203)² / (0.399 1.197) Kc 0.086 Equilibrium Expressions Involving Partial Pressure, Number of Moles and Mole Fraction. Consider the general gaseous reversible reaction. aA(g) bB(g) cC(g) dD(g) For gases the expression is often expressed in terms of partial pressure of each gas. According to Henrys law At constant temperature, the partial pressure of a gas is directly proportional to its molar concentration.

Equilibrium constant Kp in term of partial pressures is given by: Kp (PC)ᶜ (PD)ᵈ / (PA)ᵃ (PB)ᵇ Where PA, PB, PC and PD are partial pressures of gas A, B, C and D respectively. Kp is related with Kc by the following equation. Kp Kc (RT)Δn Where Δn is the difference between the total number of moles of the products and the total number of moles of the reactants as shown by the balanced equation. When the equilibrium concentrations of reactants and products are expressed in terms of their moles, the equilibrium constant is represented by Kn and is given by the following equation. Kn (nC)ᶜ (nD)ᵈ / (nA)ᵃ (nB)ᵇ Where nA, nB, nC and nD are the moles of A, B, C and D respectively at the equilibrium state. Kn is also related with Kp. Kn Kp (RT / P)Δn Where P is the pressure of reaction mixture at equilibrium and n is the total number of moles. When the equilibrium concentration of the reactants and products are expressed by their mole fractions, the equilibrium constant is represented by Kx and is given by the following equation. Kx (XC)ᶜ (XD)ᵈ / (XA)ᵃ (XB)ᵇ Where XA, XB, XC and XD are mole fractions of A, B, C and D respectively. Kx is related with Kp by the following expression. Kx Kp (P)-Δn Where P is the pressure of the equilibrium mixture. Example 7.4 Following reaction was studied at 25C. Calculate its Kp and Kc. 2NO(g) Cl₂(g) 2NOCl(g) The partial pressures at equilibrium were found to be PNO 1.2 atm PCl₂ 5.0 10² atm PNOCl 3.0 10¹ atm Problem Solving Strategy: Write Kp expression. SO₂ 0.59M, O₂ 0.05M, SO₃ 0.259M (Ans: 0.1576) Types of Equilibrium With respect to the physical states of reactants and products, there are two types of Chemical Equilibrium. Homogeneous Equilibria An equilibrium system in which all of the reactants and products are in the same phase. For example: N₂(g) 3H₂(g) 2NH₃(g) 2SO₂(g) O₂(g) 2SO₃(g) 2NO(g) Cl₂(g) 2NOCl(g) CH₃COOH(l) C₂H₅OH(l) CH₃COOC₂H₅(l) H₂O(l) Heterogeneous Equilibria Equilibria which involve more than one phase are called Heterogeneous equilibria.

This physical property is measured during the course of reaction without removing the sample from the reaction mixture. We will discuss spectrometric method. This method is applicable if a reactant or product absorbs ultraviolet, visible or infrared radiation. The concentration can be determined by measuring the amount of radiation absorbed. Equilibrium constant for N₂O₄ - NO₂ system can be determined by the spectrophotometer. N₂O₄(g) 2NO₂(g) (Colourless) (Reddish brown) N₂O₄ is a colourless gas whereas NO₂ is reddish brown gas. The progress of the reaction can be studied by measuring the absorbance at regular intervals. Absorbance is proportional to the concentration of NO₂. At equilibrium spectrophotometer will show constant value of absorbance. Suppose reaction is started with a moles of N₂O₄ at 100C and x moles of it is converted to NO₂. By applying stoichiometry, the amount of NO₂ present in equilibrium will be 2x, which is measured by the spectrophotometer. Suppose the volume of the reaction mixture is V dm³, then we can write.
