INTRODUCTION In this chapter we will discuss the shapes of molecules on the theoretical basis and some factors affecting their shapes and behaviours.

We start by describing the VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) model, which allows us to connect two dimensional Lewis structures into three dimensional shapes. You will see how molecular shape and bond polarity combine to create a polarity for these molecules and how molecular shape influences biological function. Then we consider bonding theories based on quantum mechanics. Valence bond theory explains how the molecular shape arises from the interactions of atomic orbitals. Molecular orbital theory explains the existence of orbitals that extend over the whole molecule. The Lewis concept of formation of covalent bond as a shared pair of electrons between two atoms does not explain shapes of molecules. Similarly, many other properties such as bond energy, relative strengths of bonds, and paramagnetism cannot be explained on the basis of this concept. However, modern theories of chemical bonding not only explain all of our experimental observations, but also allow us to predict the shapes and many other properties of molecules. These theories can also be used to predict many physical and chemical properties of molecules. SHAPES OF MOLECULES The shapes of molecules can be predicted by Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion Theory (VSEPR). This theory was suggested by Sidgwick and Powell (1940). According to this theory; the shape of a molecule or ion depends on the number of shared pairs as well as the unshared electrons around the central atom of the molecule or ion. Gillespie and Nyholm in 1957 proposed that the arrangement of atoms in a molecule is determined by the repulsive interactions among all electron pairs in the valence shell of central atom. Basic postulates of VSEPR theory are as follows: The electron pairs present around the central polyvalent atom are arranged in space as far apart as possible so that, there is minimum repulsion between them. A non-bonding pair or lone pair of electron occupies more space on the surface of an atom than a bonding pair. Both the lone pairs as well as bond pairs determine the geometry of the molecules. The magnitude of repulsion between the electron pairs in a given molecule decreases in the following order: Lone pair - Lone pair Lone pair - Bond pair Bond pair - Bond pair Lone pair causes deviation from ideal bond angles, which in turn change regular geometry. The two electron pairs of a double and three electron pairs of a triple bond contain a higher electron charge density. Therefore, they occupy more space than one electron pair of a single bond. However they behave like a single electron pair in determining the geometry of the molecules. Applications of VSEPR Theory The molecules and ions are classified according to the number of electron pairs present around central atom, irrespective of the fact whether they are of bonding or nonbonding type. In order to describe this theory, consider hypothetical molecules having central atom "A" with more than one terminal atoms bonded with it. Lone pair if present in the molecules is represented by "E".

Shapes of molecules containing two electron pairs around a central atom: AB2 Type. A molecule having two bond pairs of electrons but no lone pair around a central atom always has a linear geometry, because such an arrangement of atoms keeps the two bonding pairs as far as possible. The bond angle will be 180. Shapes of molecules containing three electron pairs around a central atom: AB3 type with no lone pair. A molecule having three bond pairs of electrons but no lone pairs around a central atom always has trigonal planar geometry, because such an arrangement of atoms keeps the three pairs of electrons as far apart as possible. The bond angle will be 120. Boron trifluoride is an example of molecules, which have three bond pairs of electrons. BF3 has trigonal planar geometry and each F-B-F bond angle will be 120. Other examples of such molecules are BCl3, AlCl3, GaBr3, InI3, etc. AB2E type with one lone pair and two bond pairs. In case of PbCl2 and SnCl2 molecules, there are three electron pairs around the central atoms, one lone pair and two bond pairs. According to VSEPR concept the lone pair (non-bonding) of electron occupies more space and exerts a greater repulsion on the bond pairs resulting in the shortening of Cl-Pb-Cl angle. Thus, the shape of PbCl2 molecule is distorted and becomes angular or V-shape with Cl-Pb-Cl bond angle less than 120. AB2 type with multiple bonds. Examples: SO2. In SO2, all the three regions are occupied by S-O bonds. There is no lone pair hence the structure will be perfectly triangular having 120. Shapes of molecules containing four electron pairs around a central atom: AB4, AB3E, AB2E2. AB4 type with no lone pair: A molecule having four bond pairs of electrons but no lone pairs around a central atom always has regular tetrahedral geometry, because such an arrangement of atoms keeps the four pairs of electrons as far as possible. The bond angle will be 109.5. The atoms are at four corners of a regular tetrahedron. Examples: CH4 (Methane), CCl4, SiF4, SnCl4 etc. Methane is a typical example of this type. AB3E type with one lone pair and three bond pairs: A molecule having three bond pairs and a lone pair around the central atom has triangular pyramidal geometry instead of tetrahedral. Due to repulsions between lone pair and bond pairs, the bond angles are reduced to 107.5 instead of 109.5. NH3 is a typical example. Other examples: PH3, AsH3, SbH3, etc. AB2E2 type with two lone pairs and two bond pairs: The presence of two lone pairs, introduces three types of repulsions: lone pair-lone pair, lone pair-bond pair and bond pair-bond pair. In H2O, out of the four corners of a tetrahedron two are occupied by two lone pairs and remaining two by bond pairs.

The lone pairs repel each other and their repulsion among themselves and with the bond pairs cause the bond angle to be reduced to 104.5 and geometry becomes V shaped. Table: Bonding and the shape of Molecules Number of electron pairs around central atom Number of bond pairs Number of lone pairs Shape Examples 2 2 0 Linear BeCl2, HgCl2, CO2 3 3 0 Trigonal planar BF3, BCl3, CH2O 3 2 1 Bent SO2, O3 4 4 0 Tetrahedral CH4, CBr4, SiCl4 4 3 1 Pyramidal NH3, PCl3 4 2 2 Bent H2O, H2S, SCl2 5 5 0 Trigonal bipyramid PCl5 6 6 0 Octahedral SF6 Shapes of molecules containing five electron pairs around a central atom: AB5 type. With more than four electron pairs, it becomes increasingly difficult to visualize geometries of molecules. Thus a central atom containing five electron pairs around it has trigonal bipyramidal geometry. A trigonal bipyramidal arrangement of atoms is the structure in which five electron pairs can have minimum repulsion. In PCl5, there are five electron pairs in the valence shell of central P atom. All of them are bonding pairs and thus PCl5 adopts trigonal bipyramidal structure. Shapes of molecules containing six electron pairs (AB6 type): Molecules in which the central atom has six electron pairs, adopt octahedral geometry. The examples of such molecules are SF6, PoCl6 etc. Steps to predict the shape of molecules: The following steps are generally required to predict geometry or shape by VSEPR method. Draw dot diagram for the molecule. Determine the number of valence electrons surrounding the central atom. Determine the number of bond pairs and lone pairs of electrons. Determine the geometrical distribution of electron pairs so that they are as far apart as possible. Example: Predict the shape of H2S. Valence electrons of S-atom 6 Electrons contributed by H atoms 2 Total no. of electrons around S-atom 8 Electron pairs 4 Bond pairs 2 Lone pairs 2 Thus H2S is AB2E2 type molecule. It will possess V-shaped geometry. THEORIES OF COVALENT BONDING Basically, there are two theories which are used to understand the nature of covalent bond. These are: Valence bond theory (VBT) and Molecular Orbital theory (MOT). Valence Bond Theory (VBT) It is a quantum mechanical treatment of molecules and was presented by Heitler and London (1927) and further developed by Pauling and Slater. The main points of this theory are: A covalent bond is formed by the overlap of half filled atomic orbitals of two atoms. During overlapping, atomic orbitals retain their identity. The overlapping orbitals must have electrons of opposite spin. The number of covalent bonds formed by an atom is equal to the number of unpaired electrons in the valence shell of the atom. When two orbitals overlap, a single bond is formed. If additional orbitals of atoms overlap, then multiple bonds are formed. In order to form a bond, the overlapping orbitals must have the same symmetry with respect to the bond axis.

A line joining the nuclei of two bonded atoms is called bond axis. During overlapping of orbitals energy is released. The greater the overlap between the orbitals, the greater is the energy released and the stronger is the bond formed. Types of Overlapping and Nature of Covalent Bonds There are two main types of covalent bonds which are obtained by overlapping. These are: Sigma bond (σ) and Pi Bond (π). Sigma bond (σ): Any first bond formed between two partially filled atomic orbitals by head on overlap is called sigma bond. In a sigma bond, the region of highest electron density is symmetrically distributed along the bond axis. The electron density is maximum in the region between the two nuclei. The first bond formed between any two atoms is the sigma bond. All single covalent bonds are sigma bonds, and the electrons occupying a sigma bond are called σ electrons. A sigma bond is formed by the overlapping of the following types as shown: s-s, s-p, p-p. Pi bond (π): A pi bond is formed between two already σ bonded atoms by the sidewise overlap of their two half filled atomic orbitals whose axes are parallel. In pi bond formation, the two overlapping atomic orbitals do not lie on the bond axis. The overlap of p-orbitals in pi bond formation is not as good as that in a sigma bond. One or two pi bonds can form between two atoms. A pi bond is formed by side wise or lateral overlap between two p-orbitals which have their axes parallel to the molecular axis. The side wise overlap is not too efficient, so that is why sigma bond is always stronger than a pi bond. In pi bond formation which is over a covalent bond, the electron density is greatest above and below the line joining the two nuclei and this is also called nodal plane. In figure, parallel, co-planar, half filled p-orbitals on adjacent atoms can form a π bond. Only one bond in any multiple bonds can be a sigma bond, the remaining bonds are pi bonds. On the basis of hybridization, the overlapping of any hybrid-orbitals always produces a sigma (σ) bond. Examples of Valence Bond Formation Formation of H2 molecule: Each H atom has the electron configuration 1s1. As two hydrogen atoms approach each other, their half filled 1s orbitals overlap, giving a H-H bond. The overlap of orbitals provides a means for sharing electrons, thereby helping each H to complete its valence shell. The electron density is concentrated in the region along the line joining the two nuclei. The bond thus formed is a sigma (σ) bond. Formation of Cl2 molecule: Electronic configuration of chlorine is: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3px2 3py2 3pz1. In Cl2 molecule, the half-filled 3pz orbital of one chlorine atom overlaps with the half-filled 3pz orbital of another chlorine atom along the inter-nuclear axis to form a sigma bond.

Formation of HF molecule: Electronic configurations of F and H atoms are: F: 1s2 2s2 2px2 2py2 2pz1; H: 1s1. In the formation of HF molecule, the half-filled 1s orbital of H atom overlaps with the half-filled 2pz orbital of F to form σ bond. Formation of O2 molecule: In oxygen molecule, O2 is obtained by the combination of two oxygen atoms. Electronic configuration of an oxygen atom: 1s2 2s2 2px2 2py1 2pz1. Each oxygen atom has two unpaired electrons in two half-filled 2p orbitals in the valence shell. On the basis of VBT, two covalent bonds should be formed between two O atoms. One bond is formed by the head on overlapping of 2pz and 2pz orbitals on each oxygen atom. This gives a σ bond. The other bond is formed by the side-to-side overlap of half-filled 2py orbitals on each oxygen atom. This gives a π bond. Thus a double bond is formed between two oxygen atoms. One is σ bond and the other is π bond. Formation of N2 molecule: In nitrogen molecule, N2 is formed by the combination of two N atoms. The electronic configuration of N atom is: 1s2 2s2 2px1 2py1 2pz1. Each N atom has three half-filled p orbitals. On the basis of VBT, three covalent bonds should be formed between two nitrogen atoms. When the two nitrogen atoms approach each other, the two 2pz orbitals undergo end-to-end overlap, giving a σ bond. The end-to-end overlap brings the two nitrogen atoms so close together that their parallel 2p orbitals can undergo side-to-side overlap to produce two pi bonds. Note that each π bond is in two parts surrounding a σ bond. There are five distinct regions of electron charge in nitrogen molecule: two electrons between the nuclei forming a σ bond, two electrons above and below the σ electrons forming a π bond, two electrons in front of and behind the σ electrons forming another π bond. Thus a triple bond is formed between two nitrogen atoms; one is σ bond while the other two are π bonds. Hybrid Atomic Orbitals The valency of an element generally corresponds to the number of unpaired electrons in the valence shell of an atom of that element. However this is not always true. For example, the valency of beryllium (Be) is two and carbon (C) has a valency of four, while both have no unpaired electrons in ground state. Boron (B) has a valency of three and carbon has a valency of four, while both have only one and two unpaired electrons respectively. Pauling resolved this discrepancy by introducing the concept of orbital hybridization. Hybridization involves mixing of the pure s and p (one or more) orbitals of an atom to give new equivalent orbitals, before the bonding process takes place. The number of hybridized orbitals is equal to the number of atomic orbitals overlapped.

A bonding process can then be visualized as a process of overlapping the hybrid atomic orbital of one atom with a pure atomic orbital of another. We know simple valence Bond theory does not explain the covalent bond formation in many elements. So modification in this theory was made in the form of hybridization concept. The process of mixing atomic orbitals of different energy and shape to form a set of new orbitals of the same energy and same shape is called hybridization and the orbitals so obtained are called hybrid orbitals. According to this concept atomic orbitals differing slightly in energy intermix to form new orbitals of equal energies and shape called hybrid orbitals which differ from the parent atomic orbitals in shape and energy and possess specific geometry. It also gives a satisfactory explanation for the valency of the elements. In this process, the electron belonging to ground state structure are promoted to the excited state as a result of which there is an increase in the number of unpaired electrons. The energy required for the excitation is compensated by the energy released during the process of bond formation with other atoms. Depending upon the nature of orbitals involved there are many types of hybridization. For example, sp3, sp2, sp hybridization. sp3 Hybridization: The process of mixing one s orbital and three p orbitals to form four new equivalent sp3 hybrid orbitals is called sp3 hybridization. Let us discuss the structure of methane, ammonia and water by understanding the sp3 hybridization of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen atoms. Structure of Methane: C (ground state) 1s2, 2s2 2px1 2py1 2pz0; C (excited state) 1s2, 2s1 2px1 2py1 2pz1; C (hybridized state) 1s2, (sp3)1 (sp3)1 (sp3)1 (sp3)1. In methane molecule, carbon is attached to four hydrogen atoms by the formation of four sp3-s sigma bonds. Carbon atom is at the centre of tetrahedral geometry with hydrogen atoms at the four corners. Remember that the angle between them is 109.5. Each bond is formed by the overlap of sp3 hybrid orbitals of carbon with 1s orbitals of hydrogen atoms separately to form four sigma bonds. The molecule possesses a tetrahedral geometry. The C-H bonds which result are directed towards the corners of a regular tetrahedron. Each H-C-H bond angle is 109.5. The tetrahedral structure of CH4 molecule has four faces and four corners. Structure of Ammonia, NH3: In NH3 molecule, the central atom is nitrogen. It contains five electrons in its valence shell. N (ground state)1s2 2s2 2px1 2py1 2pz1. N (hybridized state) 1s2 sp3 sp3 sp3 sp3. One s and three p orbitals of nitrogen atom hybridize to form four sp3 hybrid orbitals. They are directed towards the four corners of a tetrahedron. One of the hybrid orbitals is completely filled with one pair of electrons and the remaining three orbitals are half filled. The half filled sp3 hybridized orbitals of nitrogen overlap with three 1s-orbitals of three hydrogen atoms.

The three hydrogen atoms are located at three corners, whereas the lone pair of electrons at the fourth corner of the tetrahedron. This results in a pyramidal molecule. The three hydrogen atoms form the base and the lone pair of electrons the apex. The experimentally determined value of H-N-H bond angle in NH3 molecule is 107.5, which is less than the normal tetrahedral value of 109.5. The deviation from the tetrahedral angle is explained on the basis of repulsion between lone pair and bond pairs. The lone pair-bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair-bond pair repulsion. As a result, the bond pairs move away from the lone pair and are pushed closer together. Hence, the angle between bond pairs is reduced. Structure of Water, H2O: In H2O molecule, the central atom is oxygen. It contains six electrons in its valence shell. O (ground state)1s2 2s2 2px2 2py1 2pz1. O (hybridized state) 1s2 (sp3)2 (sp3)1 (sp3)1. One s and three p orbitals of oxygen atom intermix to give four sp3 hybrid orbitals which are directed towards the four corners of a regular tetrahedron. Two of these orbitals are completely filled and remaining two sp3 hybrid orbitals are partially filled. Thus the two partially filled sp3 hybrid orbitals overlap with two 1s orbitals of two hydrogen atoms to form two sigma bonds. Each bond is formed by sp3-s overlap. The two hydrogen atoms are located at two corners of tetrahedron, whereas the two lone pairs at the remaining two corners of the tetrahedron. The result is a V-shaped molecule. The experimentally determined value of H-O-H bond angle in H2O molecule is 104.5, which is lesser than the normal tetrahedral value. The deviation from the tetrahedral angle is explained on the basis of repulsion between lone pairs and bond pairs. The repulsion of lone pair-lone pair lone pair-bond pair bond pair-bond pair. As a result, the bond pairs move away from the lone pairs and come closer to each other. Hence the angle between bond pairs decreases up to 104.5. sp2 Hybridization: The mixing of one s and two p orbitals of the same atom to form three identical orbitals is called sp2-hybridization. The three sp2 hybrid orbitals are directed towards the three corners of an equilateral triangle. The bond angle between any two hybrid orbitals is 120. Each sp2 hybrid orbital has 33.3 s-character and 66.6 p-character. The sp2 hybrid orbitals can form only sigma bonds by overlapping with other atomic orbitals. Structure of Boron trifluoride, BF3: In BF3 molecule, the central atom is boron. It contains three electrons in its valence shell. The electronic configuration of valence shell of B-atom in the ground and excited states: B: 1s2 2s2 2px1 (ground state); 1s2 2s1 2px1 2py1 (excited state). One s and two 2p orbitals of boron atom intermix to give three sp2 hybridized orbitals. The three sp2 hybrid orbitals lie in the same plane and are directed towards the corners of an equilateral triangle with boron atom at the centre.

The bond angle between any two sp2 orbitals is 120. The three sp2 orbitals contain one electron each and are thus partially filled. The partially filled 2pz orbitals of three fluorine atoms overlap with each sp2 hybrid orbitals of boron atom to form three sp2-pz sigma bonds. As a result, BF3 molecule has triangular planar structure. Structure of Ethene, CH2 CH2: The electronic configuration of carbon atom is: C (ground state) 1s2, 2s2 2px1 2py1 2pz0; C (Excited state ) 1s2, 2s1 2px1 2py1 2pz1; C (hybrid state) 1s2, (sp2)1 (sp2)1 (sp2)1 2pz1. In CH2 CH2 molecule, one s and two p orbitals of each C-atom intermix to form three sp2 hybrid orbitals. The sp2 hybrid orbitals are triangular planar oriented at the angle of 120 to each other. Each carbon atom is left with one unhybridized p-orbital perpendicular to the plane of sp2 hybrid orbitals. One sp2 hybrid orbital of each C-atom overlaps linearly to form the C-C σ bond. Remaining two sp2 orbitals of each C-atom overlap with 1s atomic orbital of hydrogen atom to form two C-H single bonds. A π bond is formed by the sidewise overlap of two half-filled pz atomic orbitals in such a way that the probability of finding electrons is maximum above and below the line joining the nuclei. sp Hybridization: The mixing of one s and one p orbital of the same atom to form two identical orbitals is called sp-hybridization. The two sp-hybrid orbitals are directed at an angle of 180 to each other. Each sp hybrid orbital has 50 s-character and 50 p-character. The sp-hybrid orbitals can form only sigma bonds by overlapping with other atomic orbitals. Examples: BeCl2, C2H2. Structure of BeCl2 (Beryllium chloride): In BeCl2 molecule, the central atom is beryllium atom. Beryllium atom contains two electrons in its valence shell. The electronic configuration of valence shell of beryllium atom in ground state and excited state: Be: 1s2, 2s2, 2px0, 2py0, 2pz0 (ground state); 1s2, 2s1 2px1, 2py0, 2pz0 (excited state). One 2s and one 2p orbitals of beryllium atom intermix to form two sp hybrid orbitals. Each sp hybrid orbital contains one electron. The two sp hybrid orbital lie in a straight line with beryllium at the centre. One sp hybrid orbital overlaps linearly with p-orbital of one chlorine atom to form a sigma bond. Similarly, another sp hybrid orbital overlaps with p-orbital of second chlorine atom to form another sigma bond. Thus BeCl2 molecule has a linear shape. Structure of Ethyne, CHCH: Electronic configuration of carbon atom in the ground and excited states: C (ground state) 1s2, 2s2 2px1 2py1 2pz0; C (hybrid state) 1s2, (sp)1 (sp)1 2py1 2pz1. One 2s and one 2p orbitals of carbon atom intermix to give two sp hybrid orbitals. The 2py and 2pz orbitals remain unhybridized. Each sp hybrid orbital contains one electron. The two sp hybrid orbitals are directed along a straight line at an angle of 180 between them.

The two unhybridized p orbitals are perpendicular to each other and also perpendicular to the plane of the two sp hybrid orbitals. Thus each carbon atom possesses two sp hybrid orbitals and two pure p atomic orbitals. Each C-atom undergoes sp-s overlap with 1s orbital of H-atoms and sp-sp overlap with other carbon atom to form two σ-bonds. The two half-filled p orbitals of two carbon atoms overlap sideways to form two π-bonds. Thus ethyne molecule contains one σ-bond and two π-bonds between two carbon atoms and two carbon-hydrogen σ-bonds. The electronic clouds of two π-bonds merge into each other to form cylindrical shaped π-electron cloud. The molecule is linear in shape. Drawbacks of Valence Bond Theory It fails to explain: (a) The formation of coordinate covalent bond. (b) The formation of odd electron molecules or ions. (c) The paramagnetic behaviour of oxygen molecule. Molecular Orbital Theory The method of molecular orbital theory was developed in 1927-1928 by Hund and Mulliken and in 1929 by Lennard-Jones. It is assumed that linear combination of atomic orbitals form new orbitals called molecular orbitals which are characteristics of the whole molecule. The molecular orbitals extend over more nuclei of the bonded atoms. Two atomic orbitals after combining give two molecular orbitals which differ in energy. One of them, having lower energy is called bonding molecular orbital (BMO) while the other having high energy is called anti-bonding molecular orbital (ABMO). The bonding molecular orbital is formed by the linear combination (addition) of atomic orbitals while the anti-bonding molecular orbital is formed by the subtractive combination of atomic orbitals. Electrons occupy molecular orbitals according to Aufbau principle and Hund's rule. The electrons from each atom fill the bonding molecular orbital or π orbital while the anti-bonding σ orbital or π orbital may have zero, one or two electrons. The following diagram illustrates the formation of the molecular orbitals (lower energy and higher energy) and also the order of filling of electrons according to rules mentioned above. In this type of diagram, the combining atomic orbitals are shown on two extremes and the resulting molecular orbitals (MO) are represented in the middle column. Atomic orbitals of same energy are shown at the same level. The difference between the energies of atomic orbitals and the bonding MOs depend upon the extent of overlap of atomic orbitals. A large overlap results in greater lowering of the energy of bonding MO (and a corresponding large rise in energy in the anti-bonding MO). Larger the overlap, stronger will be the resulting bond. According to the above diagram, the sequence of energy levels in which electrons are filled up is: σ1s σ1s σ2s σ2s σ2pz π2py π2pz π2py π2pz σ2pz. There are two types of overlapping in molecular orbital theory: Head on approach (linear overlapping) or linear combination and Sideways approach (parallel overlapping). Head on approach can take place between s-s, s-p and p-p atomic orbitals. When two s atomic orbitals overlap, they form two molecular orbitals.

Molecular orbital which has low energy than an atomic orbital is called σ orbital. Molecular orbital which has high energy than an atomic orbital is called σ orbital as shown in the figure. Sideways approach or parallel overlapping: When axes of two p orbitals (i.e py or pz orbitals) are parallel to each other, they overlap sidewise. This results in formation of two molecular orbitals. The bonding molecular orbital π(2py) or π(2pz) has zero electron density on the nuclei. The electron density is uniformly distributed above and below the molecular axis. On the other hand, π(2py) or π(2pz) anti-bonding molecular orbital has node region. Since the 2py and 2pz atomic orbitals are of equal energy, the molecular orbitals arising from them are also of equal energy i.e., degenerate orbitals. Bond Order Bond order between two atoms after the atomic orbitals overlap is taken as half of the difference between the number of bonding and anti-bonding electrons. Bond order (No. of electrons in BMOs - No. of electrons in ABMOs)/2. For example, bond order formed in hydrogen molecule may be calculated as follows. Number of electrons in the bonding orbitals 2. Number of electrons in the anti-bonding orbitals 0. Bond order (2-0)/2 1. It is a common practice that only MOs formed from valence orbital are considered in bond order calculations. It should be noted that a bond between two atoms can be formed only when the number of electrons in the bonding orbital must be greater than the number of electrons in the anti-bonding molecular orbitals. Relative Energies of the Molecular Orbitals The relative energies of the molecular orbitals formed from 2s and 2p atomic orbitals are generally obtained by spectroscopic measurements. The molecular orbitals of diatomic molecules such as O2, F2 and their positive and negative ions can be shown in the following increasing order of energy: σ1s σ1s σ2s σ2s σ2px π2py π2pz π2py π2pz σ2px. Diatomic molecule such as H2, He2, B2, C2, and N2 (lighter molecules) show slightly different energy order: σ1s σ1s σ2s σ2s π2py π2pz σ2px π2py π2pz σ2px. As seen in the energy order of lighter molecules like B2, C2, N2, σ2px is higher in energy than π2py π2pz group orbitals. This reversal is due to mixing of 2s and 2px atomic orbitals. When the energy difference of 2s and 2p atomic orbitals is small; there is a possibility of mixing of s and p orbitals (hybridization of A.O.). As a result σ2s and σ2s MO do not retain pure s-character and σ2px and σ2px MOs do not have pure p-character. All the four MOs acquire mixed s and p character. Consequently, their energies change in such a way that MOs σ2s and σ2s are lowered in energy while MOs σ2px and σ2px become less stable. The energies of π2py π2pz and π2py π2pz remains unchanged. σ2px is raised to such a level that it becomes higher than π2py and π2pz.

In O2 and F2 there is 2600 kJ/mol energy difference of their 2s and 2p orbitals which is too high to allow mixing, so their energy order is normal. Energy level diagrams, Electronic structures and Bonding properties of some Homonuclear diatomic molecules. Hydrogen molecule H2: The hydrogen molecule is formed from the overlap of 1s atomic orbitals of two hydrogen atoms. The two electrons occupy the lower energy σ1s orbital as shown in the diagram. The electronic configuration of the molecule is represented by the equation: 2H (1s1) H2 (σ1s)2. Bond order (2-0)/2 1. Thus the two hydrogen atoms are bonded through a single bond in the molecule. We conclude that the H2 molecule is stable. It has bond dissociation energy of 436 kJ/mol and is diamagnetic in nature i.e., atoms, ions or molecules in which electrons are all paired in their molecular electronic configuration are diamagnetic. They are repelled by both poles of magnet. Helium Molecule He2: He: 1s2. The energy level diagram for He2 is similar to that of H2 except that it has two more electrons which occupy the anti-bonding σ1s orbital shown in the diagram. 2He (1s2) He2 (σ1s)2 (σ1s)2. Bond order (2-2)/2 0. Thus its bond order is zero and we conclude that the molecule is not stable. In fact, He2 is not known, helium exists as mono-atomic molecules. Lithium Molecule Li2: Li: 1s2 2s1. The electronic configuration for Li2 has a total of six electrons. Two in σ1s, two in σ1s and two in σ2s molecular orbitals. In spectroscopic notation this can be represented as Li2 KK (σ2s)2. There are two more electrons in the anti-bonding orbitals and the bond order is one. We conclude that the molecule is stable. Indeed it is known to exist in the vapour phase and is diamagnetic. Beryllium Molecule Be2: Be: 1s2 2s2. The energy level diagram for Be2 is similar to that of Li2 except that it has two more electrons which occupy the anti-bonding σ2s orbital. Bond order (2-2)/2 0. The electronic configuration is Be2 KK (σ2s)2 (σ2s)2. Be2 is very unstable. Boron Molecule B2: B: 1s2 2s2 2p1. Boron atom has the configuration of 1s2, 2s2, 2p1. Boron is the first element with five electrons to be considered for bonding. Spectroscopic study has suggested that for B2, C2 and N2 molecules π2p orbitals are lower in energy than σ2p orbital. Thus the electronic configuration of B2 is: 2B (1s2 2s2 2p1) B2KK(σ2s)2(σ2s)2 (π2py)1 (π2pz)1. Bond order (4-2)/21. Thus the two B-atoms are bonded through only one bond in the molecule. The experiments verify not only that the molecule exists in vapour phase but that it is paramagnetic (atoms, ions or molecules) with two unpaired electrons. The bond energy is 270 kJ/mol. Paramagnetic species which have one or more unpaired electrons in their molecular electronic configuration are paramagnetic. They are attracted to magnetic field. Nitrogen Molecule N2: N: 1s2 2s2 2px1 2py1 2pz1.

In the electronic configuration, only 2s and three 2p orbitals from each N atom are to be considered in the bond formation. The electronic configuration of N2 molecule is: N2 KK (σ2s)2(σ2s)2(π2py)2(π2pz)2(σ2px)2. Bond order (8-2)/2 3. Thus the two N-atoms are bonded through a triple bond. N2 is a very stable molecule and has a very high bond energy i.e., 945 kJ/mol and is diamagnetic in nature. This is consistent with MOT. It is diamagnetic due to no unpaired electron. It has a very short bond length. Oxygen Molecule O2: O: 1s2 2s2 2px2 2py1 2pz1. Lewis theory predicts that O2 would be diamagnetic. However experimental evidence indicates oxygen as being paramagnetic having two unpaired electrons. A structure consistent with this fact is given by MOT. Spectroscopic evidence indicates that for O2, the σ2p orbital lies lower in energy than π2p orbitals. The electronic configuration of O2 molecule is: O2 KK (σ2s)2(σ2s)2(σ2px)2(π2py)2(π2pz)2(π2py)1(π2pz)1. Bond order (8-4)/2 2. It suggests that the two oxygen atoms are bonded through a double bond. The two unpaired electrons in the degenerate anti-bonding orbitals make O2 paramagnetic, hence it is paramagnetic in nature. So we conclude that the molecule should be very stable as it has high bond energy i.e. 498 kJ/mol with bond length 1.21 Å. Fluorine Molecule F2: F: 1s2 2s2 2p5. Each fluorine atom has the 1s2 2s2 2p5 configuration. The corresponding electronic configuration of F2 molecule is: F2 KK(σ2s)2(σ2s)2(σ2px)2(π2py)2(π2pz)2(π2py)2(π2pz)2. Bond order (8-6)/2 1. It predicts that two F-atoms are bonded through a single bond. The F-F bond distance is longer (1.43 Å) than that for O2 (1.21 Å) and N2 (1.09 Å). The bond energy of F2 molecule is quite low and it is diamagnetic in nature. Comparison of Valence Bond and Molecular Orbital Theories The similarities of the two theories are: Both explain the formation of covalent bond. According to both theories, a covalent bond is formed by the overlapping of atomic orbitals along the molecular axis. In both theories, the electron charge resides in the region between the two nuclei. The differences of the two theories are: According to valence bond theory, only half-filled atomic orbitals of interacting atoms are involved in bond formation. In valence bond theory, the concerned atomic orbitals retain their individual identity. It fails to explain the paramagnetic behaviour of molecules like O2 molecule i.e., electrical properties. It does not give idea about the bond order. According to molecular orbital theory, all the atomic orbitals of interacting atoms are involved in bond formation. In MOT, the two atomic orbitals lose their individual identity. It explains the paramagnetic behaviour of molecules like O2 molecule i.e., electrical properties. It gives idea about bond order by which we can determine that whether the bond is single, double or triple. It explains the non-existence of He2 molecule.

BOND ENERGY (BOND ENTHALPY) When a bond is formed between two atoms, energy is released (exothermic process), the same amount of energy is absorbed (endothermic process) when the bond is broken to form neutral atoms. So the bond energy is the amount of energy required to break all bonds of a particular type in one mole of the substance. The strength of a bond is measured by its bond energy. The higher the bond energy, the stronger is the bond. It is determined experimentally by measuring the heat involved in a chemical reaction. It is also called bond enthalpy, as it is measure of enthalpy change at 298K. The enthalpy change in splitting a substance into its component atoms is called enthalpy of atomization. It is expressed in kilojoules per mole (kJmol1). It is the energy required to break up an Avogadros number (6.02x1023) of bonds i.e., one mole of bond. It is found that energies of multiple bonds are greater than those of single bonds. But a double bond is not twice as strong as a single bond and a triple bond is not thrice as strong as a single bond. It means that a σ bond is stronger than a π bond. Also, a polar covalent bond is stronger than a non-polar covalent bond. Bond energy of H-H in H2 molecule at 25C (298K) is 436 kJ/mole. The bond energy of Cl-Cl bond in Cl2 molecule at 25C is 242 kJ/mole. Bond energy of H-Cl bond in HCl molecule at 25C is 431 kJ/mole. Bond energy is a measure of bond strength. Higher the bond energy, the stronger is the bond. It depends upon the following factors: The greater the difference of electronegativity between the bonded atoms, the greater is the bond energy and stronger is the bond. For example, in H-F, the electronegativity difference is 1.9 and bond energy is 567 kJ/mol. In H-Cl, the electronegativity difference is 0.9 and bond energy is 431 kJ/mol. In H-Br, the electronegativity difference is 0.7 and bond energy is 366 kJ/mol. In H-I, the electronegativity difference is 0.4 and bond energy is 299 kJ/mol. From the above data it is observed that HF molecule has higher bond energy (567 kJmol-1) due to greater electronegativity difference i.e., 1.9. The smaller the size of the bonded atoms, the greater is the bond energy and stronger is the bond. The bond energy of H-H bond is 436 kJmol-1 and that Cl-Cl is 242 kJmol-1. This is due to the shorter bond length in H2 molecule and greater bond length in Cl2 molecule (larger size of Cl atom than H atom). Multiple bonds also affect the bond energy, greater the no. of bonds greater will be the bond energy. Table: Average Bond energies (kJmol-1) of single bonds.

Bond Theoretical Experimental H-F 338.9 567 H-Cl 338.9 431 H-Br 338.9 366 H-I 338.9 299 BOND LENGTH It may be defined as the distance between the nuclei of atoms joined by a covalent bond.

This distance between the bonded atoms is not constant, because the bonded atoms are always vibrating with respect to each other. Therefore, average of minimum and maximum distance is considered as bond length or bond distance. Thus bond length may also be defined as the internuclear distance when the maximum possible overlap of concerned atomic orbitals occurs. It is measured by techniques such as X-ray diffraction, neutron diffraction and microwave spectroscopy. Measuring units: It is measured in Å or picometer: 1 pm 10-12 m, 100 pm 1 Å 10-10 m. It is observed that its measurements may vary in accuracy but similar bonds have fairly constant lengths in different molecules, variation generally being less than 1. In most of the compounds, the C-C single bond length is very close to 1.54 Å. For example in ethane molecule the C-C bond length is 1.54 Å and in ethyl chloride (C2H5Cl) the C-C bond length is 1.55 Å. One half of the bond length between nuclei of two similar atoms joined by single covalent bond is called the covalent radius of that atom. For example, the covalent radius of Carbon is 0.77 Å i.e., half of the C-C bond length which is 1.54 Å. For example, C-Cl bond length in CH3Cl is 1.76 Å, which is exactly the sum of the covalent radius of carbon (0.77 Å) and chlorine (0.99 Å). However, in most cases, the length of a covalent bond between two unlike atoms is markedly shorter than the sum of the two covalent radii. DIPOLE MOMENT (MEASURE OF POLARITY OF MOLECULES) The polarity of a molecule can be expressed in terms of dipole moment. It is a product of the charge (positive or negative) and the distance between the charges. If q is the magnitude of charge at each end of dipole and r is the distance between them, then dipole moment represented as μ is given by μ q x r. The SI unit of dipole moment is Coulomb-meter (C.m) but most common units used is Debye (D). 1 D 3.336 x 10-30 C.m. A symmetrical molecule like CO2 has zero dipole moment, so it is non polar. But chloroform (CHCl3) has a dipole moment of 1.2 D, so it is polar. The measurement of dipole moment also finds applications in stereochemistry. For example dipole moments of isomer 1,2-dichloroethene have been calculated are given below: Trans 0 D; Cis 1.89 D. By knowing the dipole moment of the given sample of 1,2-dichloroethene, one can predict whether it is Cis or trans isomer. The dipole moment helps to calculate the percentage ionic character in a bond. For example, observed dipole moment of HF is 1.90 D. Find the percentage ionic character in HF bond. The distance between the charges is 0.917 x 10-10 m. Unit positive charge 1.6022 x 10-19 C. Suppose that HF molecule is 100 ionic. It means that H has full positive charge and F has full negative charge. To calculate their dipole moments multiply the bond length with the charges of electron or proton i.e., 1.6022 x 10-19. This dipole moment is called theoretical dipole moment. μ theoretical (1.6022 x 10-19 C) (0.917 x 10-10 m) 1.469 x 10-29 C.m. Since 1 D 3.336 x 10-30 C.m. So μ theoretical (1.469 x 10-29 C.m) / (3.336 x 10-30 C.m/D) 4.4 D. Actual dipole moment as it is observed, μ actual 1.90 D. ionic character (1.90 D / 4.4 D) x 100 43.2. Thus H-F bond is 43 ionic and 57 covalent. The bond is predominantly covalent, because the ionic character is less than 50.

EFFECT OF BONDING ON THE PROPERTIES OF COMPOUNDS Solubility of Ionic Compounds: Ionic compounds are soluble in water but insoluble in non-aqueous solvents. When a crystal of ionic compound is placed in water, the polar water molecules surround each cation and anion from the crystal lattice by their electrostatic attraction. The ions are detached from the crystal lattice by hydration. This happens when the hydration energy is equal to or greater than lattice energy. The energy released in hydration is used to overcome the repulsion between the ions are freed from their positions in the crystal. Ionic compounds do not dissolve in water because the attraction of water molecules is not enough to overcome the attraction between the ions. Their lattice energy dominates over hydration energy. For the same reasons, the non-polar solvents benzene and carbon tetrachloride cannot dissolve in ionic compounds. Solubility of Covalent Compounds: Covalent compounds dissolve in non-polar organic solvents such as benzene, ether, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. Covalent compounds are insoluble in water. However, some of them dissolve in water. The attractive forces of solvent molecules in non-polar solvents are enough for separating the intermolecular forces of attraction in covalent compounds. Hence covalent compounds dissolve easily in non-polar organic solvents. Solubility of covalent compounds in water depends on their ability to form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Many organic compounds containing oxygen or nitrogen like carboxylic acids, alcohols and amines are soluble in water due to hydrogen bonding. Directional nature of Ionic Bonds: Ionic bonds are non-directional and rigid in nature. They do not show the phenomenon of isomerism. Directional Nature of Covalent Bonds: Covalent bonds are of directional nature. They show the phenomenon of isomerism. Due to non-rigid and directional nature of the covalent bond, covalent compounds have different arrangements of atoms in space. Hence many covalent compounds show the phenomenon of isomerism. For example C2H6O show structural isomerism: CH3-O-CH3 (Dimethyl Ether) and CH3-CH2-OH (Ethyl alcohol). Electrical Conductivity: Ionic compounds conduct electricity in the form of ions in an aqueous solution. The ionic compounds have already separated ions which act as carriers of charge, so the reaction is so rapid because no bond formation or bond breaking is involved. Electrical Conductivity of Covalent Compounds: Covalent compounds do not conduct electricity because they do not have free ions in solution. They are neutral molecules. The bonds are generally much slower to react as they involve both bond breaking and bond making. The molecules undergo a chemical change as a whole. It is necessary to break the covalent bonds. Covalent compounds react in a variety of ways. The reactivity of covalent compounds depends upon the way a reaction proceeds and the product obtained at the end of a reaction. Density: The strong electrostatic force of attraction existing between the cations and anions in an ionic compound packs these ions very close to one another. This decreases the volume of the crystal and consequently the ionic crystals have high density.

Types of Solids: A Solid is a structural unit of atoms, molecules or ions, which are held together strongly enough to give a rigid structure. Four types of solids exist namely Molecular solids: Consists of atoms or molecules held together by inter-molecular forces. Solid water (ice) and solid CO2 (dry ice) are common examples. Metallic Solids: Consists of atoms held together by metallic bonding, examples silver, copper and gold. Ionic Solids: Consists of cations and anions held together by virtue of electrostatic attraction of the opposite charges. Examples are NaCl and CaCl2. Covalent Network Solids: Consists of atoms held together in large network or chains by covalent bonds. Diamond, graphite are typical examples. Difference between Covalent Network Solids and Molecular Network Solids (Metallic Solids) In Metallic Solids: Metallic solids consist of infinite arrays of bonded atoms; each cation in a metal has a coordination number sometimes four or six, but more often eight or twelve they are good conductor of heat and electricity. In Covalent Network Solids: Consist of infinite arrays of bonded atoms; no individual molecules can be distinguished (each piece of network solid may be considered a giant, covalently bonded molecule). They are non conductor of heat and electricity. Strong covalent bonds throughout these solids, give them great strength and high melting points.

INTRODUCTION Every process in this universe whether it occurs in living cells, or in test tubes, or in the atmosphere or in water etc. is accompanied by an energy change. Some processes release energy, other require energy. However, in all these cases total amount of energy in the universe remains constant. The branch of thermodynamics that examines the heat involved in chemical reactions is called thermochemistry. In this chapter we will discuss the principles that govern energy changes. We will examine the role of energy in chemical reactions. We will also discuss how heat of a chemical reaction is measured in order to focus on the central topic of the chapter i.e., the amount of heat released or absorbed in a reaction. The study of all types of energy changes associated with physical and chemical changes is known as thermodynamics. ENERGY IN CHEMICAL REACTIONS The energy in the form of heat is either evolved or absorbed as a result of chemical reaction. This is because, in a chemical reaction old bonds are broken and new bonds are formed. Bond breaking always consumes energy and bond making always releases energy. When the energy released by bond formation is greater than the energy consumed by bond breaking, there is a net release of chemical energy. Whereas energy is absorbed, when the energy consumed by bond breaking is greater than the energy released by bond formation. Thus in chemical reactions energy is exchanged with the surroundings. UNITS OF THERMAL ENERGY Unit of heat or thermal energy used in SI system is the Joule (J). It is defined as the energy required to move an object or a particle through a distance of one meter by a force of one Newton. Another common unit of heat is the calorie. It is defined as the heat or thermal energy required to raise the temperature of one gram of water from 14.5C to 15.5C. 1 Calorie 4.18 Joules SYSTEM, SURROUNDINGS AND BOUNDARY The part of the universe on which we wish to focus our attention is called a system. The remaining part of the universe is called surroundings. The real or imaginary surface separating the system from its surroundings is called the boundary. A system in chemistry is usually the substance undergoing physical or chemical change.

For example, in the study of reaction between limestone and hydrochloric acid solution in a test tube, limestone and hydrochloric acid solution form a system. The test tube and everything around the test tube is surroundings. Similarly in the study of thermal decomposition of a compound, the sample of the compound would be the system, whereas the beaker, the source of heat and everything else would be surroundings. THERMOCHEMICAL REACTIONS When a chemical change takes place, energy is exchanged between system and its surroundings. Energy has many forms such as heat, light, work etc. A chemical reaction which proceeds with the evolution or absorption of heat is called a thermochemical reaction. A balanced chemical equation which also shows heat change of a chemical reaction is called thermochemical equation. The branch of chemistry which deals with the heat or thermal energy changes in chemical reactions is called thermochemistry. For example C(s) O2(g) CO2(g) ΔH 393.5kJ There are two types of thermochemical reactions: EXOTHERMIC REACTIONS A chemical reaction that proceeds with the evolution of heat is called an exothermic reaction. In an exothermic reaction the chemical system transfers energy to the surroundings as the reactants are converted to products e.g. burning of fuels is a highly exothermic reaction. The energy released can be used to heat a room, or to drive an engine or to cook food. Examples of exothermic reactions are given below: (i) C(s) O2(g) CO2(g) ΔH 393.5kJ (ii) 2H2(g) O2(g) 2H2O(l) ΔH 571.6kJ ENDOTHERMIC REACTIONS A chemical reaction that proceeds with the absorption of heat is called an endothermic reaction. In these reactions heat is transferred from surrounding to the system. Examples of endothermic reactions are given below: (i) H2(g) I2(g) 2HI(g) ΔH 53.8kJ (ii) C(s) H2O(g) CO(g) H2(g) ΔH 134.4kJ (iii) 2NO2(g) N2O4(g) ΔH 58.0kJ (iv) 2NO(g) O2(g) 2NO2(g) ΔH 114.0kJ (v) N2(g) O2(g) 2NO(g) ΔH 180.5kJ Self Check Exercise 11.1 Classify the following processes as exothermic or endothermic. (a) Freezing of water (b) Combustion of methane (c) Sublimation of dry ice (d) H2O(g) H2O(l) (e) decomposition of limestone. HEAT OF REACTION The amount of energy released or absorbed depends on the amount of substances that react. For example, as more fuel burns, more energy is released. Thus when we report an energy change we must also report the amounts of the chemical substances that generate the energy change. For this purpose energy changes are expressed in terms of molar quantities of reactants and products. The amount of heat evolved or absorbed in a chemical reaction, when molar quantities of reactants and product are same as shown in a chemical reaction is called heat of reaction.

Heat of reaction measured at 25C (or 298K) and one atmospheric pressure is known as standard enthalpy change denoted by ΔH (for detail see section 11.5.1) (i) C(s) O2(g) CO2(g) ΔH -393.5kJ This equation shows that 1 mole of solid carbon (12g) reacts with 1 mole of oxygen gas (32g) to give 1 mole of CO2 gas (44g) at 25C and 1 atmospheric pressure and 393.5 KJ heat is evolved. What does the following equation show? (ii) H2(g) I2(g) 2HI(g) ΔH 53.8kJ If a reaction is exothermic when going in one direction, it will be endothermic in the reverse direction. When a reaction is reversed, the magnitude of ΔH remains the same but its sign changes. Thus above two thermochemical reactions in the reverse direction would be represented as follows: CO2(g) C(s) O2(g) ΔH 393.5kJ 2HI(g) H2(g) I2(g) ΔH -53.8kJ THERMODYNAMICS The study of all types of energy changes associated with chemical and physical changes is known as thermodynamics. STATE FUNCTION A complete description of a system, which includes its quantity, temperature, pressure and volume describe the state of the system. There are three types of systems, open system, closed system and isolated system. In an open system reactants and energy may be exchanged with its surroundings. In a closed system only energy may be exchanged with surroundings but not material. Whereas in an isolated system no energy and no material may be exchanged with its surroundings. In fact there is no ideally isolated system. It is hypothetical system used for a comparison. The condition of a system when various properties like temperature, pressure, volume, number of moles etc. of system have definite values is called state of the system. The initial state of a system is its state before it undergoes a change. Whereas the final state is its state after the change has occurred. In a chemical reaction, the description of the products defines the final state. Variables such as pressure, temperature, volume and energy depend only on the state of the system. A change in any of these variables depends only on the difference between initial and final conditions, but does not depend on the path followed. Such variables are called state functions or state variables. The properties that are determined by the state of the system regardless of how that condition was achieved are called state functions. Change in any property of a system is determined by the difference in the value of that property in the final state and the value of the same property in the initial state. For example Let V1 is the initial volume of H2 gas confined in a cylinder at temperature T1, and pressure P1. When temperature is increased from T1 to T2, its volume becomes V2 and pressure changes to P2. The change in volume (ΔV) is given by the following equation. ΔV V2 V1 Similarly change in temperature ΔT and change in pressure ΔP are given by the equations.

ΔT T2 T1 ΔP P2 P1 Spontaneous and non-spontaneous reactions: The reactions which proceed on their own and do not need any external energy to proceed are called spontaneous reactions. For example emission of rays from radioactive elements, burning of methane and coal. On the other hand the reactions which require external energy to proceed are called non-spontaneous reactions. For example reaction of nitrogen and oxygen to form nitric oxide, thermal decomposition of PbO2 etc. INTERNAL ENERGY In every chemical process energy is transformed from one form to another. The amount of energy transformed depends upon the energy contents of reactants and products. Every system has definite amount of energy present in it. This energy is due to kinetic as well as potential energies of the particles present in the system. The kinetic energy of the particles is due to the translational, rotational and vibrational motions of particles. The average distance between the nucleus and the outermost orbit of an atom/ion is called atomic/ionic radius. Trends. The number of shells in all the elements of a given period remains the same, but the effective nuclear charge increases from left to right. Ionization energy is the minimum amount of energy required to remove one mole of the most loosely held electrons from one mole of isolated gaseous atoms to produce one mole of unipositive gaseous ion. That is why ionization energy of Mg is higher than that of Al. Electron affinity generally increases with increase in the effective nuclear charge across a period and decreases with increase in atomic number down a group as atomic size increases due to shielding effect. Anomalous Trend. Halogens have high electron affinities which decreases from Chlorine to Iodine. Chlorine in this group has the highest electron affinity (-349 kJ mol¹). The lower value of electron affinity for fluorine (-328 kJ mol¹) is due to its small size and inter electronic repulsion between electron added and electrons already present (i.e. compact 2p orbital of F atom). 4. Electronegativity. Electronegativity is a measure of the tendency of an atom to attract a shared pair of electrons towards itself. Electronegativity has no units. The most commonly used scale for its measurement is the Pauling scale. According to this scale, fluorine (the most electronegative element) is assigned a value of 4.0, and values range down to Caesium and Francium which are the least electronegative elements. Trends. (i) On moving from left to right in a period, there is a decrease in the size of the atoms. Smaller atoms have greater tendency to attract the electrons towards themselves i.e. smaller atoms have higher electronegativity values. (ii) In going down a group, there is an increase in the size of atom, so electronegativity decreases. (b) Physical Properties. We will discuss electrical conductivity, melting point and boiling point in this section. 1. Electrical Conductivity. Electrical conductivity is the ability of a substance to conduct the electric current due to the presence of charged particles (free electrons, ions). Trends. Electrical conductivity of elements of period 3 increases as we move from sodium to aluminium and then decreases at the end of the period. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are all good conductors of electricity. Conductivity increases as we move from sodium to aluminium due to increase in number of delocalized electrons. These delocalised electrons are free to move throughout the solid or the liquid metal. Silicon is a semiconductor. The remaining elements (P, S, Cl₂, Ar) do not conduct electricity because they form simple molecular structure having no free electrons. 2. Melting and Boiling Points. The melting and boiling points tell us about the strength of forces present among atoms, ions and molecules within a substance. In the case of elements, the values of melting and boiling points are according to the bonding forces present in them. Trend.

As we move from left to the right in a period, the melting and boiling points increase up to the middle i.e. group IV-A and then decrease from group V-A to noble gases (zero group elements.) Reasons. (1) The melting and boiling points are high up to the middle because these elements contain increasing number of binding electrons from I to III while silicon has giant covalent structure. (2) The melting and boiling points are low from P to Ar because these elements exist in the form of simple molecules and have weak intermolecular forces up to Argon. Quick Quiz. 1. Explain the trend of melting and boiling points of the elements of period-3. 13.1.2 Chemical Reactions of the Period 3 Elements. (a) Reactions with Water. Sodium. Sodium has a highly exothermic reaction with cold water producing hydrogen and a colourless solution of sodium hydroxide. 2Na 2H₂O 2NaOH H₂ (exothermic). Magnesium. Magnesium has a very slight reaction with cold water to form magnesium hydroxide and hydrogen but burns in steam with its typical white flame forming magnesium oxide and hydrogen. Mg 2H₂O (cold) Mg(OH)₂ H₂. Mg H₂O (steam) MgO H₂. Aluminium. Aluminium powder heated in steam produces aluminium oxide and hydrogen gas. The reaction is relatively slow because of the protective layer of aluminium oxide on its surface, and the build-up of even more oxide during the reaction. 2Al 3H₂O (steam) Al₂O₃ 3H₂. Silicon, Phosphorus and Sulphur. They have no reaction with water. Chlorine. Chlorine dissolves in water to some extent to give a green solution. A reversible reaction takes place to produce a mixture of hydrochloric acid and chloric (I) acid (hypochlorous acid). Cl₂ H₂O HCl HOCl. In the presence of sunlight, the chloric (I) acid slowly decomposes to produce more hydrochloric acid. 2Cl₂ 2H₂O (sunlight) 4HCl O₂. Argon. There is no reaction between argon and water. (b) Reactions with Oxygen. Sodium. Sodium burns in oxygen with yellow flame to produce a white solid mixture of sodium oxide and sodium peroxide. 4Na O₂ 2Na₂O (sodium oxide). 2Na O₂ Na₂O₂ (sodium peroxide). Magnesium. Magnesium burns in oxygen with an intense white flame to give white solid magnesium oxide. 2Mg O₂ 2MgO. Aluminium. Aluminium combines with oxygen on heating to produce a thin protective layer of aluminium oxide which protects the metal from further corrosion. 4Al 3O₂ 2Al₂O₃. Silicon. Silicon will burn in oxygen if heated strongly. Silicon dioxide is produced. Si O₂ SiO₂. Phosphorus. White phosphorus catches fire spontaneously in air, burning with a white flame and producing clouds of white smoke (mixture of phosphorus (III) oxide and phosphorus (V) oxide). The proportions of these oxides depend on the amount of oxygen available. In an excess of oxygen, the product will be almost entirely phosphorus (V) oxide. For the phosphorus (III) oxide: P₄ 3O₂ P₄O₆. For the phosphorus (V) oxide: P₄ 5O₂ P₄O₁₀. Sulphur.

Sulphur burns in air or oxygen with a pale blue flame. It produces colourless sulphur dioxide gas. S O₂ SO₂. Chlorine and Argon. Despite having several oxides, chlorine would not react directly with oxygen. Argon does not react either. (c) Reactions with Chlorine. Sodium. Sodium burns in chlorine with a bright orange flame. White solid of sodium chloride is produced. 2Na Cl₂ 2NaCl. Magnesium. Magnesium burns with its usual intense white flame to give white magnesium chloride. Mg Cl₂ MgCl₂. Aluminium. Aluminium is often reacted with chlorine by passing dry chlorine over aluminium foil heated in a long tube to produce very pale-yellow aluminium chloride. 2Al 3Cl₂ 2AlCl₃. Silicon. When chlorine is passed over silicon powder heated in a tube, it reacts to produce colourless silicon tetrachloride. Si 2Cl₂ SiCl₄. Phosphorus. White phosphorus burns in chlorine to produce a mixture of two chlorides, phosphorus (III) chloride (PCl₃) and phosphorus (V) chloride (PCl₅). Phosphorus (III) chloride is a colourless fuming liquid. P₄ 6Cl₂ 4PCl₃. Phosphorus(V) chloride is an off-white (going towards yellow) solid. P₄ 10Cl₂ 4PCl₅. Sulphur. When a stream of chlorine is passed over some heated sulphur, it reacts to form an orange evil-smelling liquid, disulphur dichloride, S₂Cl₂. 2S Cl₂ S₂Cl₂. Chlorine and Argon. It obviously does not make sense to talk about chlorine reacting with itself, and argon does not react with chlorine. 13.1.3 Physical Properties of the Oxides. The Oxides. The oxides we shall be looking at are: Na₂O, MgO, Al₂O₃, SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇. The oxides in the top row are known as the highest oxides of period-3 elements. These are the oxides where the Period 3 elements are in their highest oxidation states. In these oxides, all the outer electrons in the Period 3 elements are being involved in the bond formation just as one with sodium, to all seven of chlorine's outer electrons. I. Structures. The trend in structure is from the metallic oxides containing giant structures of ions on the left of the period via a giant covalent oxide (silicon dioxide) in the middle to molecular oxides on the right. II. Melting and Boiling Points. The giant structures (the metal oxides and silicon dioxide) will have high melting and boiling points because a lot of energy is needed to break the strong bonds (ionic or covalent) operating in three dimensions. The oxides of phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine consist of individual molecules. The attractive forces between these molecules will be Vander Waals dispersion and dipole-dipole interactions. These vary depending on the size, shape and polarity of the various molecules - but will always be much weaker than the ionic or covalent bonds. These oxides are either gases, liquids or low melting point solids. III. Electrical Conductivity. The ionic oxides of Na, Mg and Al are good conductors in solution form or molten state. These ionic solids are bad conductors in solid state. The oxides of silicon, phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine are non-ionizable, hence are non-conductors. 13.1.4. Acid-Base Behaviour of the Oxides. I.

Trend in Acid-Base Behaviour. In period-3, the trend is from strongly basic oxides on the left-hand side to strongly acidic ones on the right, via an amphoteric oxide (aluminium oxide) in the middle. An amphoteric oxide is one which shows both acidic and basic properties (see table 13.3). II. Reactions of Oxides with Water, Acids and Bases. (a) Sodium oxide (Na₂O). Sodium oxide is a simple strongly basic oxide. It is basic because it contains the oxide ion, O², which is a very strong base with a high tendency to combine with hydrogen ions. O² H₂O 2OH. Reaction with Water. Sodium oxide reacts exothermically with cold water to produce sodium hydroxide solution. Depending on its concentration, this will have a pH around 14. Na₂O H₂O 2NaOH. Reaction with Acids. As a strong base, sodium oxide also reacts with acids. For example, it would react with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce sodium chloride solution. Na₂O 2HCl 2NaCl H₂O. (b) Magnesium oxide (MgO). Magnesium oxide is again a simple basic oxide, because it also contains oxide ions. However, it is not as strongly basic as sodium oxide because the oxide ions are not so free. In the sodium oxide case, the solid is held together by attractions between Na and O² ions. In the magnesium oxide case, the attractions are between Mg² and O². It takes more energy to break the crystal lattice of MgO having smaller ions. Thus, lattice energy of MgO is greater than Na₂O. Reaction with Water. When we shake some white magnesium oxide powder with water, some magnesium hydroxide is formed in the reaction, but this is almost insoluble and so not many hydroxide ions actually get into solution. The pH of an aqueous solution of magnesium oxide is around 9 showing that it is slightly alkaline. MgO H₂O Mg(OH)₂. Reaction with Acids. It reacts with warm dilute hydrochloric acid to give magnesium chloride solution. MgO 2HCl MgCl₂ H₂O. (c) Aluminium oxide (Al₂O₃). As it is an amphoteric oxide, it has reactions as both a base and an acid. Aluminium oxide is an ionic oxide which allows it to act as a base. The ions in it have high charge density and hence it has a partial covalent character allowing it to act as an acidic oxide as well. Reaction with Water. Aluminium oxide does not react with water and does not dissolve in it because ions are held too strongly in the solid lattice to react with water. Reaction with Acids. Aluminium oxide will react with hot dilute hydrochloric acid to give aluminium chloride solution. Al₂O₃ 6HCl 2AlCl₃ 3H₂O. Reaction with Bases. With hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide solution, aluminium oxide reacts to give a colourless solution of sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate. Al₂O₃ 2NaOH 3H₂O 2NaAl(OH)₄. (d) Silicon dioxide (SiO₂). Reaction with water. It is insoluble in water because of the difficulty of breaking up the large and giant covalent structure. Reaction with Bases. It has got an acidic character.

It reacts with hot and concentrated sodium hydroxide to form sodium silicate. SiO₂ 2NaOH (hot and conc.) Na₂SiO₃ H₂O. It also reacts with basic metal oxides (Na₂O, K₂O, CaO, PbO, ZnO or mixture of oxides) forming silicates and glasses. (e) Phosphorus (V) oxide (P₄O₁₀). Reaction with Water. Phosphorus (V) oxide reacts violently with water to give a solution containing a mixture of acids, the nature of which depends on the conditions. We usually consider one of these, phosphoric (V) acid, H₃PO₄ (also known as phosphoric acid or as orthophosphoric acid). P₄O₁₀ 6H₂O 4H₃PO₄. Reaction with Base. As it is acidic, it reacts with NaOH as follows: NaOH H₃PO₄ NaH₂PO₄ H₂O. 2NaOH H₃PO₄ Na₂HPO₄ 2H₂O. 3NaOH H₃PO₄ Na₃PO₄ 3H₂O. When phosphorus (V) oxide reacts with sodium hydroxide solution, we would end up with the same possible salts rather than making the acid first. 12NaOH P₄O₁₀ 4Na₃PO₄ 6H₂O. (f) Sulphur oxides (SO₂ and SO₃). Sulphur has two oxides i.e., sulphur dioxide, (SO₂), and sulphur trioxide, (SO₃). (i) Sulphur dioxide (SO₂). Reaction with Water. Sulphur dioxide is fairly soluble in water. It reacts to give a solution of sulphurous acid, H₂SO₃. SO₂ H₂O H₂SO₃. Reaction with Base. As it is acidic, it reacts with NaOH and CaO as follows: CaO SO₂ CaSO₃. (ii) Sulphur trioxide (SO₃). Reaction with water. Sulphur trioxide reacts violently with water to produce a fog of concentrated sulphuric acid droplets. SO₃ H₂O H₂SO₄. Reaction with Base. Sulphur trioxide itself will also react directly with bases to form sulphates. For example, it will react with Sodium hydroxide and calcium oxide to form sodium sulphate and calcium sulphate, respectively. 2NaOH SO₃ Na₂SO₄ H₂O. CaO SO₃ CaSO₄. (g) Chlorine oxides (Cl₂Oₓ). Chlorine forms several oxides, but the only two are chlorine (VII) oxide, Cl₂O₇, and chlorine (I) oxide, Cl₂O are given here. Chlorine (VII) oxide is also known as dichlorine heptoxide, and chlorine (I) oxide as dichlorine monoxide. (i) Chlorine (VII) oxide. Chlorine (VII) oxide is the highest oxide of chlorine. In this oxide, chlorine is in its maximum oxidation state of 7. It continues the trend of the highest oxides of the Period 3 elements towards being stronger acids. Reaction with Water. Chlorine (VII) oxide reacts with water to give the very strong acid, chloric (VII) acid - also known as perchloric acid. The pH of typical solutions will, like sulphuric acid, be around 0. Cl₂O₇ H₂O 2HClO₄. Reaction with Base. Chlorine (VII) oxide reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give a solution of sodium chlorate(VII). 2NaOH Cl₂O₇ 2NaClO₄ H₂O. Chloric (VII) acid itself also reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to form the same product. NaOH HClO₄ NaClO₄ H₂O. (ii) Chlorine (I) oxide. Reaction with Water. Chlorine (I) oxide is far less acidic than chlorine (VII) oxide. It reacts with water to some extent to give chloric(I) acid, HOCl - also known as hypochlorous acid. Cl₂O H₂O 2HOCl. Reaction with Base. Chloric (I) acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give a solution of sodium hypochlorite. NaOH HOCl NaOCl H₂O.

Chlorine (I) oxide also reacts directly with sodium hydroxide to give the same product. 2NaOH Cl₂O 2NaOCl H₂O. Table 13.3: Properties of the oxides of elements in period 3. 1. In this topic, the structures of the chlorides of the Period 3 elements (sodium to sulphur), their physical properties and their reactions with water will be brought under discussion. Sodium Chloride, NaCl. Sodium chloride is a simple ionic compound consisting of a giant array of sodium and chloride ions having strong electrostatic forces of attraction between the positive and negative ions. Therefore, it needs a lot of heat energy to break, so sodium chloride has high melting and boiling points. It does not conduct electricity in the solid state but is a conductor in aqueous state or molten state. Sodium chloride simply dissolves in water to give a neutral solution (hydration). NaCl(s) H₂O(l) Na(aq) Cl(aq). Magnesium Chloride, MgCl₂. Magnesium chloride is also ionic and a lot of heat energy is needed to overcome the strong electrostatic forces of attractions between the ions, and so the melting and boiling points are high. Solid magnesium chloride is a non-conductor of electricity because the ions are not free to move. However, it is a conductor in molten state and in aqueous solution. Magnesium chloride dissolves in water to give a faintly acidic solution of pH approximately 6. (hydrolysis). When magnesium ions are broken off from the solid lattice and go into solution, there is enough attraction between the Mg² ions and the water molecules to form co-ordinate covalent bonds to form hexaaquamagnesium ions Mg(H₂O)₆² and Chloride ions. MgCl₂ 6H₂O Mg(H₂O)₆² 2Cl. Aluminium Chloride, AlCl₃. Solid aluminium chloride does not conduct electricity at room temperature because the ions are not free to move. Molten aluminium chloride (only possible at increased pressures) does not conduct electricity because there are not any ions any more. The aluminium chloride reacts with water to form hexaaquaaluminium ions and chloride ions. AlCl₃(s) 6H₂O(l) Al(H₂O)₆³ 3Cl. As this reaction is exothermic, heat released is used to break the O-H bond of water molecule, so steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride gas is formed. AlCl₃ 3H₂O Al(OH)₃ 3HCl. This explains why aqueous aluminium chloride is acidic. Silicon Tetrachloride, (SiCl₄). Silicon tetrachloride is a colourless liquid and forms a simple covalent structure. It contains weak Vander Waals forces so low boiling liquid. It does not conduct electricity because having no mobile electrons. If we add water to silicon tetrachloride, there is a violent reaction to produce silicon dioxide and steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride. SiCl₄ 2H₂O SiO₂ 4HCl. The Phosphorus Chlorides (PCl₃ and PCl₅). There are two phosphorus chlorides - phosphorus(III) chloride, (PCl₃), and phosphorus(V) chloride, (PCl₅). Phosphorus (III) Chloride (PCl₃).

Phosphorus trichloride is a simple covalent fuming liquid, containing Vander Waals dispersion forces. It does not conduct electricity because it has no free electrons. Phosphorus (III) chloride reacts violently with water to form phosphorous acid, H₃PO₃, and fumes of hydrogen chloride. PCl₃ 3H₂O H₃PO₃ 3HCl. Phosphorus (V) Chloride (PCl₅). Phosphorus (V) chloride is a simple covalent white solid which sublimes at 163C. As we increase the temperature, it dissociates reversibly to give PCl₃ and Cl₂. PCl₅ PCl₃ Cl₂. Solid phosphorus (V) chloride contains ions thats why it is solid at room temperature. The formation of the ions involve two molecules of PCl₅. PCl₅ PCl₅ PCl₄ PCl₆. Phosphorus (V) chloride has a violent reaction with water producing fumes of hydrogen chloride. The reaction occurs in two stages. In the first, with cold water, phosphorus oxychloride, POCl₃, is produced along with HCl. PCl₅ H₂O POCl₃ 2HCl. If the water is boiling, the phosphorus (V) chloride reacts further to give phosphoric (V) acid and more HCl. POCl₃ 3H₂O H₃PO₄ 3HCl. Disulphur dichloride, (S₂Cl₂). It is a simple covalent liquid (orange and smelly), containing Vander Waals forces. It does not conduct electricity because of lack of free electrons. Disulphur dichloride reacts slowly with water to produce a complex mixture of hydrochloric acid, sulphur, hydrogen sulphide and various sulphur containing acids and anions (negative ions). This topic consists on the brief account, how the chemistry of the "hydroxides" of the Period 3 elements from sodium to chlorine varies, across the period. Sodium and magnesium hydroxides are ionic compounds and are simple basic hydroxides. Both react with acids to form salts. For example, with dilute hydrochloric acid, colourless solution of sodium chloride or magnesium chloride are formed. NaOH HCl NaCl H₂O. Mg(OH)₂ 2HCl MgCl₂ 2H₂O. Aluminium hydroxide, like aluminium oxide, is amphoteric (both basic and acidic properties).

With dilute hydrochloric acid, a colourless solution of aluminium chloride is formed. Al(OH)₃ 3HCl AlCl₃ 3H₂O. But aluminium hydroxide also has an acidic side character. It will react with sodium hydroxide solution to give a colourless solution of sodium tetrahydroxoaluminate. Al(OH)₃ NaOH NaAl(OH)₄. Hydroxides of Si, P, S and Cl have hydroxides -OH groups covalently bonded to the atoms. These compounds are all acidic ranging from the very weakly acidic silicic acids to the very strong sulphuric or Chloric acids. There are other acids (also containing -OH groups) formed by these elements, but these are the ones where the Period 3 element is in its highest oxidation state. Orthosilicic acid is very weak.
