This section explores the trends in some atomic and physical properties of the Group I elements - lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium and caesium. 1. Trends in Atomic Radius. As we move from lithium to caesium, an extra shell of electrons is added to each element. Due to the increase in shielding effect, the effective nuclear charge decreases down the group. We find, therefore, that there is an increase of atomic and ionic radii (of M ions) as we move from lithium to caesium. This can be seen in the table 13.5. Table 13.5 Some Physical Properties of Alkali Metals. 2. Trends in First Ionization Energy. The first ionization energy falls as we go down the group. We know that alkali metals have only one electron in their outermost shell (ns¹ electron). This ns¹ electron is so weakly held with the nucleus that it can be removed very easily. Alkali metals, therefore, have low ionization energies. As the distance of ns¹ electron from the nucleus increases, on moving from Li to Cs, its removal becomes more and more easy i.e. the amount of energy (ionization energy) used in the removal of ns¹ electron is maximum in case of Li and minimum in case of Cs. The first ionization energy of alkali metals are shown in the table 13.5. The second ionisation energy is fairly high, since the loss of the second electron from M cation which has a noble gas configuration is quite difficult (size of M is smaller than M). 3. Trends in Electronegativity. Because of this electropositive character, these metals have very little electronegative character. Therefore, we can say that alkali metals are the least electronegative and their electronegativity values decrease down the group (due to the increase in size of atom) (Table 13.5). 4. Trends in Melting and Boiling Points.

We see that both the melting points and boiling points fall as we go down the Group. (Table 13.5.) The melting and boiling points are very low because of the presence of weak metallic bonds (fewer no of free electrons) in the solid state of the alkali metals. 5. Trends in Density. The densities of alkali metals are quite low due to the large atomic volumes. Li, Na and K are lighter in atomic size from Li to Cs. K however is, lighter than Na which is due to an unusual increase in atomic size of K. (Table 13.5). Quick Quiz 5. 1. Why is K lighter than Na? 2. Explain that 2nd ionization energy is greater than 1st ionization energy for alkali metals. 3. Why are melting points of alkali metals low? 13.2.2 Trends in Reactivity with Water. The reaction of alkali metals with water is highly exothermic. A small piece of Li, Na and K floats on water. They react vigorously and liberate metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas. These reactions are highly exothermic. The energy which is produced can burn the hydrogen gas. It is for this reason that alkali metals are stored in kerosene or paraffin oil. 2Na 2H₂O 2NaOH H₂ ΔH -ve. The reactivity of alkali metals with water becomes more and more vigorous as we move down the group. K, Rb and Cs are so reactive with water that they react with ice at 100C. 13.2.3. Reactions with Oxygen. Alkali metals react with O₂, or air rapidly and thus get tarnished due to the formation of their oxide. Li when burnt in O₂, mainly gives lithium monoxide, (normal oxide) Li₂O. 4Li O₂ 2Li₂O. Na burnt with golden yellow flame in O₂ forms sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂. 2Na O₂ Na₂O₂. Other alkali metals (M K, Rb, Cs) react with O₂ to form super oxide of MO₂ type. Since the normal oxides of alkali metals other than that of Li (Li₂O) are not formed by the direct reaction between the metals and O₂, they are formed by indirect methods, e.g. by reducing peroxides, nitrite and nitrates with the metals itself. 2Na₂O₂ 4Na 4Na₂O. 2NaNO₂ 6Na 4Na₂O N₂. 2NaNO₃ 10Na 6Na₂O N₂. Properties: Normal oxides (O²) react with H₂O to form hydroxides by proton exchange. O² H₂O OH OH. The peroxides (O₂²) and superoxides (O₂) are strong oxidising agents and react with H₂O to give H₂O₂ and O₂. Peroxides: O₂² 2H₂O 2H₂O₂. Superoxides: 2O₂ 2H₂O 2H₂O₂ O₂. Reactions of the Oxides with Water and Dilute Acids. I. The simple oxides, M₂O. Reaction with Water. The simple oxides react with water to give metal hydroxide. For example, lithium oxide reacts with water to give a colourless solution of lithium hydroxide. M₂O H₂O 2MOH ; Li₂O H₂O 2LiOH. Reaction with dilute Acids. The simple oxides react with an acid to give a salt and water. For example, sodium oxide will react with dilute hydrochloric acid to give colourless sodium chloride solution and water.

M₂O 2HCl 2MCl H₂O ; Na₂O 2HCl 2NaCl H₂O. II. The peroxides, M₂O₂. Reaction with Water. If the reaction is done in ice cold water (and the temperature controlled so that it does not rise even though these reactions are strongly exothermic), a solution of the metal hydroxide and hydrogen peroxide is formed. If the temperature increases (as it inevitably will unless the peroxide is added to water very slowly), the hydrogen peroxide produced decomposes into water and oxygen. The reaction can be very violent overall. 2H₂O₂ 2H₂O O₂. Reaction with dilute Acids. These reactions are even more exothermic than the ones with water. A solution containing a salt and hydrogen peroxide is formed. The hydrogen peroxide will decompose to give water and oxygen if the temperature rises again, it is almost impossible to avoid this. III. The Superoxides, MO₂. Reaction with Water. When superoxides react with water, a solution of the metal hydroxide and hydrogen peroxide is formed, but oxygen gas is given off as well. Once again, these are strongly exothermic reactions and the heat produced will inevitably decompose the hydrogen peroxide to water and more oxygen. Reaction with dilute Acids. When these oxides react with HCl, a solution containing a salt and hydrogen peroxide is formed together with oxygen gas. The hydrogen peroxide will again decompose into water and oxygen as the temperature rises. 13.2.4 Reactions of the Alkali metals with Chlorine. Alkali metals react with halogens (chlorine) to give halides (chlorides). Li and Na react slowly with chlorine at room temperature to give LiCl and NaCl. Molten Na burns with a brilliant yellow flame in the atmosphere of chlorine to form NaCl. 2Na Cl₂ 2NaCl. K, Rb and Cs react vigorously with all the halogens to form metal halides. 13.2.5. Effect of heat on Nitrates and Carbonates. The carbonates (M₂CO₃) are highly stable to heat. With increase of electropositive character from Li to Cs, the stability of these salts increases. Their nitrates decompose on strong heating to the corresponding nitrite and O₂, (Exception is LiNO₃). 4LiNO₃ 2Li₂O 4NO₂ O₂. 2NaNO₃ 2NaNO₂ O₂. Quick Quiz 6. 1. Give trend of stability of carbonates of alkali metals along the group. 2. Why are alkali metals stored in kerosene / paraffin oil? 13.2.6 Flame Tests. A flame test is an analytical procedure used to detect the presence of certain metal ions, based on each elements characteristic emission spectrum. Flame tests are used to identify the presence of a relatively small number of metal ions in a compound. Not all metal ions give flame colours. Procedure. Clean a platinum or nichrome (a nickel-chromium alloy) wire by dipping it into concentrated hydrochloric acid and then heat it in a hot Bunsen flame until the wire does not produce any colour in the flame. When the wire is clean, moisten it again with some of the acid and then dip it into a small amount of the solid to be tested.

Place the wire back in the flame again, an intense flash of colour is imparted to the flame. Different colours shown by different elements are given below. Elements: Li - crimson red; Na - golden yellow; K - violet; Rb - reddish-violet; Cs - Blue; Ca - brick red; Sr - crimson red; Ba - pale green/grassy green; Cu - blue-green (often with white flashes); Pb - greyish-white. The Origin of Flame Colours. When an alkali or alkaline earth metal or any of their compound is heated in a Bunsen flame, the electrons get excited to higher energy levels. These electrons on de-excitation, release the excitation energy in the form of light in the visible region of the spectrum. Since the amount of energy absorbed during the excitation process is different in different atoms, different colours are imparted by the atoms to the flame. Quick Quiz 7. 1. Write electronic configuration for alkali metal atoms. 2. Explain periodicity in ionisation energy, electronegativity and atomic radii on passing from Li to Rb. 3. Explain the following: a) Alkali metals show an oxidation state 1 only. b) Alkali metals are good reducing agents. c) Alkali metals have low melting points. d) Alkali metals give characteristic colour to the Bunsen flame. e) Na is stored under kerosene oil. f) Alkali metals form M cations instead of M² cations. g) Alkali metals have low ionisation potentials. 13.3 GROUP II ELEMENTS (Alkaline Earth Metals). 13.3.1 Atomic and Physical Properties. This section explores the trends in some atomic and physical properties of the Group II elements - beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium and radium. 1. Trends in Atomic Radius. We can see that the atomic radius increases as we go down the Group. Reason: As we go down the group, extra shells are added and the atomic volume increases from Be to Ra. With the increase of atomic volume, the atomic and ionic radii (of M² ions) also increase from Be to Ra. The atomic radii of these elements are, however, smaller than those of alkali metals in the same period. This is due to the fact that the alkaline earth metals have higher nuclear charge which tends to draw the orbit electrons towards the nucleus. The smaller values of atomic radii result in that the alkaline earth metals are harder, have higher densities and higher melting points than alkali metals. Table 13.6: Some physical properties of alkaline earth metals. 2. Trends in First Ionization Energy. The first ionisation energy decreases down the group. Reason: The first and second ionisation energies of these elements decreases with the increase of atomic radii from Be to Ba. However, the values for Ra is slightly higher than those of Ba (for values see table no 13.6). 3. Trends in Electronegativity. The electronegativity values fall as we go down the group (table 13.6), because of the increase of atomic radii from Be to Ba. 4. Trends in Melting Point and Boiling Point.

The melting and boiling points of group II elements are higher than group I elements. The reason is that the group II elements have stronger metallic bond due to the presence of two valence electrons. Anyhow there is no regular trend present which can be observed. 13.3.2 Trends in Reactivity with Water. The group II metals become more reactive towards water as we go down the group. For example: Beryllium: Beryllium has no reaction with water or steam even when red hot. Magnesium: Magnesium burns in steam to produce white magnesium oxide and hydrogen gas. Mg(s) H₂O(g) MgO(s) H₂(g). Very clean magnesium ribbon has a very slight reaction with cold water. After several minutes, some bubbles of hydrogen form on its surface, and the coil of magnesium ribbon usually floats to the surface. However, the reaction soon stops because the magnesium hydroxide formed is almost insoluble in water and forms a protective layer on the magnesium preventing further reaction. Mg(s) 2H₂O(l) Mg(OH)₂(s) H₂(g). Calcium, Strontium and Barium: They react with cold water with increasing vigour to give the metal hydroxide and hydrogen. Strontium and barium have reactivities similar to lithium in Group I of the Periodic Table. Calcium, for example, reacts fairly vigorously with cold water in an exothermic reaction. Bubbles of hydrogen gas are given off, and a white precipitate (of calcium hydroxide) is formed, together with an alkaline solution as; Ca 2H₂O Ca(OH)₂ H₂. 13.3.3 Reactions with Oxygen and Nitrogen. I. Reactions of the Group 2 Elements with Air or Oxygen. (a) Formation of Simple Oxides. Preparation: The alkaline earth metals form the normal oxides (MO) which are obtained by heating the metal in O₂, or by heating their carbonates at high temperature e.g. 2Ca O₂ 2CaO. CaCO₃ (heat) CaO CO₂. Properties: (i) These white crystalline oxides are extremely stable due to their high crystal lattice energy. (ii) BeO and MgO are quite insoluble in H₂O while CaO, SrO and BaO react with H₂O to give soluble hydroxides, M(OH)₂ which are strong bases. (iii) BeO is not at all basic in nature; in fact, it is amphoteric since it reacts with acids to form salts and with alkalis to give beryllates. BeO 2HCl BeCl₂ 2H₂O. BeO 2NaOH Na₂BeO₂ 2H₂O. The oxides of other metals are basic in character. Their basic character increases down the group. (iv) Due to the small size of Be² ion, BeO is covalent while other oxides are ionic. Although BeO is covalent yet it has a higher melting point and is harder than the oxides of other metals as it is polymeric. Each Be atom is tetrahedrally coordinated by four oxygen atoms. (b) Peroxides: Preparation: The peroxides of heavier metals (Sr, Ba etc.) can be obtained on heating the normal oxides with O₂ at high temperature. 2BaO O₂ (High Temp.) 2BaO₂. Properties: The peroxides are white, ionic solids having peroxide anion, O-O². They react with acids to produce H₂O₂. BaO₂ H₂SO₄ BaSO₄ H₂O₂. II. Reactions of the Group II element with Nitrogen.

All the elements burn in nitrogen to form nitrides, M₃N₂ e.g. 3Ca N₂ Ca₃N₂. These metal nitrides react with H₂O to liberate NH₃ e.g. Ca₃N₂ 6H₂O 3Ca(OH)₂ 2NH₃. Be₃N₂ is volatile while other nitrides are non-volatile. 13.3.4 Trends in Solubility of the Hydroxides, Sulphates and Carbonates. I. Solubility of the Hydroxides. Group II metal hydroxides become more soluble as we go down the group because the lattice energy decreases down the group due to the increase in size. Be(OH)₂ and Mg(OH)₂ are almost insoluble in H₂O while the hydroxides of other metals are slightly soluble. Magnesium Hydroxide is insoluble and shows slightly alkaline nature in water. Suspension of Mg (OH)₂ is called milk of magnesia. It is used to remove stomach acidity. Calcium Hydroxide solution is used as "lime water". 1 litre of pure water will dissolve about 1 gram of calcium hydroxide at room temperature. Barium Hydroxide is soluble enough to be able to produce a solution with a concentration of around 0.1 mol dm³ at room temperature. II. Solubility of the Sulphates. The sulphates become less soluble as we go down the Group e.g., BeSO₄ and MgSO₄ are fairly water soluble, calcium sulphate is sufficiently soluble in water while strontium and Barium sulphates are almost insoluble. III. Solubility of the Carbonates. The carbonates tend to become less soluble as we go down the Group. Carbonates are insoluble in water and therefore occur as solid rock minerals in nature. However, they dissolve in H₂O containing CO₂ due to the formation of bicarbonates. 13.3.5. Trends in Thermal Stability of the Carbonates and Nitrates. The effect of heat on the Group 2 Carbonates. All carbonates decompose on heating at appropriate temperature evolving CO₂. MCO₃ CO₂ MO. The stability of the carbonates of these metals increase on moving down the group. This is illustrated by the values of the decomposition temperatures of these carbonates as given below: BeCO₃ 25C, MgCO₃ 540C, CaCO₃ 900C, SrCO₃ 1290C, BaCO₃ 1360C. Reason: Cations of group II elements have smaller sizes and greater charge densities than the cations of group I elements. The cations of small size and high charge densities have greater ability to distort or polarize the carbonate ion and hence facilitate its decomposition. Thus the carbonates of group I are more stable than group II carbonates. The effect of heat on the Group II Nitrates. All the nitrates in this Group undergo thermal decomposition to give the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen e.g., 2Mg (NO₃)₂ 2MgO 4NO₂ O₂. 2Ba (NO₃)₂ 2BaO 4NO₂ O₂. The nitrates are white solids, and the oxides produced are also white solids. Brown nitrogen dioxide gas is given off together with oxygen. Magnesium and calcium nitrates normally have water of crystallisation, and the solid may dissolve in its own water of crystallisation to make a colourless solution before it starts to decompose. Thermal stability of nitrates increases down the group. 13.3.6. How Beryllium Differ from other Members of its Group?

Beryllium, the first element of the group, differs from rest of alkaline earth metals due to its small atomic size and comparatively high electronegativity. The main points of difference are: 1. Hardness: Beryllium is the hardest of all the elements of its group. 2. Melting and Boiling Points: The melting and boiling points of beryllium are the highest. 3. Formation of Covalent Compounds: Beryllium has a tendency to form covalent compounds. Thus when it reacts with other elements, the electronegativity difference is not so large and the bond is therefore covalent. 4. Reaction with Water: Beryllium does not react with water even at high temperature. Other alkaline earth metals decompose water liberating H₂ gas. Mg H₂O MgO H₂. 5. Reaction with Hydrogen: Beryllium does not react with hydrogen directly to form its hydride. Its hydride however has been prepared indirectly. The rest of the alkaline earth metals combine with hydrogen to form hydrides. The hydrides of Be and Mg are covalent, whereas the hydrides of other metals are ionic. M H₂ MH₂. 6. Reaction with Alkalis: Beryllium reacts with alkalis to form hydrogen gas. Be 2NaOH Na₂BeO₂ H₂. Other alkaline earth metals do not react with alkalis. 7. Behaviour of Oxides and Hydroxides: The oxides and hydroxides of beryllium are amphoteric, i.e. dissolve both in acids and alkalis to form salts. BeO 2HCl BeCl₂ H₂O. BeO 2NaOH Na₂BeO₂ H₂O. The oxides and hydroxides of other group II elements are basic. 8. Behaviour of Carbides: Beryllium carbide is decomposed by water to form methane (CH₄). Be₂C 4H₂O 2Be(OH)₂ CH₄. The carbide of other alkaline earth metals are decomposed by water to form acetylene (C₂H₂). For example: CaC₂ 2H₂O Ca(OH)₂ C₂H₂. 9. Behaviour of Nitrides: Be₃N₂ is volatile while the nitrides of other alkaline earth metals are non-volatile. 10. Number of Molecules of Water of Crystallisation: The salts of Be² ion cannot have more than four molecules of water of crystallisation while other alkaline earth metals have more than four molecules of water of crystallisation because in case of Be² ion there are only four orbitals. One orbital can accept lone pairs of electrons donated by O-atoms on each of the water molecules. On the other hand, other alkaline earth metals like Mg can extend their coordination number to six by using one 3s, three 3p and two 3d orbitals belonging to their outermost shell. 11. Formation of Complex Compounds: Be² ion, on account of its small size, forms stable complex compounds like BeF₃, BeF₄² while M² ions derived from other alkaline earth metals form very few complex compounds. Melting Points and Boiling Points. As we move down the group from C to Pb, the melting points as well as boiling points generally decrease, decrease in melting points as well as in boiling points indicate that inter-atomic forces also decrease in the same direction. The melting and boiling points of C and Si are notably high because of the tendencies of these elements to form giant covalent molecules. The low value for tin's melting point compared with lead is presumably due to forming a distorted 12 co-ordinated structure rather than a pure one. The tin values in the chart refer to metallic white tin. 13.4.2 The Trend from Non-Metal to Metal in the Group IV Elements. The change from non-metallic to metallic character with the increase in atomic number is the best illustrated by the elements of this group. The first two elements i.e C and Si are distinctly non-metals, although electrical properties of Si are like those of a semi-metal (i.e a metalloid); the third element i.e Ge is partly a metal and partly a non-metal, while the last two elements i.e. Sn and Pb are distinctly metals. Thus: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb. Non-metals, Metalloid, Metals. Metallic Character increases. The change from non-metallic to metallic character with the increase in atomic number is due to the decrease in effective nuclear charge and an increase in the size of the atoms. 13.4.3 Oxidation State. The elements of group IVA exist in two oxidation states 2 and 4. In carbon and silicon compounds the 4 state is very stable relative to 2. The 2 state is rare and easily oxidized to 4. The steady increase in the stability of the lower oxidation state relative to the higher oxidation state on moving down the group from carbon to lead is due to inert pair effect. 13.4.4 Possible Oxidation States; (a). Inert pair effect and positive oxidation states: Carbon and silicon show 4 oxidation states while Ge, Sn and Pb show 2 and 4 oxidation states. When only two np electrons from the ns²np² configuration are lost, we get the elements in 2 oxidation states.

The ns² electron pair remains inert and does not take part in bond formation. This pair of ns² electrons is called inert pair of electrons and the effect is called inert pair effect. Since in the group the stability of 2 oxidation state also increases from Ge² to Pb² i.e. Ge² Sn² Pb². Oxidizing and reducing properties: When all the four ns²np² electrons are lost, M⁴ cations are formed. On descending the group stability of 4 oxidation state decrease i.e. the stability of M⁴ cations decrease from Ge⁴ to Pb⁴ i.e. Ge⁴ Sn⁴ Pb⁴. Compounds of Ge² are less stable than those of Ge⁴. Hence the compounds of Ge² are readily oxidised into Ge⁴. In other words, compounds of Ge² act as strong reducing agents while those of Ge⁴ act as oxidising agents. Ge² compounds Oxidation Ge⁴ compounds (Less stable, Reducing agent). Ge⁴ compounds Reduction Ge² compounds (More stable, Oxidising agent). On similar grounds it can be shown that the compounds of Sn² are less stable than those of Sn⁴. In other words, compounds of Sn² act as strong reducing agents while those of Sn⁴ act as oxidising agents. Sn² compounds Oxidation Sn⁴ compounds (Less stable, Reducing agent). Sn⁴ compounds Reduction Sn² compounds (More stable, Oxidising agent). When we compare the stability of the compounds of Pb⁴ and Pb² ions, we find that Pb⁴ compounds are less stable than those of Pb² (PbCl₄). Hence the compounds of Pb⁴ are readily changed (reduced) into those of Pb². In other words, compounds of Pb⁴ act as strong oxidising agents while those of Pb² act as reducing agents. Pb⁴ compounds Reduction Pb² compounds (Less stable, Oxidising agent). Pb² compounds Oxidation Pb⁴ compounds (More stable, Reducing agent). The stability of M⁴ and M² cations of Ge, Sn and Pb, are as follows: Ge² Ge⁴; Sn² Sn⁴; Pb² Pb⁴. (b). Negative Oxidation State. Since the electronegativities of these elements are low, they do not have much tendency to form the negative ion. However, carbon forms C⁴ and C₂² ions in certain compounds, e.g. Na₄C (Na and C⁴ ions), CaC₂ (Ca² and C₂² ions). (c) Nature of M² and M⁴ compounds (Fajan Rule). The nature of the compounds of M² and M⁴ cations can be predicted by Fajans rule which states that: The smaller cation with high charge density makes the bond more covalent. The members of group IVA elements show M² and M⁴ oxidation states. Therefore, these members can form covalent as well as ionic bonds depending upon the size of cation. According to Fajans rule, molecules containing M² ions (low charge density) are ionic in nature, while compounds containing M⁴ ions (high charge density) are covalent in nature. Example SnCl₂ and SnCl₄. Sn⁴ ion is smaller than Sn², the compounds of Sn⁴ are covalent in nature while those of Sn² are ionic. Similarly Pb⁴ compounds are covalent and those of Pb² are ionic. The tendency of given cations to form ionic compounds increases down the group. 13.4.5 The Chlorides of Carbon, Silicon and Lead.

Carbon, Silicon and Lead Tetrachlorides. These all have the formula XCl₄. They are all simple covalent molecules with a typical tetrahedral shape. All of them are liquids at room temperature. (Although at room temperature, lead(IV) chloride will tend to decompose to give lead(II) chloride and chlorine gas). PbCl₄ PbCl₂ Cl₂ (white solid). Stability. At the top of Group 4, the most stable oxidation state shown by carbon and silicon is 4 in CCl₄ and SiCl₄ and have no tendency to decompose into dichlorides (in 2 Oxidation state). The thermal stability of the chlorides of group IVA decreases down the group. Reaction with water (hydrolysis). Actually the hydrolysis of tetra halides takes place through the following two steps: 1st step: In this step, oxygen atoms of H₂O which acts as an electron donor, attack the central atoms to form a coordinate bond with it and thus produces an unstable intermediate compound MX₄4H₂O. 2nd step: In this step, four HX molecules are eliminated from this unstable intermediate compound and hydroxide of the central element is formed. Thus X atoms of MX₄ molecule are replaced by OH ions. The tetrahalides of C are not hydrolysed while those of Si, Ge and Sn get readily hydrolysed: Reason: We know that C atom being a member of second period of the periodic table, has no d-orbitals in its valence shell and hence is unable to accommodate the lone pair donated by the donor oxygen atom of H₂O molecule to form an unstable intermediate compound. Thus the tetrahalides of C are not hydrolysed. On the other hand, Si, Ge and Sn have vacant d-orbitals which can accept the lone pair and thus their tetrahalides get readily hydrolysed. Trends: The ease with which the tetrahalides are hydrolysed by H₂O decreases from Si to Sn as the metallic character of the central atom increases in this order. Thus GeX₄ and SnX₄ tetrahalides are less readily hydrolysed than SiX₄ tetrahalides. It may be mentioned here that empty orbitals are always available with any atom and they can be utilised if sufficient energy is provided for the reaction to occur, e.g., CCl₄ undergoes hydrolysis when superheated steam is used. CCl₄ H₂O (superheated steam) COCl₂ 2HCl (Phosgene gas). Hydrolysis of tetrahalides of Pb follows essentially the same pattern but due to the instability of tetravalent compounds of Pb, some decomposition of PbCl₄ to PbCl₂ also takes place. PbCl₄ is hydrolysed by H₂O as follows: PbCl₄ 2H₂O PbO₂ 4HCl. Complex formation: Except carbon, the tetrahalides of Si, Ge, Sn and Pb react with halide ions and form the hexahalo complex ions like SiF₆², GeX₆². SiF₄ 2F SiF₆². 13.4.6 Oxides. The elements of group IVA form three types of oxides i.e., Monoxides (MO type oxides); Dioxide (MO₂ type); other oxides like C₃O₂, Pb₃O₄, PbO, PbO₂ etc. But we will discuss only the structural differences between carbon dioxide and silicon dioxide, and the trends in acid-base behaviour of the oxides as we go down Group IV. The Structures of Carbon Dioxide and Silicon Dioxide.

Carbon dioxide is a gas whereas silicon dioxide is a hard and high melting point solid. The other dioxides in Group IV are also solids. The Structure of Carbon Dioxide: 1. It is a triatomic simple covalent molecule. 2. It has two double bonds between carbon and oxygen atoms. 3. Carbon is sp-hybridized and oxygen is sp²-hybridized. 4. The molecule of CO₂ is linear and net dipole moment is zero. 5. The solid CO₂ has a face-centred cubic structure. 6. The bond lengths between carbon and oxygen have values 115 pm. 7. All three atoms have completed their octet. So the molecule of CO₂ is stable. The Structure of Silicon Dioxide: Silicon dioxide forms a giant covalent structure in which each silicon and oxygen atom is linked together covalently in tetrahedral basic unit. Because of its structure silicon dioxide is non-volatile and hard solid unlike carbon dioxide. Both these oxides show a lot of difference in their physical properties. It is due to the fact that: (1) Silicon atoms are much larger in size than carbon atoms and thus tend to be surrounded by more oxygen atoms. (2) Silicon forms only single bond with oxygen atoms while carbon forms double bonds. (3) Carbon dioxide forms a simple molecular structure containing weak Vander Waals forces. Whereas in silicon dioxide, each silicon atom is bonded with four oxygen atoms in a tetrahedral structure. Silicon dioxide forms a giant covalent structure containing strong covalent bonds throughout the network, which need a lot of energy to break. The simplest formula for silica is SiO₂. However, the whole crystal of silicon dioxide can be considered as one molecule. The Acid-Base Behaviour of the Group IV Oxides. The oxides of the elements at the top of Group IV are acidic, but acidity of the oxides falls as we go down the Group. The oxides become more basic as we move down the group. The trend is, therefore, from acidic oxides at the top of the Group towards amphoteric ones at the bottom. Carbon and Silicon Oxides. Carbon Monoxide: Carbon monoxide is usually treated as if it is a neutral oxide. But in fact it is very, very slightly acidic. It does not react with water but it will react with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution to give a solution of sodium methanoate. NaOH CO HCOONa. Carbon and Silicon Dioxides: These are both weakly acidic. With Water: Silicon dioxide does not react with water, because of the difficulty of breaking up the giant covalent structure. Carbon dioxide reacts with water, to a slight extent, to produce hydrogen ions (strictly, hydroxonium ions) and hydrogencarbonate ions. H₂O(l) CO₂(aq) H(aq) HCO₃(aq). With Bases: Carbon dioxide reacts with sodium hydroxide solution at low temperature to give either sodium carbonate or sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, depending on the concentration of reactants. 2NaOH CO₂ Na₂CO₃ H₂O. NaOH CO₂ NaHCO₃. Silicon dioxide also reacts with sodium hydroxide solution when hot and concentrated. Sodium silicate solution is formed. 2NaOH SiO₂ Na₂SiO₃ H₂O.

Calcium oxide reacts with silicon dioxide to produce a liquid slag, calcium silicate. CaO(s) SiO₂(s) (heat) CaSiO₃(l) (Slag). Germanium, Tin and Lead Oxides. I. The Monoxides: They have general formula XO, where (X Ge, Sn, Pb). All of these oxides are amphoteric. The Basic Nature of the Oxides: These oxides react with acids to form salts. XO 2HCl(aq) XCl₂(aq) H₂O(l) (Where X can be Ge and Sn). Example: Lead (II) oxide reacts with dilute HCl and forms an insoluble layer of lead (II) chloride over the lead (II) oxide and stops the reaction as: PbO(s) 2HCl(aq) PbCl₂(s) H₂O(l). But when we use Conc. HCl insolubility disappears and PbCl₄² complex is formed, which is soluble in water. PbCl₂(s) 2Cl(aq) PbCl₄²(aq). The Acidic Nature of the Oxides: All of these oxides also react with bases like sodium hydroxide solution. XO(s) 2NaOH(aq) Na₂XO₂(aq) H₂O(l). II. The Dioxides: They have general formula XO₂, where (X Ge, Sn, Pb). These dioxides are again amphoteric - showing both basic and acidic properties. The Basic Nature of the Dioxides: The dioxides react with concentrated hydrochloric acid first to give compounds of the type XCl₄: XO₂(s) 4HCl(aq) XCl₄(aq) 2H₂O(l). XCl₄ will react with excess chloride ions in the hydrochloric acid to give complexes such as XCl₆². XCl₄ 2Cl XCl₆². In case of lead (IV) oxide, the reaction has to be done with ice-cold hydrochloric acid. In warm condition, the lead (IV) chloride decomposes to give lead (II) chloride and chlorine gas. This is an effect of the preferred oxidation state of lead being 2 rather than 4. PbCl₄ PbCl₂ Cl₂. The Acidic Nature of the Dioxides: The dioxides will react with hot concentrated sodium hydroxide solution to give soluble complexes of the form X(OH)₆². Quick Quiz 9. 1. Give the trend of conductivity of group IV elements. 2. Which of the following metals are semiconductors Pb, C, Si, Ge? 3. Arrange following cation in increasing order of their stability. Sn², Sn⁴, Ge⁴, Pb⁴. 13.5 GROUP VII ELEMENTS (HALOGENS). 13.5.1 Atomic and Physical Properties. 1. Trends in Atomic Radius. Atomic radius increases as we go down the group due to the increase in number of shells, greater shielding effect. 2. Trends in Electronegativity. Halogens have large values of electronegativity. These values decrease as we proceed from F to I in the group. Large electronegativity values of halogen atoms indicate that they have a strong tendency to form halide ions. 3. Trends in Electron Affinity (E.A). Halogens have high electron affinities which decrease from chlorine to iodine. Chlorine in the group has the highest electron affinity. The lower value of E.A for F is due to its small size and interelectronic repulsion between the electron added and electrons already present (i.e compact 2p orbital of F atom). 4. Trends in Melting and Boiling Points. The melting and boiling points of the halogens regularly increase from F₂ to I₂. Halogens contain instantaneous dipole induce dipole forces.

These attractive forces between molecules become progressively more prominent as the molecules increase in size and mass. This effect is also reflected in the physical states of halogens. F₂ and Cl₂ are gases at ordinary temperature, Br₂ is a heavy liquid while I₂ is a solid. 5. Bond enthalpies (bond energies or bond strengths). Bond enthalpy is the heat needed to break one mole of a covalent bond to produce individual atoms. For example: Cl-Cl(g) 2Cl(g). For bromine, the reaction is still from gaseous bromine molecules to separate gaseous atoms. Br-Br(g) 2Br(g). Bond enthalpy in the halogens, X₂. The bond enthalpies of the Cl-Cl, Br-Br and I-I bonds fall just as we would expect, but the F-F bond is deviated from the sequence. Reason: Due to the very small size of fluorine atom in F₂ molecule, repulsions between the non-bonding electrons is very large as compared to other halogens. This makes the F atoms in F₂ molecule repel each other and helps in the dissociation of F₂ molecule into F atoms. That is why the bond enthalpy of F₂ is less than expected. Bond Enthalpies in the Hydrogen Halides, HX. As the halogen atom gets bigger, the bonding pair gets more and more distant from the nucleus. The attraction becomes less, and the bond gets weaker and can easily be broken down. 13.5.2 Strength of Halogens as Oxidising Agents: The halogens due to high electron affinity values have a great tendency to accept electron and hence acts as strong oxidising agent. The oxidising property of a halogen molecule, X₂ is represented by; ½X₂ (s,l,g) e H₂O X(aq) Energy. It has been seen that the values of E.A are decreasing from fluorine to iodine. The oxidising power of halogens is also decreasing in the same direction i.e. the oxidising power of halogen is in the order: F₂Cl₂Br₂I₂. Since F₂ is the strongest oxidising agent in the series, it will oxidise other halide ions to halogens in solution or when dry, i.e., F₂ displaces other halogens from their corresponding halides. For example. F₂ 2X 2F X₂. Similarly Cl₂ will displace Br and I ions from their solutions and Br₂ will displace I ions from their solutions. Cl₂ 2X 2Cl X₂. Br₂ 2I 2Br I₂. 13.5.3 The Acidity of the Hydrogen Halides. All the halogen acids in the gaseous state are essentially covalent but in the aqueous solution they ionise to give solvated proton (H₃O) and hence acts as acids. H₂O HX H₃O X. HF ionises only slightly while HCl, HBr, and HI ionise completely. Hence HF is the weakest acid and strength of these acids increase from HF to HI, i.e. HF HCl HBr HI (weakest acid) (strongest acid). Acidic character of HX increases from HF to HI. As we move down the group, size of halogen atom increases which causes the decrease in forces of attraction between H and X. so the ability to release proton (H) increases which makes the acid strong.

13.5.4 Halide Ions as Reducing Agents and Trends in Reducing Strength. Ability of Halide Ions (The Redox Reactions between Halide Ions and Concentrated Sulphuric Acid). (i) With Chloride Ions: The chloride ions will not reduce the concentrated sulphuric acid. 2NaCl H₂SO₄ Na₂SO₄ 2HCl. (ii) With Bromide Ions: Bromide ions are strong reducing agents and reduce the concentrated sulphuric acid. In this process, the bromide ions are oxidised to bromine. The oxidation state of sulphur decreases from 6 in the sulphuric acid to 4 in the sulphur dioxide. (iii) With Iodide Ions: Iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than bromide ions. They are oxidised to iodine by the concentrated sulphuric acid. 8NaI 4H₂SO₄ 4Na₂SO₄ 8HI. 8HI H₂SO₄ 4I₂ H₂S 4H₂O. The iodide ions reduce H₂SO₄ to H₂S. Thus, the oxidation state of sulphur decreases from 6 to -2. Trends in reducing strength: The reducing ability of the halide ions increases as we go down the group; F Cl Br I. When a halide ion acts as a reducing agent, it has to lose electrons, itself. The bigger the halide ion, the farther the outer electrons are from the nucleus, and the more they are screened from it by inner electrons. It, therefore, gets easier for the halide ions to lose electrons as we go down the group because there is less attraction between the outer electrons and the nucleus. Quick Quiz 10. 1. Give reasons of the following: (a) HI is stronger acid than HF. (b) Electron affinity of fluorine is less than chlorine. (c) The iodide ions are powerful reducing agent. 2. As early as 1940, can manufacturers began to explore adapting cans to package carbonated soft drinks. In addition, beer ages naturally, so it has a limited shelf life of about three months in any package. In contrast, the food acids, including carbonic, citric and phosphoric, in soft drinks present a risk for rapid corrosion of exposed tin and iron in the can. At this point, the can was upgraded by improving the organic coatings used to line the inside, making cans heavier and more encasing. Elements/Metals Their Mining and Extraction. Different elements/metals are obtained after passing through different steps. These steps are discussed as follows: 1. Mining and enrichment, 2. Reduction, 3. Refining and Casting. In fact, some special methods are used to obtain each metal from its ores and to develop it into useful articles. Yet a few steps are common in the metallurgy of every metal.

Which are follows: 1. Mining: Obtaining ores by digging the rocks and hills is called mining. This work is done by engineers and laborers with the help of machines. But prior to this work it is confirmed by survey and analysis that obtaining metals from this is economical or not. 2. Crushing: Breaking of rocks and larger stones into smaller size stones is called crushing. This is done by jaw crushers. 3. Grinding: The crushed ore is grinded in grinding machines. 4. Hand Picking, Jugging and Shaking: In Pakistan and other under developed countries where labour is cheap, metallic stones are picked and separated by hands. Heavy metals are separated from useless material i.e. gangue, by shaking with chaage. In some countries this process is done by pressurized water. 5. Magnetic Separation: The ground ore is passed over a magnetic belt which separates the magnetic metal from gangue. This process is used for metals, which have magnetic properties like iron. Reduction: For the complete separation of a metal from gangue, ores are heated at high temperature. At its melting point, molten metal is separated from solid gangue. The process of reduction is carried out in the blast furnace. Blast Furnace: It is lined inside with fire bricks. Its height and capacity are kept according to the requirement. Hot gases enter from lower side and ores are charged from the top of the furnace. Temperature is maintained at 1500-3000C. This furnace is usually used for iron and copper metallurgy. 3. Refining of Metals: Metals extracted in the above process are further refined by the following process. Open-Hearth Process: A fire furnace is used to remove the impurities of metal. It is lined inside with fire bricks and is just like a room. Burning gases are entered from one side and exhaust gases are removed from the opposite end. The process is operated from opposite ends after an interval. Metals melt in a shorter time by this two way heating. Applications of Bleaching Powder. Bleaching powder is actually a mixture of calcium hypochlorite Ca(OCl)₂ and the basic chloride CaCl₂H₂O with some slaked lime, Ca(OH)₂. 1. Bleaching powder is highly effective for cleaning inside the home and outdoors. It can be used for removing mildew from fabric, cleaning countertops and for removing mold from grout between tiles, bathmats and shower curtains. 2. Bleaching powder can be used to disinfect safely and sterilize many things around the home including second hand goods, trash cans, pet accessories and baby toys and furniture. 3. Bleaching powder is used for the disinfection of drinking water or swimming pool water. 4. Bleaching powder is used for bleaching cotton and linen. Iodine Deficiency: Iodine is an element that is needed for the production of thyroid hormone. The human body cannot synthesize iodine, so it is an essential element. The deficiency of iodine leads to enlargement of thyroid a condition called goiter. Hypothyroidism and mental retardation in children and infants is observed if their mothers suffer from iodine deficiency during pregnancy. Before 1920, iodine deficiency was common in Appalachian, north-western US regions, and in most of Canada. Approximately, 40 of the worlds population remains at the risk of iodine deficiency. Goiter: The term goiter refers to the abnormal enlargement of thyroid gland due to deficiency of iodine in diet. It results in swelling in neck. It is important to know that the presence of goiter does not necessarily mean that the thyroid gland is malfunctioning (hypothyroidism). A goiter can also occur in a gland that is producing too much thyroid hormone (hyperthyroidism) or even the correct amount of hormone (euthyroidism). A goiter indicates that there is a condition present which is causing the thyroid to grow abnormally. Fluoride Deficiency and Toxicity. Fluoride Toxicity: Fluoride toxicity or fluoride poisoning is a condition in which more fluoride is taken than the amount required for normal growth, development and metabolism. Fluoride toxicity is characterised by a variety of signs and symptoms. Poisoning most commonly occurs following ingestion of conspicuous amount of fluoride containing products. Symptoms appear within minutes of exposure. Fluoride is found in many common household products e.g. toothpaste, dietary supplements, insecticides, rodenticides etc. fluoride toxicity results: 1. Fluoride deficiency results in Brittle bones or demineralization of bones, Cavities, Weakened tooth enamel. Definition of Transition Elements: "The elements which have partially filled d or f-orbitals either in atomic state or in any one of their possible oxidation states are called transition elements." They are called d-block elements (outer transition elements) and f-block elements (inner transition elements). Why are they called Transition Elements? They are called transition elements because they show properties which are transition in between s-block and p-block elements. Series of Transition Elements: The d-block elements consist of the following four series; 1. First Outer Transition Series: From Scandium (Sc 21) to Zinc (Zn 30) 3d-series. 2. Second Outer Transition Series: From Yttrium (Y 39) to Cadmium (Cd 48) 4d-series. 3. Third Outer Transition Series: From Lanthanum (La 57) to Mercury (Hg 80) 5d-series. 4. Fourth Outer Transition Series: From Actinium (Ac89) onwards 6d-series. The general outermost electronic configuration of the first outer transition series (d-block elements) is: (n-1)d¹¹⁰ns¹². The f-block elements constitute two series, which are: 1. First Inner Transition Series: From Cerium (Ce 58) to Lutetium (Lu 71) which are called Lanthanides 4f-series. 2. Second Inner Transition Series: From Thorium (Th90) to Lawrencium (Lr 103) which are called Actinides 5f-series. Zn-group (IIB): Zn, Cd and Hg are not regarded as transition elements because they have completely filled d-orbitals. It is appropriate to include these in transition elements because they form complexes with ammonia, halide ions and amines and their chemical behaviour is similar to transition elements. Coinage Metals (IB): Coinage metals (Cu,Ag,Au) are transition elements since Cu² has 3d⁹ configuration, Ag has a 4d¹⁰ and Au³ has 5d⁸ configuration, although all these metals have d¹⁰s¹ configuration in atomic states. Typical and non-Typical Transition Elements: The elements of the group II-B and III-B have the electronic distribution as follows: II-B: ₃₀Zn .....4s²3d¹⁰, ₄₈Cd .....5s²4d¹⁰, ₈₀Hg .....6s²5d¹⁰. III-B: ₂₁Sc .....4s²3d¹, ₃₉Y ......5s²4d¹, ₅₇La ....6s²5d¹. It is clear that the elements of II-B i.e. Zn, Cd and Hg do not have partially filled d-subshell in the elemental state or ionic state. They do not show the typical properties of the transition elements to an appreciable extent. The elements of the group III-B are ₂₁Sc, ₃₉Y and ₅₇La. They do not show many of the typical properties of transition elements. In the compound state, they show tri-positive ion i.e.

Sc³, Y³ and La³. In this way, they do not have any electron in d-orbital. For this reason, the elements of group II-B and III-B are non-typical transition elements. 14.1 GENERAL FEATURES. 14.1.1 General Features of Transition Elements. 1. They are all metallic in nature. 2. Some of the transition elements play an important role in the industry. These metals are Ti, Cr, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mo, W, Zr, Nb, Ta and Th etc. 3. They are all hard and strong metal with high melting and boiling points. They are good conductors of heat and electricity. 4. They form alloys with one another and other elements of periodic table as well. 5. With a few exceptions, they show variable oxidation states. 6. Their ions and compounds are coloured in the solid state and the solution state. 7. Transition elements and their compounds are usually used as catalysts in some reactions. 8. In order to understand the mechanical properties of transition elements, we should understand the binding energies (metallic bond). Transition elements are hard, tough, having high density, malleable and ductile. Their melting and boiling temperatures are higher than those of s-block metals. All these properties are a measure of the strength of the metallic bond. Along with electrons of d-orbital, s-orbital electrons are involved in delocalisation. The metallic bond is strong in transition metals. Variation in Binding Energies: When we move from left to the right in any d-block series, the number of unpaired electrons increase up to group V-B; that is vanadium family and VI-B i.e.

Cr family. After that the pairing of electron starts. The unpaired electrons become zero at group II-B. It means that binding forces go on increasing up to V and then decrease after that. This is shown for the elements of 3d series. 14.1.4 Variable Oxidation States. Transition elements are electropositive, so they have positive oxidation states. All 3d series elements show an oxidation state of 2 in addition to higher oxidation states when the electrons of 4s-orbital take part in bonding. They show variable oxidation states. The reason is that they have d-electrons in addition to s-electron for the purpose of bond formation. These elements have several (n-1)d and ns electrons. The energies of (n-1)d and ns orbitals are very close to each other. The (n-1)d electrons are as easily lost as ns electrons. In the highest oxidation states of the first five elements, all s and d-electrons are used for bonding. Among the 3d series, Mn has the maximum oxidation states of 7. The compounds of transition metals are also catalysts. The reason is that the transition metals show variety of oxidation states. In this way, they can form intermediate products with various reactants. They also form interstitial compounds which can adsorb the reacting species. The substances attracted into the magnetic field are called paramagnetic. Paramagnetism is due to the unpaired electrons present in the metals and their compounds. The substances which can be magnetized are called ferromagnetic. For example, Fe, Co and Ni are ferromagnetic. Some substances in which even number of electrons are present, and have paired spins are diamagnetic. They are slightly repelled by magnetic field.

The magnetic moment (μ) is related to the number of unpaired electrons (n) by the equation: μ n(n 2). It is measured in Bohr magneton, BM. By measuring magnetic moment, the nature of transition metal compound and oxidation state of transition metal can be calculated. 14.1.7 Alloy Formation. Alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more than two metals. Transition metals form alloys with each other. Reason: Transition elements have almost similar sizes. Hence atoms of one metal can easily take up positions in crystal lattice of the other. They form substitution alloys among themselves. Examples: 1. Those compounds which contain complex molecules or complex ions capable of independent existence are called coordination compounds or complex compounds. Such compounds are formed by the coordination of an electron pair from donor to metal atom or an ion. Explanation. In order to understand the complex compounds, let us mix aqueous solutions of two substances that is KCN and Fe(CN)₂. When this mixture is evaporated, a new compound is obtained. This compound when dissolved in water ionizes into K and Fe(CN)₆⁴. On this basis, the new compound has been given the formula K₄Fe(CN)₆ (potassium ferrocyanide). 4KCN Fe(CN)₂ K₄Fe(CN)₆. K₄Fe(CN)₆ 4K Fe(CN)₆⁴. Fe(CN)₆⁴ is called complex ion. A complex ion is shown by square brackets. Parts of Complex Compound on the basis of ions. A complex compound is mostly made up of two parts: 1.

Positively charged ion or cation. 2. Negatively charged ion or anion. For example in K₄Fe(CN)₆ , K is a cation and Fe(CN)₆⁴ is the anion. Complex ion as cation. In some of the complexes, the positively charged ion is complex ion. Example: Cu(NH₃)₄SO₄ Cu(NH₃)₄² SO₄². Complex cation. Complex Ion as anion. In some of the complexes, the negatively charged ion is the complex ion. For example: K₄Fe(CN)₆ 4K Fe(CN)₆⁴. Complex anion. 14.2.1 Components of Complex Compounds. A complex compound consists of three components: 1. A positively or negatively charged ion which is not complex. 2. A central metal atom or ion which is usually a transition element. 3. Electron pair donor specie (ligand) which may be negatively charged, positively charged or neutral. a) Central Metal Atom or Ion. A central metal atom or ion is usually a transition element. It is surrounded by a number of ligands. Examples: 1. In K₄Fe(CN)₆, Fe² is the central metal ion. 2. In K₃Fe(CN)₆, Fe³ is the central metal ion. 3. In Cu(NH₃)₄SO₄, Cu² is the central metal ion. 4. In Ag(NH₃)₂Cl, Ag is the central metal ion. b) Ligand. A Substance usually negatively charged, neutral molecule or sometimes positively charged surrounding the central metal atom or ion by donating the electron pair is called ligand. Examples: 1) In K₄Fe(CN)₆ and K₃Fe(CN)₆, CN is the negatively charged ligand. 2) In Cu(NH₃)₄SO₄ and Ag(NH₃)₂Cl, NH₃ is the neutral ligand. Types of Ligands. Depending upon the number of donatable electron pairs, ligands are of many types: 1) Monodentate Ligands. Those ligands which have only one donatable electron pair are called monodentate ligands. Such ligands may be negatively charged, or neutral. Examples: 1) Negatively charged ligands: F, Cl, Br, I, OH, CN. 2) Neutral ligands: H₂O, NH₃, CO. 2) Bidentate Ligands. Those ligands which have two donatable electron pairs are called bidentate ligands. Examples: CO₃², SO₄², (COO)₂², NH₂-NH₂, NH₂-CH₂-CH₂-NH₂. Carbonate ion, Sulphate ion, Oxalate ion, Hydrazine, Ethylenediamine (en). 3) Tridentate Ligands. Those ligands which have three donatable electron pairs are called tridentate ligands. Example: H₂N - CH₂ - CH₂ - NH - CH₂ - CH₂ - NH₂. Diethylenetriamine. 4) Hexadentate Ligands. Those ligands which have six donatable electron pairs are called hexadentate ligands. Example: Ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion (EDTA). c) Coordination Number (CN). It is the total number of electron pairs donated by ligands to the central metal atom or ion. Numerically coordination number represents the total number of the chemical bonds formed between the central metal atom or ion and the donor atoms of the ligands. Example: 1) In K₄Fe(CN)₆, the coordination number of Fe² is six. 2) In Cu(NH₃)₄SO₄, the coordination number of Cu² is four. 3) In Ag(NH₃)₂, the coordination number of Ag is two. 4) In Ni(CO)₄, the coordination number of Ni⁰ is four. d) Coordination Sphere. The central neutral metal atom or ion along with ligand is called coordination sphere. It is usually placed in the square brackets. It may be positively charged, negatively charged or neutral.

Examples: 1) In K₄Fe(CN)₆, the Fe(CN)₆⁴ is the coordination sphere of this complex compound. 2) In Cu(NH₃)₄SO₄, the ion Cu(NH₃)₄² is the coordination sphere of this complex compound. 3) In K₃Fe(CN)₆, the ion Fe(CN)₆³ is the coordination sphere of this complex compound. 4) In Ag(NH₃)₂Cl, the ion Ag(NH₃)₂ is the coordination sphere of this complex compound. 5) In Ni(CO)₄, the Ni(CO)₄ is the coordination sphere of this complex compound. e) Charge on the Coordination Sphere. It is the algebraic sum of charges present on the central metal ion and total charge on the ligands. Example: In K₄Fe(CN)₆ the charge on the coordination sphere can be calculated as follows; Since charge on each ligand is -1. Charge on 6CN -6. Charge on iron 2. So the charge on the coordination sphere -62 -4. 14.2.2 Nomenclature of Complex Compounds. Complex compounds are named according to following rules given by IUPAC. 1) Order of Ions. Cations are named first and then the anions. For example in K₄Fe(CN)₆, we will call K first and then Fe(CN)₆⁴. In naming Cu(NH₃)₄ SO₄, write the name of Cu(NH₃)₄² first and then SO₄². 2) Naming of Ligands. a) The ligands which are negatively charged end in O. For example: F Fluoro, Cl Chloro, Br Bromo, I Iodo, CN Cyano, CH₃COO Acetato, C₂O₄² Oxalato. b) Neutral ligands are called as such. For example: H₂O Aqua, NH₃ Ammine, CO carbonyl. c) Positively charged ligands end in ium. For example: NH₂NH₃ Hydrazinium, NO Nitrosonium. 3) Order of Ligands. All ligands are arranged alphabetically. The numerical prefixes (di, tri, etc) are not considered. 4) More than one same type of Ligands. In order to indicate more than one ligands, use prefixes as di for two, tri for three, tetra for four, penta for five and hexa for six. 5) Termination of name of Metal. If the complex ion is negatively charged then the name of the metal ends in ate. For example: In K₄Fe(CN)₆, the name is potassium hexacyanoferrate (II). 6) Oxidation Number of Metal Ion. The oxidation number of the metal ion is represented by Roman numeral in parenthesis following the name of the metal. 7) More than one Polydentate Ligands. If polydentate ligands are there, then in order to indicate their number, use bis for two, tris for three. Examples: Keeping in view all the above rules the following names are proposed for the complex compounds according to IUPAC system: (a) In the following Complexes, the Complex Ion has Negative Charge. So, the name of the Metal ends in ate. (1) K₄Fe(CN)₆ Potassium hexacyanoferrate (II). (2) K₃Fe(CN)₆ Potassium hexacyanoferrate (III). (3) NaMn(CO)₅ Sodium pentacarbonylmanganate (-I). (4) K₂PtCl₆ Potassium hexachloroplatinate (IV). (5) Na₂Ni(CN)₄ Sodium tetracyanonickelate (II). (b) In the following Complexes the Complex Ion has Positive Charge. So the name of the Metal is called as such: (1) Co(NH₃)₆Cl₃ Hexaamminecobalt (III) chloride. (2) Cr(H₂O)₆Cl₃ Hexaaquochromium (III) chloride. (3) Co(en)₂Cl₂Cl Dichlorobisethylendiamminecobalt (III) chloride. (4) Ni(CO)₄ Tetracarbonylnickel (0). (5) PtCl(NO₂)(NH₃)₄SO₄ Tetraamminechloronitroplatinum (IV) sulphate. (6) Co(NO₂)₃(NH₃)₃ Triamminetrinitrocobalt (III).

14.2.3 Shapes of Complex Ions with Coordination Number 2, 4 and 6. The coordination number shown by metals in complexes is 2 to 9. The most common are 2, 4 and 6. Geometries corresponding to C.Ns 2, 4 and 6 are shown. 1) Coordination Number 2. The complexes having Coordination number 2 are linear, since this geometry provides minimum ligand-ligand repulsion. Cu, Ag and in some cases Hg² form such complexes, e.g. Cu(CN)₂, Cu(NH₃)₂, Ag(NH₃)₂, Ag(CN)₂, Au(CN)₂, Hg(NH₃)₂², Hg(CN)₂. 2) Coordination Number 4. Complexes with Coordination number 4 may be tetrahedral or square planar in geometry, depending upon the type of hybridization. i. Tetrahedral (Sp³-hybridization): ZnCl₄², Cu(CN)₄³, Ni(CO)₄⁰, Zn(CN)₄², Zn(NH₃)₄². ii. Square planar geometry (dsp²-hybridization): Pt(NH₃)₄², PdCl₄², AuCl₄. 3) Coordination Number 6 (d²sp³-hybridization). Complexes with Coordination number 6 are the most common ones formed by transition metal ions. Six ligands in a 6 coordination compound can only be arranged around the central metal ion as octahedron. 14.2.4 Colour of Complexes. When white light is allowed to fall on a complex, the following process may occur: (1) The complex may absorb the whole of white light. In this case complex appears black. (ii) The complex may reflect or transmit the whole light. In this case it appears white. (iii) The complex may absorb some of it and may reflect or transmit the remaining light. Colour is produced in the substances due to absorption and emission of the photon, in visible region of the spectrum. Explanation: When transition elements make the compounds, then the electrons of d-orbital are involved in bonding. When ligands approach the transition metal ion, the d-orbitals split into two energy levels t₂g (lower energy) and eg (higher energy). This is called d-d splitting. The electrons, present in lower d-orbital absorb the photons of energy and are promoted to higher level. The photon, which is involved for the jumping of electron, is responsible for showing definite colour of complex. Basically, unabsorbed light is transmitted and it decides the nature of colour. This transition is called d-d transition. Examples: All simple transition metal ions which possess unpaired electrons are coloured. The colour of the ions is related to the number of unpaired electrons. Sc³ colourless, Ti³ purple, V³ green, Cr³ violet, Mn² pale pink, Fe² green, Fe³ yellow, Co² pink, Ni² green, Cu² blue. Quick Quiz 3. 1. Why do most of the transition metal ions possess a definite colour? 2. When does complex compound appear black? 3. What will be geometry of complex compound having co-ordination number 2, 4 and 6? 4. Give examples of hexadentate and tridentate ligand. 14.3 CHEMISTRY OF SOME IMPORTANT TRANSITION ELEMENTS. Some important transition elements of the first outer transition series are Vanadium, Chromium, Manganese, Iron and copper etc. 14.3.1 Vanadium. It is a silvery white metallic element. It was discovered by Andres Manuel in 1801 in Mexico, considering as a form of Chromium. Later it was re-discovered in 1830 by Nils Gabriel a Swedish chemist. 14.3.1.1 Vanadium's Oxidation States.

Vanadium shows -1,0,1,2,3,4 and 5 oxidation states. Compounds in lower oxidation states are very unstable and act as powerful reducing agents. The most stable oxidation states are 4 and 5. Reason: It uses d-electrons in addition to s-electrons for the purpose of bond formation. The energy of (n-1)d and ns orbital are very close to each other. In higher oxidation states all s- and d-electrons are used for bonding. Examples: V(-1) compounds: V(CN)₅(NO)³, V(CO)₆ etc. V(0) compounds: V(CO)₆, V(dipy)₃ etc. V(1) compounds: V₂O₂², V(dipy)₃ etc. V(2) compounds: VO or V₂O₂, VX₂, VSO₄.7H₂O. V(3) compounds: V₂O₃, V₂(SO₄)₃, V₂S₃ VX₃, VOX etc. V(4) compounds: VO₂ or V₂O₄, VOSO₄, VX₄, VOX₂, (VCl₆)² etc. V(5) compounds: VX₅, V₂O₅, VOX₃ etc. Physical state and dissociation of V₂O₅. It is a yellowish-red poisonous powder having m.p 670 C. It is slightly soluble in H₂O and resulting pale yellow solution in acidic nature. It undergoes reversible dissociation in the temperature ranges 700-1125C. 2V₂O₅ 4VO₂ O₂ (700-1125C). Colour of complexes of Vanadium in different oxidation states. Vanadium shows the following different colours in different oxidation states. 5 Yellow, 4 Blue, 3 Green, 2 Purple. The reduction of V⁵ to V² is taking place in the presence of Zn/HCl. Due to the change in oxidation state of vanadium from 5 to 4, the change of colour also takes place. The green colour in transition state is a mixture of 5 (yellow) and 4 (blue). Further reduction of vanadium from 4 to 3 and 3 to 2 changes the colour from blue to green and then green to purple. Vanadium (V) Oxide (V₂O₅) as an oxidizing agent: (i) Reaction with Hydrochloric acid. V₂O₅ oxidizes HCl into vanadium oxydichloride (VOCl₂) and VCl₄. V₂O₅ 6HCl 2VOCl₂ 3H₂O Cl₂. (ii) Reaction with Nitric acid. The reaction of V₂O₅ with HNO₃ gives meta vanadic acid HVO₃. (iii) Vanadium (V) Oxide as a Catalyst. During the Contact Process for manufacturing sulphuric acid, Sulphur dioxide has to be converted into Sulphur trioxide. This is done by passing Sulphur dioxide and oxygen over a solid vanadium (V) oxide catalyst. 2SO₂ O₂ 2SO₃ (V₂O₅ catalyst). Mechanism. This is a good example of the ability of transition metals and their compounds to act as catalysts because of their ability to change their oxidation state (oxidation number). The Sulphur dioxide is oxidized to Sulphur trioxide by the vanadium (V) oxide. In the process, the vanadium (V) oxide is reduced to vanadium (IV) oxide. SO₂ V₂O₅ SO₃ V₂O₄. The vanadium (IV) oxide is then re-oxidized by oxygen. 2V₂O₄ O₂ 2V₂O₅. Although the catalyst has been temporarily changed during the reaction, at the end it is chemically the same as it started. Quick Quiz 4. 1. How re-oxidation of lower oxidation state of vanadium is prevented? 2. How is V₂O₅ used as a catalyst for the oxidation of SO₂ to SO₃ in contact process? 14.3.2 Chromium. It is a shining, metallic and corrosion resistant element. It was discovered in 1797 by French Chemist Louis Nicolas. 14.3.2.1 The Oxidation of Chromium(III) to Chromium(VI).

When a few drops of sodium hydroxide is added to a solution of hexaaquachromium (III) ions, green precipitate of chromium(III) hydroxide is formed. Cr(H₂O)₆³ 3OH Cr(H₂O)₃(OH)₃ 3H₂O. Green solution, Green ppt. An excess of sodium hydroxide solution when added to Chromium (III) hydroxide Cr(H₂O)₃(OH)₃, green precipitate is dissolved and green solution of hexahydroxo chromate(III) ions is produced. Cr(H₂O)₃(OH)₃ 3OH Cr(OH)₆³ 3H₂O. Green ppt. Green solution. Afterwards this is oxidised by warming it with hydrogen peroxide solution. You eventually get a bright yellow solution containing chromate (VI) ions. The equation for the oxidation stage is as below: 2Cr(OH)₆³ 3H₂O₂ 2CrO₄² 2OH 8H₂O. 14.3.2.2 Chromium(VI) Chemistry. 1. The Chromate(VI)-Dichromate(VI) Equilibrium. Chromates are soluble in water and give brilliant yellow solution. When acid is added to chromate (VI) (CrO₄²) ions, an equilibrium is established and dichromate(Cr₂O₇²) ion is formed. 2CrO₄² 2H Cr₂O₇² H₂O. yellow, Orange. If alkali (hydroxide) is added to the above equilibrium mixture, concentration of hydrogen ion decreases. Therefore, the reaction will move in backward direction and concentration of chromate (VI) ion increases. Cr₂O₇² 2OH 2CrO₄² 4H₂O. Orange, yellow. 2.Reaction with Zn. When K₂CrO₄ is added to the neutral solution of zinc salt, basic zinc chromates Zn(OH)₂ZnCrO₄H₂O is obtained. K₂CrO₄ 2Zn² H₂O Zn(OH)₂ZnCrO₄H₂O 2K. 3. Reaction with acid. Acidified solution of K₂Cr₂O₇ act as an oxidizing agent. 14.3.2.4 Potassium Dichromate (VI) as an Oxidizing Agent. Potassium dichromate(VI) solution acidified with dilute sulphuric acid is commonly used as an oxidising agent. It reduces itself and oxidises other substances. Following is the half ionic equation of acidified dichromate ion; Cr₂O₇² 14H 6e 2Cr³ 7H₂O. 1. The Reduction of Acidified Dichromate (VI) ion with Zinc. For the reduction from 6 to 3: Cr₂O₇² 14H 3Zn 2Cr³ 7H₂O 3Zn². For the reduction from 3 to 2: 2Cr³ Zn 2Cr² Zn². 2. Reaction with Oxalic Acid. When acidified solution of potassium dichromate is added to oxalic acid, it oxidises oxalic acid to carbon dioxide and reduces itself from 6 to 3 in chromium sulphate. K₂Cr₂O₇ 4H₂SO₄ 3(COOH)₂ K₂SO₄ Cr₂(SO₄)₃ 6CO₂ 7H₂O. 3. Reaction with Mohrs Salt. Mohrs salt is a double salt (NH₄)₂SO₄FeSO₄6H₂O. Acidified solution of potassium dichromate oxidises Fe of Mohrs salt from 2 to 3. K₂Cr₂O₇ 7H₂SO₄ 6(NH₄)₂SO₄FeSO₄6H₂O K₂SO₄ Cr₂(SO₄)₃ 43H₂O 3Fe₂(SO₄)₃ 6(NH₄)₂SO₄. Quick Quiz 5. 1. How is dichromate ion converted into chromate and vice versa? 2. Acidified solution of potassium dichromate acts as an oxidising agent. Explain with the help of examples. 14.3.3. Manganese. It is a silvery white metallic element. It was first isolated by a Swedish chemist John Gihan in 1774. 14.3.3.1 The Oxidation States. Manganese can exist in a number of oxidation states. The most stable oxidation states are 2, 4 or 7. 14.3.3.2 Potassium Manganate(VII) as an Oxidizing Agent. KMnO₄ is a powerful oxidizing agent. The course of reaction depends on whether the oxidation takes place in alkaline, neutral or acidic solution. i) In alkaline Medium: In alkaline solution Mn of MnO₄ ion is first reduced from 7 to 6 and then to insoluble MnO₂ (Mn 4).

The solution first changes from purple (due to MnO₄) to green (due to MnO₄²) and finally it becomes brown (MnO₂). 2KMnO₄ 2H₂O 2MnO₂ 4KOH 2O. ii) In acidic Medium: In acidic medium (dil.H₂SO₄), MnO₄ ion is reduced to Mn² ion and five nascent oxygen atoms are produced. 2KMnO₄ 3H₂SO₄(dilute) K₂SO₄ 2MnSO₄ 3H₂O 5 O. Ionic equation is shown as: 2MnO₄ 6H 2Mn² 3H₂O 5 O. Potassium manganate(VII) solution is used to find the concentration of all sorts of reducing agents. It is always used in acidic solution. KMnO₄ as an Oxidizing agent. 1. Reaction with iron (II) sulphate. 2KMnO₄ 8H₂SO₄ 10FeSO₄ K₂SO₄ 2MnSO₄ 5Fe₂(SO₄)₃ 8H₂O. 2. Reaction with oxalic acid. Oxalic acid (ethandioic acid) oxidises to carbon dioxide and potassium manganate reduces itself from 7 to 2. This reaction has to be done in hot state. 2KMnO₄ 3H₂SO₄ K₂SO₄ 2MnSO₄ 3H₂O 5O. 3. Reaction with Mohrs Salt. Acidified solution of potassium permanganate oxidises iron (II) to Iron (III) and reduces itself from Mn⁷ to Mn². 2KMnO₄ 7H₂SO₄ 10(NH₄)₂ SO₄FeSO₄6H₂O K₂SO₄ 5Fe₂(SO₄)₃ 2MnSO₄ 10(NH₄)₂ SO₄ 67H₂O. Titration. The potassium manganate(VII) solution is always taken in the burette, and the other solution in the flask is acidified with dilute sulphuric acid. As the potassium manganate(VII) solution is run into the flask, it becomes colourless. The end point is the first faint trace of permanent pink colour in the solution showing that there is a tiny excess of manganate(VII) ions present. Quick Quiz 6. 1. Give half equation for manganate (VII) ion in acid solution. 2. Write equations for the oxidation of oxalic acid by potassium permanganate. 14.3.4 Iron. 14.3.4.1 Oxidation State. Iron exists in two common oxidation states, 2 (Fe²) and 3 (Fe³). In aqueous solution, iron is readily oxidized from Fe² to Fe³. Fe²(aq) Fe³(aq) e. The Fe² ion is thus a reducing agent. Concentrations of Fe² in solution can be determined by titration with oxidizing agents. 14.3.4.2 Catalytic properties of Iron. Iron as Catalyst in the Haber process (Manufacture of ammonia). In Haber Process nitrogen and hydrogen combine to form ammonia. Nitrogen comes from the air (by the fractional distillation of liquid air) and hydrogen is obtained mainly from natural gas (methane) (by Cracking of oil). Iron is used as a catalyst. N₂(g) 3H₂(g) 2NH₃(g) (Fe catalyst). 14.3.4.3 Iron ions as a Catalyst in the reaction between Persulphate ions and Iodide ions. The reaction between persulphate ions (peroxodisulphate ions), S₂O₈², and iodide ions in solution can be catalysed using either iron(II) or iron(III) ions. S₂O₈² 2I 2SO₄² I₂. Mechanism. The reaction takes place in two steps. S₂O₈² 2Fe² 2SO₄² 2Fe³. 2Fe³ 2I 2Fe² I₂. As Fe² ion is regenerated in the second step, so it acts as a catalyst. If we use iron(III) ions, the second of these reactions happens, first. This is a good example of the use of transition metal compounds as catalysts because of their ability to change oxidation state. 14.3.4.4 Reactions of Iron ions in Solution. In water it exists as: The hexaaquairon(II) ion - Fe(H₂O)₆².

The hexaaquairon(III) ion - Fe(H₂O)₆³. (a) Reactions of the Iron ions with Sodium hydroxide. Hydroxide ions from a base such as sodium hydroxide solution remove hydrogen ions from the water ligands attached to the iron (II) ion to form a new complex with formula Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂. This is insoluble in water and a green precipitate is formed. In case of Iron (III) ion reddish brown precipitate of complex with formula Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃ is formed. Iron (II) ions: Fe(H₂O)₆² 2OH Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂ 2H₂O. Hexaaquairon(II)ion, Tetraaquadihydroxoiron(II). Green sol., Green ppt. Iron(III) ions: Fe(H₂O)₆³ 3OH Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃ 3H₂O. Hexaaquairon(III)ion, Triaquatrihydroxoiron(III). Yellow sol., Brown ppt. Oxygen in the air oxidises the iron(II) hydroxide precipitate to iron(III) hydroxide especially around the top of the tube. The darkening of the precipitate comes from the same effect. (b) Reactions of the Iron ions with Ammonia Solution. Ammonia can act as both a base and a ligand. In these cases, it simply acts as a base - removing hydrogen ions from the aqua complex and green precipitates of hydroxide is formed. Reaction of Iron (II) ions: Fe(H₂O)₆² 2NH₃ Fe(H₂O)₄(OH)₂ 2NH₄. The precipitate again changes colour as the iron(II) hydroxide complex is oxidised by the air to iron(III) hydroxide. Reaction of iron(III) ions: Fe(H₂O)₆³ 3NH₃ Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃ 3NH₄. Yellow, Reddish brown ppt. 14.3.4.5 Reactions of the Iron (II) and (III) ions with Carbonate Ions and Thiocyanate ions. There is an important difference here between the behaviour of iron(II) and iron(III) ions. (a) Reaction of Iron(II) ions with carbonate. When Iron (II) ion reacts with carbonate ion, green ppt of Iron(II) carbonate is formed. Fe² CO₃² FeCO₃. (b) Reaction of Iron(III) ions with carbonate. The hexaaquairon(III) ion is sufficiently acidic to react with the weakly basic carbonate ion. If we add sodium carbonate solution to a solution of hexaaquairon(III) ions, Carbonate ions remove hydrogen ion from water ligand to form hydrogen carbonate ion or carbon dioxide and reddish-brown precipitates of hydroxide of iron (III) complex is formed. 2Fe(H₂O)₆³ 3CO₃² 2Fe(H₂O)₃(OH)₃ 3CO₂ 3H₂O. Yellow, Reddish brown ppt. (c) Reaction of Iron(III) ions with Thiocyanate ion. This is identifying test for iron(III) ions in solution. If we add thiocyanate ions, SCN of potassium or ammonium to a solution containing iron(III) ions, we get an intense blood red solution containing the ion Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅². Fe(H₂O)₆³ SCN Fe(H₂O)₅(SCN)² H₂O. Yellow, Blood Red Sol. Quick Quiz 7. 1. Give role of ammonia in reaction of it with iron ion solution. 2. In which form iron ions are present in aqueous solution? 3. Explain the catalytic role of Iron ions in the reaction between per sulphate ion and iodide ion. 4. How thiocyanate ion is used for testing of Fe(III)? 14.3.5 Copper. It is brown red metallic element and is one of the most widely used metal. 14.3.5.1 The Oxidation States. Copper exists in two oxidation states: cuprous or copper (I) (Cu) and cupric or copper(II) (Cu²). Most of the cuprous compounds are usually colourless and diamagnetic as 3d orbital is completely filled (Cu 3d¹⁰).

Most of the anhydrous cupric compounds are colourless while the hydrated cupric compounds are blue due to the formation of hydrated ion, Cu(H₂O)₄² or Cu(H₂O)₆². Solutions of Cu² salts are acidic in nature due to hydrolysis. Cu² H₂O Cu(OH) H. Since the outer most shell of Cu² ion has one unpaired electron (d⁹ configuration), Cu² compounds are paramagnetic. Reaction of Hexaaquacopper(II) ions with Hydroxide Ions. Hydroxide ions from a base such as sodium hydroxide solution remove hydrogen ions from the water ligands attached to the copper ion complex to form blue precipitates of tetraaquadihydroxocoppper(II) complex is formed. Cu(H₂O)₆² 2OH Cu(H₂O)₄(OH)₂ 2H₂O. Reactions of Hexaaquacopper(II) ions with Ammonia Solution. Ammonia as a base. When a few drops of aqueous ammonia is added to hexaaquacopper (II) ion, hydrogen ion of water ligand is removed by ammonia and blue precipitate of hydroxide of copper is formed. In this reaction ammonia acts as a base (Proton acceptor). Cu(H₂O)₆² 2NH₃ Cu(OH)₂(H₂O)₄ 2NH₄. Blue ppt. Ammonia as a ligand. When excess of aqueous ammonia is added to hexaaquacopper (II) ion, precipitate dissolves and deep blue solution of tetraamminecopper (II) ion complex is formed. In this reaction ammonia acts as a ligand. Cu(H₂O)₆² 4NH₃ Cu(NH₃)₄² 6H₂O. deep blue Sol. Reaction of Hexaaquacopper(II) Ions with Carbonate Ions. When carbonate is added to copper (II) ion, blue precipitate of copper (II) carbonate is formed. Cu² CO₃² CuCO₃. Quick Quiz 8. 1. Ammonia acts as a base as well as a ligand. Prove this statement by the reaction with copper ion. 2. When copper ion reacts with carbonate. What will you expect? Which colour of precipitate is formed?
