Describe isomerism in alcohols and phenols. Identify ethers from their formula. The structures of alcohols, phenols and ethers are much closer to water. Alcohols and phenols both contain hydroxyl (OH) group attached to alkyl and phenyl groups, respectively. In ether, both hydrogen atoms of water are replaced by alkyl or phenyl groups. Water Alcohol Phenol Ether 1 ALCOHOLS Aliphatic organic compounds containing hydroxyl group OH, as functional group are called alcohols. Alcohols containing one OH group are called monohydric alcohols and those containing two or more hydroxyl groups are known as polyhydric alcohols. Monohydric alcohol Dihydric alcohol Classification of Monohydric Alcohols Monohydric alcohols are classified into the following three families: (1) Primary alcohols (2) Secondary alcohols and (3) Tertiary alcohols. Examples: Ethyl alcohol (Primary alcohol) Isopropyl alcohol (Secondary alcohol) tert-Butyl alcohol (Tertiary alcohol) 1 Nomenclature: Common System of Naming In common system, alcohols are named by adding the word alcohol after the name of the alkyl group to which the OH group is attached. Ethyl alcohol Benzyl alcohol IUPAC System According to this system: (i) The longest chain of carbon atoms containing the hydroxyl group is selected as the parent hydrocarbon. (ii) The ending e of the parent hydrocarbon (alkane) is replaced by ol. (iii) The position of OH group is indicated by placing the number of carbon to which OH is attached before the name of the alcohol. (iv) The carbon chain bearing OH group is numbered, beginning from that end which would assign the lowest possible number to the carbon atom linked to the OH group. (v) The presence of more than one OH groups is indicated by suffixes -diol, -triol, etc. and repeating the number of carbon atoms to which OH groups are attached. 1,2-ethanediol (Glycol) 1,2,3-propanetriol (Glycerol) (Common names are given in brackets) (vi) In unsaturated alcohol, the hydroxyl group gets lower number than the double bond. 2-butene-1-ol 2 Physical Properties Alcohols up to butanol are generally colorless liquids with characteristic sweet smell and burning taste. They are readily soluble in water. The solubility of alcohols in water is due to hydrogen bonding which is significant in lower alcohols but decreases in higher alcohols. Melting and boiling points of alcohols are higher than corresponding alkanes. This is due to hydrogen bonding which is present in alcohols but absent in alkanes.

(Hydrogen bonding in alcohol) (Hydrogen bonding in water) 3 Structure The carbon-oxygen (C-O) bond in alcohol is formed by sp3-sp3 overlap. The alcohol functional group consists of an O atom bonded to a C atom and an H atom via sigma bonds. Both the C-O and the O-H bonds are polar due to high electronegativity of the O atom. 4 Acidity Due to the electronegativity of the O atoms, alcohols are slightly acidic. The anion derived by the deprotonation of an alcohol is the alkoxide, which is a Lewis base (Nucleophile). Alcohols react with Na (or K) like water to give the alkoxide: 2R-OH 2Na - 2R-ONa H2 2Na 2H-OH - 2NaOH H2 5 Preparations of Alcohols Hydration of Alkenes Alkenes react with water in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid to form alcohol. Alkenes on reaction with cold concentrated sulfuric acid form an alkyl hydrogen sulphate. These alkyl hydrogen sulphates on boiling with water decompose to give corresponding alcohols. Ethyl hydrogen sulphate Ethanol Hydrolysis of Alkyl halides When alkyl halides react with aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide, alcohols are formed. CH3CH2Cl NaOH - CH3CH2OH NaCl Reactions of Grignards reagent with Aldehydes and Ketones Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols can be prepared by the reaction of Grignards reagent with carbonyl compounds. (As discussed in chapter 17) Reduction of Aldehydes and Ketones (a) Catalytic reduction Hydrogenation of aldehydes and ketones in the presence of Ni, Pd or Pt as a catalyst gives alcohols. Aldehyde reduces to primary alcohol and ketone reduces to secondary alcohol. Propanal H2 - Propan-1-ol Butan-2-one H2 - Butan-2-ol (b) Reduction with reducing agents Carbonyl compounds are also reduced to respective alcohols by using reducing agents such as NaBH4 or LiAlH4. Aldehyde LiAlH4 - Primary Alcohol Ketone LiAlH4 - Secondary Alcohol Reaction of RMgX with Esters Esters react with Grignards reagents to form carbonyl compounds. Alkyl methanoate produces an aldehyde while another ester produces a ketone. Aldehyde reacts with another molecule of Grignard reagent to form primary alcohol while ketone produces tertiary alcohol. Alkyl methanoate CH3MgBr - Aldehyde - Secondary alcohol Ester CH3MgBr - Ketone - Tertiary alcohol Reduction of Carboxylic Acids and Esters Carboxylic acids and esters can be reduced to alcohols with the help of reducing agents such as NaBH4 or LiAlH4. Propanoic acid LiAlH4 - Propan-1-ol Methyl propionate LiAlH4 - Propan-1-ol Methanol 6 Reactivity of Alcohols An alcohol reacts with other agents due to the breaking of C-O and O-H bonds. Breaking of these bonds depends upon the nature of the attacking reagent. If a nucleophile attacks, the C-O bond breaks and if an electrophile attacks the O-H bond breaks. Reactivity of alcohols with respect to the cleavage of C-O bond is: Tertiary alcohol Secondary alcohol Primary alcohol. Reactivity of alcohol with respect to O-H bond cleavage is: Primary alcohol Secondary alcohol Tertiary alcohol.

7 Reactions of Alcohols The reactions of alcohols may be divided into four types: a) Reactions in which C-O bond is broken Reaction with HX to give Alkyl Halides In this substitution reaction, the OH group of alcohol is replaced by a halogen atom of hydrogen halide to produce alkyl halide. R-OH H-Br - R-Br H2O Lucas Test: (Test used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols) Alcohols on reaction with Lucas reagent (ZnCl2 / HCl) gives an oily layer of haloalkanes. R-OH H-Cl (ZnCl2) - R-Cl H2O Different alcohols react with Lucas reagent with different rates. Examples with Observations: i. Tertiary alcohols form an oily layer immediately. tert-Butyl alcohol HCl - tert-Butyl Chloride H2O ii. Secondary alcohols form an oily layer in 5 to 10 minutes. Isopropyl alcohol HCl - Isopropyl Chloride H2O iii. Primary alcohols form an oily layer on heating. Ethyl alcohol HCl - Ethyl Chloride H2O Reaction with SOCl2, PX3 to give Alkyl Halides When alcohols react with Thionyl chloride in the presence of pyridine as a solvent it gives alkyl chloride. RCH2OH SOCl2 - RCH2Cl SO2 HCl Alcohols react with Phosphorus Tribromide and Triiodide (PBr3 and PI3) to form corresponding alkyl halides. 3ROH PI3 - 3RI H3PO3 Alkyl bromides and iodides are best prepared by treating alcohols with PBr3 and PI3. Acid catalyzed Dehydration of alcohol When dehydration of alcohol takes place, two different types of products are formed under different set of conditions. Concentrated Sulphuric acid is used as a dehydrating agent. Ethanol (conc. H2SO4, 180C) - Ethene H2O 2 Ethanol (conc. H2SO4, 140C) - Diethyl ether H2O MECHANISM FOR ALCOHOL CONDENSATION TO GIVE AN ETHER Step 1: An acid/base reaction. Protonation of the alcoholic oxygen to make a better leaving group. This step is very fast and reversible. The lone pair on oxygen atom attacks on proton to form an Oxonium ion. Step 2: The oxygen atom of the second alcohol molecule attacks on the Oxonium ion to form another Oxonium ion intermediate. Step 3: The lone pair of oxygen atom of water attacks on Oxonium ion to form an ether. b) Reactions in which O-H bond is broken and oxygen of an alcohol acts as a base Preparation of Esters (Reaction with Carboxylic Acid) When alcohols react with carboxylic acid in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid as a catalyst, they give ester and water. This reaction is known as esterification. CH3COOH C2H5OH - CH3COOC2H5 H2O c) Oxidation of alcohols. Alcohols undergo oxidation easily by alkaline KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7 H2SO4 solutions to give different products. (i) Primary Alcohol: A primary alcohol is first oxidized to an aldehyde, which is further oxidized to a carboxylic acid. CH3CH2OH - CH3CHO - CH3COOH (ii) Secondary Alcohol: A secondary alcohol is oxidized under similar condition to give a ketone which is not further oxidized. 2-Propanol - Acetone (iii) Tertiary Alcohol: A tertiary alcohol is not oxidized by alkaline KMnO4.

When heated with a mixture of K2Cr2O7 and H2SO4, it is dehydrated to form an alkene in the presence of an acid. 2-methyl-2-butanol - 2-methyl-2-butene Cleavage of 1, 2-Diols (Oxidative Cleavage of Diols) 1,2- or vicinal diols are cleaved by the periodic acid, HIO4, into two carbonyl compounds. The reaction is selective for 1,2-diols. This can be used as a functional group test for 1,2-diols. 8 The Sulfur Analogues (Thiols, RSH) Nomenclature: Thiols are the sulfur analogues of alcohols. These are named by adding the suffix thiol to the name of corresponding alkanes. e.g. H3CSH (Thiomethanol) Physical Properties: Hydrogen bonding is much weaker than that in alcohols. Lower boiling points than similar alcohols. Structure: Generally similar to alcohols, but bonds to S are longer and weaker than those to O. The thiol functional group consists of an S atom bonded to a C atom and a H atom via sigma bonds. The S-H bond is less polar than that in alcohols since S is less electronegative than O. Reactivity: Thiols are much more acidic than similar alcohols, e.g. RSH (pKa 10) versus ROH (pKa 16 to 19). Thiols are also much more nucleophilic than similar alcohols, in fact RSH is about as nucleophilic as RO-. Thiols are readily oxidized to S-O systems rather than CS systems. Thiols are commonly oxidized to disulfides, R-S-S-R, a biologically important reaction. Quick Quiz 1 What are monohydric and polyhydric alcohols? Why are some alcohols readily soluble in water? Write general formulas of primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols. How Grignards reagent is used for the preparation of primary alcohols? 2 PHENOLS Introduction First prepared by Runge in 1834. Melting point of phenol is 41C. Boiling point of phenol is 182C. Simplest example is phenol, also known as carbolic acid. "Aromatic compounds containing one or more OH groups, directly attached with carbon of benzene ring, are called phenols". The simplest example is phenol, which is also known as carbolic acid, i.e., C6H5OH; it was first obtained from coal tar by Runge in 1834. Phenol is derived from the old name of benzene (phene), to include the suffix indicating that it possesses a hydroxyl group. Phenols are acidic and important intermediates in the preparation of aryl ethers, C6H5-OR. 1 Nomenclature In IUPAC system, OH group is represented by the name hydroxyl. It is used as a prefix. The benzene part of the molecule is used as a suffix. Some common names, and their IUPAC names are given below: Phenol 1,2-Dihydroxybenzene (Catechol) 1,3-Dihydroxybenzene (Resorcinol) 1,4-Dihydroxybenzene (Hydroquinone) 2-Nitrophenol 4-Nitrophenol 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (Picric acid) 2 Structure The -O-H group consists of an O atom bonded to a sp2-hybridized aromatic C atom and an H atom via sigma bonds. Both the C-O and the O-H bonds are polar due to high electronegativity of the O atom. Conjugation exists between an unshared electron pair on the oxygen and the aromatic ring. Phenol differs from alcohol as: It has shorter carbon-oxygen bond distance. It has more basic hydroxyl oxygen.

It has more acidic hydroxyl proton (-OH) 3 Physical Properties Phenol is a colorless, crystalline, poisonous, solid with characteristic phenolic odor; having melting point of 41C and boiling point of 182C. It is sparingly soluble in water forming pink solution, at room temperature, but completely soluble above 68.5C. It is poisonous and causes blisters on the skin. It is used as disinfectant. It has a distinctive odour. 4 Comparison of Acidity of Phenol, alcohol and Carboxylic acid: Phenols are more acidic (pKa 10) than alcohols (pKa 16 - 20), but less acidic than carboxylic acids (pKa 5). The Acidic strength of alcohols, phenols, and carboxylic acid depends upon the stability of their conjugate bases alkoxide, phenoxide and carboxylate ion, respectively. Alcohol - Alkoxide ion H3O Phenol - Phenoxide ion H3O Carboxylic acid - Carboxylate ion H3O Carboxylate ion is a more stable conjugate base than phenoxide ion and alkoxide ions because the negative charges spread from oxygen to oxygen. Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols. In phenoxide ion, the negative charge on oxygen atom is delocalized over the whole ring, which makes it stable. In alcohol the negative charge on oxygen atom of alkoxide ion is localized and is least stable and stronger base. The acidic strength of carboxylic acid, phenol and alcohol are in the order of: RCOOH C6H5OH ROH. Effect of substituents on the acidity of Phenols Electron attracting (withdrawing) substituents tend to disperse the negative charge of the phenoxide ion, thus stabilizing the ion and increasing the acidity of phenols. Electron releasing substituents tend to intensify the charge, destabilize the ion and decrease its acidity. For example, nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol. Methyl phenol is less acidic than phenol. 5 Preparations of Phenols: Reaction of Sodium salt of Benzene Sulfonic Acid with Sodium Hydroxide Sodium benzene sulphonate on fusion with strong alkali like NaOH at 573 K gives sodium phenoxide. On further treatment with H2SO4 / HCl, it gives phenol. Sodium benzene sulphonate NaOH - Sodium phenoxide - Phenol Base Hydrolysis of Chlorobenzene (Dows Method) Chlorobenzene is hydrolyzed by heating with 10 NaOH at 623K and under high pressure to form sodium phenoxide. On further treating with HCl, it gives phenol. Chlorobenzene NaOH - Sodium Phenoxide - Phenol Acidic Oxidation of Cumene Cumene is oxidized by atmospheric oxygen in the presence of metal catalyst, into cumene hydroperoxide. The cumene hydroperoxide is converted into phenol through an acid catalyzed rearrangement. Cumene O2 - Cumene hydroperoxide - Phenol Acetone Hydrolysis of Benzene diazonium Chloride. Benzene diazonium chloride can be converted into phenols using H2O / H2SO4 / heat. Benzene diazonium chloride can be prepared by the reaction of aniline with nitrous acid (HNO2) in the presence of hydrochloric acid. If temperature is greater than 10 C, hydrolysis of benzene diazonium chloride takes place and Phenol is formed. Aniline - Benzene diazonium chloride - Phenol 6 Reactivity of phenol Reactivity of phenol is due to the OH group and the benzene ring.

The presence of OH group on benzene ring increases electron density on ortho and para position because of its electron donating effect. Therefore, it is ortho, para directing group. 7 Reactions of Phenol A. Reaction due to Benzene ring (Electrophilic Substitution reactions of Phenol) Halogenation Phenol on reaction with bromine in the presence of nonpolar solvents (CCl4 or CS2) gives a mixture of ortho and para bromophenol. Phenol Br2 - 2-bromophenol and 4-bromophenol Phenol on reaction with bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6 tribromophenol. (This is the test of phenol) Phenol Br2 (aq) - 2,4,6 tribromophenol (White ppt) Nitration Phenol reacts with dilute nitric acid to give a mixture of ortho and para nitrophenol. Phenol HNO3 - 2-nitrophenol and 4-nitrophenol With concentrated nitric acid, 2,4,6 trinitrophenol (Picric acid) is formed. Phenol 3HNO3 - 2,4,6 trinitrophenol (picric acid) 3H2O Sulphonation Sulphonation of phenol with concentrated sulphuric acid results in the formation of ortho and para hydroxy benzene sulphonic acids. At low temperature (20C) the ortho isomer is the major product whereas at high temperature (100C) para isomer is formed. Phenol H2SO4 (15-20C) - 2-hydroxy benzene sulphonic acid Phenol H2SO4 (100C) - 4-hydroxy benzene sulphonic acid Nitrosation Phenol reacts with nitrous acid to form 4-nitrosophenol along with a small amount of 2-nitrosophenol. 4-nitrosophenol exhibits tautomerism and forms yellow crystals of para benzoquinone monoxime. B. Reaction due to -OH group (Acidic Character of Phenol) Reaction with Sodium Metal (Formation of salts) Phenol is acidic and reacts with Sodium or sodium hydroxide to form salts. Phenol 2Na - Sodium Phenoxide H2 Phenol NaOH - Sodium Phenoxide H2O Phenol is a weak acid. It has no action on litmus paper and cannot evolve carbon dioxide from carbonates and bicarbonates. Carboxylation (Kolbe-Schmitt reaction) The reaction of sodium salt of phenol with CO2 is called Kolbe reaction. It is the carbonation of phenol. At low temperature, sodium salicylate (sodium-o-hydroxy benzoate) and at high temperature sodium-p-hydroxy benzoate are formed. Phenol NaOH CO2 - Sodium salicylate Sodium salicylate acid - Salicylic acid Carbon of CO2 acts as electrophilic centre in this reaction. Acidification of sodium salicylate gives corresponding hydroxy benzoic acids. C. Oxidation Phenols are reactive towards oxidizing agents. The oxidation takes place through several steps eventually destroying the ring. 8 Differences between Alcohols and Phenol The main differences between alcohols and phenols are as follow; Alcohol Alcohols are hydroxyl derivatives of alkanes. The compounds in which one hydrogen of water is replaced by an alkyl group. The general formula of alcohol is R-OH. Lower alcohols are generally colorless liquids. Alcohols have a characteristic sweet smell and burning taste. They are readily soluble in water but solubility decreases in higher alcohols. Alcohol reacts with other reagents in two ways, either in which C-O bond breaks or in which O-H bond breaks. Phenol Phenols are derivatives of benzene. The compounds in which one hydrogen of water is replaced by an aryl group. The general formula of phenol is C6H5OH. It is also known as carbolic acid.

They are colorless, crystalline, deliquescent solids. They have characteristic phenolic odor. Its melting point is 41C. Phenols are more acidic (pKa 10) than alcohols. (pKa 16 - 20). It is sparingly soluble in water forming pink solution at room temperature but completely soluble above 68.5C. Phenolate ions have resonance structures but alcohols do not have such type of structures. Quick Quiz 2 What are phenols? What is the effect of substituents on acidity of phenols? How is phenol prepared from cumene? 3 ETHERS 1 Nomenclature Common Names In Common system of Naming: In common system of naming, simple and mixed (or unsymmetrical) ethers are named by naming the two groups bonded to oxygen followed by the word ether. Dimethyl ether Phenyl methyl ether (Anisole) Isopropyl ethyl ether IUPAC System In IUPAC system of naming, simple ethers are named by naming the two groups linked by oxygen atom followed by the word ether. Dimethyl ether (Methoxy methane) Diethyl ether (Ethoxy ethane) Mixed ethers are named as alkoxy derivatives of hydrocarbons. Methoxyethane 2-Methoxy butane 2 Preparation Ethers are prepared by the following methods: (i) Williamson synthesis (conversion of alcohols to ethers) The reaction of primary alcohol with sodium gives an alkoxide. 2CH3CH2OH 2Na - 2CH3CH2ONa Alkoxide when treated with alkyl halide, forms ether. CH3CH2ONa CH3CH2Cl - CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3 NaCl (ii) Dehydration of alcohols: Ether can be prepared by heating an excess of alcohol with conc. H2SO4 at 140C. For example, ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at 140C gives diethyl ether but at 180C it gives alkene. 2CH3CH2OH - CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3 H2O Different alcohols on dehydration give mixture of ethers. For example, when methanol and ethanol are mixed and heated with conc. H2SO4, it gives mixture of ethers. Ethanol Methanol - Diethyl ether Dimethyl ether Ethyl Methyl ether (iii) Reaction of alkyl halides with dry Ag2O: When alkyl halides are heated with dry silver oxide, ethers are produced. 2R-X Ag2O - R-O-R 2AgX Ethyl chloride Ag2O - Diethyl ether 2AgCl 3 Physical Properties Ethers are colorless, low boiling, highly inflammable compounds. Their chemical inactivity and ability to dissolve fats, oil, gum and other organic compounds make them very useful as a solvent. Lower ethers act as anaesthetics. 4 Reactions of ether Reaction with H-Br The oxygen atom of an ether molecule possesses unshared electron pair which accepts a proton of H-Br to form oxonium ion. No further reaction takes place. Reaction with H-I The oxygen atom of an ether molecule possesses unshared electron pair, which accepts a proton of H-I to form oxonium, which reacts with iodide ion (I-) to form R-OH and RI. In this reaction ether acts as a Lewis base (electron donor). Diethyl ether reacts with HI to form C2H5-OH and C2H5I. C2H5-O-C2H5 HI - C2H5-OH C2H5I Quick Quiz 3 What are ethers? How is diethyl ether prepared from ethyl alcohol? Explain the reaction of diethyl ether with HI. Society, Technology and Science Antiseptics and Disinfectants Antiseptics and disinfectants are an essential part of infection control practices.

Antiseptics An antiseptic is a substance which inhibits the growth and development of microorganisms. For practical purposes, antiseptics are thought of as topical agents for application to skin, mucous membrane and inanimate objects. Their uses include cleansing of skin and wound, surgical procedures and routine disinfection. Disinfectants are widely used in the health care, food and pharmaceutical sectors to prevent unwanted micro-organisms from causing disease. Disinfectant chemicals disrupt significant cellular structures or processes in order to kill or eliminate micro-organisms. An effective Anesthetic Three of the most important early anesthetics were nitrous oxide (dinitrogen oxide, N2O), ether (ethoxyethane, CH3CH2OCH2CH3) and chloroform (trichloromethane, CHCl3). Nitrous oxide is non-toxic and non-flammable, but it only produces light anesthesia. Chloroform produces deep anesthesia and is non-flammable, but it is toxic and carries the risk of liver damage.

aldehydeandsketones2ndchemfed.txt After completing this lesson, you will be able to: Explain nomenclature and structure of aldehydes and ketones. Discuss the preparation of aldehydes and ketones by ozonolysis of alkene, hydration of alkynes, oxidation of alcohols and Friedel Craft's acylation of aromatics. Describe reactivity of aldehydes and ketones and their comparison. Describe acid and base catalyzed nucleophilic addition reaction of aldehydes and ketones. Discuss the chemistry of aldehydes and ketones by their reduction to alcohols and hydrocarbons, by using carbon nucleophiles, nitrogen nucleophiles and oxygen nucleophiles. Describe oxidation reactions of aldehydes and ketones. Describe isomerism in aldehydes and ketones. Organic compounds containing the carbonyl functional group are called aldehydes and ketones. Aldehydes: In aldehydes, the C atom of carbonyl group is attached to at least one H atom. General formula: CnH2nO or RCHO. Ketones: In ketones, the C atom of carbonyl group is attached to two alkyl or aryl groups. General formula: CnH2nO or RCOR'. An aldehyde may be represented by the general structure: R-CHO. A ketone may be represented by the general structures: RCOR', R-CO-R', Ar-CO-Ar, Ar-CO-R. Examples: Formaldehyde (HCHO), Acetaldehyde (CH3CHO), Benzaldehyde (C6H5CHO). Acetone (CH3COCH3), Acetophenone (C6H5COCH3), Benzophenone (C6H5COC6H5). 1 NOMENCLATURE Aldehydes: (a) Common names For naming substituted aldehyde, the chain is labeled by using alpha, beta, gamma, etc. The carbon next to the carbon of the carbonyl group is indicated by alpha and so on. Formaldehyde Acetaldehyde Alpha-methyl propionaldehyde Beta-chloro-alpha-methyl propionaldehyde. (b) IUPAC Names Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms containing aldehydic group as parent chain. The ending e of the alkane is replaced by al. The numbering starts from the carbon atom of the carbonyl group. The carbon atom of aldehyde group is always carbon number 1. The position of the substituent is indicated by numbers which are written before their names. Examples: Propanal 2-Methyl propanal 4-Bromo-4-methyl pentanal. Ketones: (a) Common names Ketones are named by adding the word ketone after writing the names of alkyl or aryl groups linked to carbonyl carbon in alphabetical order. Dimethyl Ketone (Acetone) Ethyl methyl Ketone. Substituted ketones are named by labelling the chain using alpha, beta, gamma, etc. The carbon next to the carbonyl group is indicated by alpha and so on. Alpha-hydroxy-methyl ethyl ketone Methyl beta-chloroethyl ketone. (b) IUPAC Names The longest chain containing the carbonyl group is taken as parent hydrocarbon. The ending e of hydrocarbon is replaced by one. The numbering starts from the end that gives the carbonyl carbon the lower number. In cyclic ketones, carbonyl carbon is number 1. The positions of substituent are indicated by numbers before their names. Examples: 2-Methyl-3-hexanone 4-Bromo-2-butanone 3-Methyl cyclohexanone 2,6-Dimethyl cyclohexanone. Quick Quiz 1 (i) Draw structures of the following compounds: (a) 2-Hexenal (b) 2,4-Dimethyl pentanal (c) 4-Bromo-2-butanone. 2 PHYSICAL PROPERTIES The polar nature of the carbonyl (CO) group (due to the electronegativity difference of the two atoms) means dipole-dipole interactions will occur. Though CO cannot form hydrogen bonds to each other, the CO can accept hydrogen bonds from hydrogen bond donors (e.g. water, alcohols).

The implications of these effects are: Higher melting and boiling points compared to analogous alkanes. Lower boiling points than analogous alcohols. More soluble than alkanes but less soluble than alcohols in aqueous media. 3 PREPARATIONS OF ALDEHYDES AND KETONES 1 Ozonolysis of Alkenes Alkenes react with ozone in the presence of dry ether to form ozonide. These ozonides are decomposed with zinc and boiling water to form aldehydes and ketones. Mechanism: Alkene O3 - Ozonide - (Zn/H2O) - Aldehydes/Ketones. If the alkene has no branching at the double bond then it produces aldehydes. This reaction is used to locate the position of double bond. 2 Hydration of Alkynes When alkynes are treated with water in the presence of H2SO4 and HgSO4, aldehydes and ketones are formed. The vinyl alcohol, that is initially produced, rearranges. Acetylene gives acetaldehyde. Propyne gives acetone. This reaction is useful for preparing methyl aryl ketones. 3 Oxidation of Primary and Secondary Alcohols Primary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes by warming with acidic potassium dichromate solution, while secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones. Butanol - Butanal. Benzyl alcohol - Benzaldehyde. 2-Propanol - Acetone. 4 Friedel-Crafts Acylation of Benzene Aromatic ketones can be obtained by treating benzene with acid halide (-COCl) in the presence of anhydrous AlCl3. Benzene R-COCl - Alkyl aryl ketone HCl. 4 REACTIVITY The double bond of the carbonyl group (CO) has a sigma bond and a pi bond. As oxygen is more electronegative, it attracts the pi-electrons to itself. Therefore, the CO bond is strongly polar. Hence, carbonyl carbon is electrophilic and is likely to be attacked by a nucleophile like CN-. Therefore, carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition reactions. 1 Relative Reactivity of Aldehydes and Ketones The reactivity of aldehydes and ketones is due to two important resonance structures which have charge separation with a positive carbon and negative oxygen. In general, the reactivity order towards nucleophiles is: aldehydes ketones. The substituents have two contributing factors on the reactivity at the carbonyl carbon: The size of the substituents attached to the CO. Larger groups will tend to sterically hinder the approach of the nucleophile. The electronic effect of the substituent. Alkyl groups are weakly electron donating so they make the carbon in the carbonyl less electrophilic and therefore less reactive towards nucleophiles. 5 REACTIONS OF ALDEHYDES AND KETONES 1 Nucleophilic Addition Reactions There are two types of nucleophilic addition reactions of carbonyl compounds: I- Base catalyzed nucleophilic addition reaction. II- Acid catalyzed nucleophilic addition reaction. I- Base Catalyzed Nucleophilic Addition Reaction A base catalyzed nucleophilic addition reaction takes place with a strong nucleophilic reagent. The base reacts with the reagent and generates the nucleophile. The addition is initiated by the attack of a nucleophile on the electrophilic carbon of the carbonyl group. General Mechanism: Base H-Nu - Nu- H2O. Nu- CO - Intermediate - Product OH-. There are five types of base catalyzed nucleophilic addition reactions of carbonyl compounds: Addition of hydrogen cyanide. Addition of Grignards reagent. Addition of sodium bisulphite. Condensation reactions.

Haloform reactions. Addition of hydrogen cyanide Hydrogen cyanide adds to aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins. The acid HCN is obtained from the reaction of sodium cyanide and HCl. NaCN HCl - HCN NaCl. The reaction is used in the synthesis of a hydroxy acid that contains one carbon atom more than the number of carbon atoms in the starting aldehydes or ketones. Formaldehyde - Formaldehyde cyanohydrin. Acetaldehyde - Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin. Acetone - Acetone cyanohydrin. Mechanism: The base (OH-) generates cyanide ions which act as nucleophile. The hydroxide ion reacts with hydrogen cyanide to produce cyanide ions, which in turn react with carbonyl compound. Addition of Grignards reagent Grignards reagents add to aldehydes and ketones to form adduct which on hydrolysis with a dilute mineral acid gives alcohols. (Chapter 17) Addition of sodium bisulphite Aldehydes and small methyl ketones react with a saturated aqueous solution of sodium bisulphite to form a crystalline white precipitate of sodium bisulphite adduct. Formaldehyde - Formaldehyde bisulphite addition product. Acetaldehyde - Acetaldehyde bisulphite addition product. Acetone - Acetone bisulphite addition product. The bisulphite adduct on heating with a dilute mineral acid (HCl or H2SO4) regenerates the parent aldehyde or ketone. The reaction is used for the separation and purification of carbonyl compounds from non-carbonyl compounds such as alcohols. Condensation reactions The reaction in which two molecules of the same or different compounds combine to form a new compound with or without the elimination of a small molecule like H2O or NH3 are called condensation reactions. (a) ALDOL CONDENSATION Definition: Aldol condensation is a reaction in which two molecules of same or different carbonyl compound containing alpha hydrogen (hydrogen attached to the carbon atom next to carbonyl group) combine to form aldol or ketol, which usually loses water molecule. Mild Alkaline conditions: Aldol condensation takes place under mild alkaline conditions. For example, in the presence of sodium carbonate, sodium bicarbonate, barium hydroxide, dilute sodium hydroxide or an alkoxide in low concentration. Types: Aldol condensation can occur: (i) Between two aldehydes (identical or different) (ii) Between an aldehyde and a ketone (iii) Between two ketones (identical or different). (i) Condensation between two aldehydes: Ethanal Ethanal - Aldol (3-hydroxybutanal). On heating aldol loses a molecule of water to form an alpha, beta-unsaturated aldehyde. Aldol - Crotonaldehyde (2-butenal). (ii) Condensation between aldehyde and ketone: Ethanal Propanone - 4-Hydroxy-2-pentanone (ketol). Mechanism of Aldol Condensation: Following steps are involved in aldol condensation. (1) Removal of a proton from alpha-carbon of aldehyde/ketone by base: (Formation of nucleophile) (2) Attack of nucleophile on carbonyl carbon to form alkoxide ion: (Formation of alkoxide ion) (3) Removal of proton from water by alkoxide ion: (Formation of aldol) (b) CANNIZZAROS REACTION Aldehydes having no alpha-hydrogen atoms undergo Cannizzaros reaction. It is a disproportionation (same element is being oxidized as well as reduced) reaction. Two molecules of the aldehyde are involved. Formaldehyde Conc. KOH - Methanol Potassium formate. Benzaldehyde Conc. NaOH - Benzyl alcohol Sodium benzoate.

The reaction is carried out with 50 aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide/potassium hydroxide at room temperature. Mechanism of Cannizzaros Reaction: The hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile. It attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon to form a complex anion. The anion transfers a hydride ion to a second molecule of formaldehyde. The methoxide ion acts as a base and abstracts a proton from formic acid to form methanol and formate ion. The formate ion in the presence of alkali gives a salt of acid. Haloform Reaction (Iodoform test) The carbonyl compounds containing CH3CO- group on reaction with iodine in the presence of alkali such as an aqueous NaOH forms a yellow crystalline solid called iodoform (CHI3). Chemical Equation: Organic compound I2 NaOH - CHI3 RCOONa NaI H2O. This test is given by alcohols, aldehydes and ketones. Examples: In primary alcohol only ethanol will give this test positive. In secondary alcohols having H3C-CH(OH)- group will give this test. This test is not given by tertiary alcohol. In aldehydes only ethanal will give this test positive. In ketones only methyl ketones will give this test. Note: Iodoform test is used for distinguishing methyl ketones from other ketones. It is also used to distinguish ethanol from methanol and other primary alcohols. It can be used to distinguish acetaldehyde from other aldehydes. II- ACID CATALYZED NUCLEOPHILIC ADDITION REACTIONS Acid increases the electrophilic character of the carbonyl carbon and the attack of the weaker nucleophile on the electrophilic carbon becomes easy. General mechanism: These are of three types: Polymerization of aldehydes. Nucleophilic addition of ammonia derivatives with aldehydes/ketones. Addition of alcohols with aldehydes. Polymerization of aldehydes: Both formaldehyde and acetaldehyde polymerize in the presence of dil. H2SO4 to give metaformaldehyde and paraldehyde respectively. Nucleophilic addition reaction of carbonyl compounds with ammonia derivatives: Aldehydes and ketones react with ammonia derivatives, G-NH2, to form compounds containing the group CN-G and water. The reaction is known as condensation reaction or addition-elimination reaction because water is lost after addition occurs. General Reaction: Where G -OH, -NH2, -NHC6H5, -NHCONH2, etc. (i) Reaction with hydroxylamine: Aldehydes and ketones react with hydroxylamine to form oximes in the presence of an acid. Ethanal - Ethanal oxime. Propanone - Propanone oxime. (ii) Reaction with hydrazine: Aldehydes and ketones react with hydrazine to form hydrazone in the presence of an acid. Acetaldehyde - Acetaldehyde hydrazone. Acetone - Acetone hydrazone. (iii) Reaction with Phenyl hydrazine: Aldehydes and ketones react with phenylhydrazine to form phenylhydrazones in the presence of an acid. Where R may be alkyl group or H atom. (iv) Reaction with 2,4-dinitrophenyl hydrazine: Aldehydes and ketones react with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) in the presence of an acid as a catalyst to form a yellow or orange precipitate of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. This is the identifying test of aldehydes and ketones. Where R and R' may be Alkyl group or H atom. Mechanism of the Reaction of ammonia derivatives: Step (i) Protonation of oxygen of the carbonyl group.

Step (ii) Nucleophilic attack of nitrogen of ammonia derivative on the electrophilic positively charged carbon and deprotonation of the adduct. Step (iii) Protonation of oxygen of hydroxyl group followed by the removal of water. Addition of alcohols with aldehydes: Aldehydes combine with alcohols in the presence of hydrogen chloride gas to form acetals. The hydrogen chloride acts as a catalyst. Acetaldehyde 2 C2H5OH - 1,1-Diethoxyethane H2O. The reaction may be used to protect the aldehyde group against alkaline oxidizing agents. To regenerate aldehyde, the acetal is hydrolyzed in the presence of an acid. Note: Ketones do not react under these conditions. 2 Reduction of Aldehydes and Ketones Reduction to Hydrocarbons: Aldehyde and ketone can be reduced to a saturated hydrocarbon by the following two methods: (i) Clemmensen Reduction (acidic conditions): In this reaction Zn(Hg) in HCl reduces the CO group of an aldehyde or ketone into -CH2- group. Ethanal - Ethane. Propanal - Propane. (ii) Wolff-Kishner Reduction (basic conditions): In this reaction NH2NH2 / KOH / ethylene glycol reduces the CO of an aldehyde or ketone into -CH2- group. These reduction methods do not reduce CC, CC or -CO2H. Hydride Reductions of Aldehydes and Ketones: When reducing agents such as sodium tetrahydridoborate (NaBH4) or Lithium tetrahydridoaluminate (LiAlH4) are added to aldehydes or ketones, they are converted to primary or secondary alcohols. The BH4- and the AlH4- ion acts as a source of H- ion (hydride ion). NaBH4 is a weak reducing agent while LiAlH4 is a strong reducing agent. During this reaction carbonyl group (CO) of aldehyde and ketone is converted to CH(OH). Methanal - Methanol. Ketone - Secondary Alcohol. Ethanal - Ethanol. Propanone - 2-Propanol. Cyanohydrin Formation (Using Carbon Nucleophiles): Cyanide ion adds to aldehydes or ketones to give a cyanohydrin. The reaction is usually carried out using NaCN or KCN with HCl. HCN is a fairly weak acid, but very toxic. Step 1: Addition of Cyanide to an Aldehyde. The nucleophilic C in the cyanide adds to the electrophilic C in the polar carbonyl group, electrons from the CO move to the electronegative O creating an intermediate alkoxide. Step 2: An acid/base reaction. Protonation of the alkoxide oxygen creates the cyanohydrin product. Using Nitrogen Nucleophiles: Primary amines, R-NH2 or ArNH2, undergo nucleophilic addition with aldehydes or ketones to give carbinolamines which then dehydrate to give substituted imines. The reactions are usually carried out in an acidic buffer to activate the CO and facilitate dehydration but without inhibiting the nucleophile. Using Oxygen Nucleophiles: Aldehydes and ketones react with water to give 1,1-geminal diols known as hydrates. In general, hydrates are not stable enough to be isolated as the equilibrium shifts back to starting materials. 4 Oxidation Reactions I. Oxidation of Aldehydes: They are easily oxidized by strong oxidizing agents such as K2Cr2O7/ H2SO4, KMnO4/ H2SO4, and dilute nitric acid. Acetaldehyde - Acetic acid. Propionaldehyde - Propionic acid. II. Oxidation of Ketones: Ketones are only oxidized by strong oxidizing agents such as K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, KMnO4/H2SO4 and conc. HNO3.

The carbon atom joined to the smaller number of hydrogen atoms is oxidized. In case of symmetrical ketones only one carbon atom adjacent to the carbonyl group is oxidized and a mixture of two carboxylic acids is always obtained. Acetone - Acetic acid Formic acid. However, in case of unsymmetrical ketones, the carbon atom joined to the carbonyl group with the smaller number of hydrogen atoms is preferentially oxidized and the carbonyl group remains with the smaller alkyl group. Butanone - Acetic acid Acetic acid. Tests used to distinguish aldehydes and ketones: Weak oxidizing agents like Tollens reagent, Fehlings solution and Benedicts solution easily oxidize aldehydes to carboxylic acids. Ketones are not oxidized by these weak oxidizing agents. Test 1: Fehling Solution Test: Fehlings solution (a mild oxidizing agent) is an alkaline solution of Cu2 ions and sodium or potassium tartrate. When Fehling solution is added to an aldehyde, a red ppt of Cu2O is formed. This test is not given by ketones. Aldehyde oxidizes to salt of carboxylic acid and Cu2 reduces itself to form Cu. Test 2: Tollens Test (Silver mirror test): When Tollen's reagent (aqueous Silver nitrate, ammonia and sodium hydroxide) is added to an aldehyde, a silver mirror (Ag) is formed. This test is not given by ketones. This test is called silver mirror test. Society, Technology and Science Sugar Glucose and Fructose - Naturally occurring carbonyl compounds. Glucose - An example of aldehyde: The two forms are readily inter-converted and in aqueous solution about 1 of glucose molecules exist in the open chain form. This form carries an aldehyde group, so glucose has several properties typical of an aldehyde. It is sometimes called an aldose. Thus, in addition to the condensation reaction already mentioned, glucose shows the reducing properties typical of an aldehyde. The reduction of Fehlings solution (or Benedicts solution) is a standard test for glucose and other reducing sugars. Fructose - An example of ketone: The open chain form of fructose is a ketose. Under the conditions of the tendency of the carbonyl group to undergo nucleophilic addition. alkylhaliandamine2ndchemfed.txt After completing this lesson, you will be able to: Name alkyl halides using IUPAC system. Discuss the structure and reactivity of RX. Describe isomerism in alkyl halides and amines. 1 ALKYL HALIDE Introduction Alkyl halides are the compounds in which one hydrogen atom of alkanes has been replaced by a halogen atom. They are also known as halogen derivatives of alkanes. The general formula of alkyl halide is R-X. Types They may be mono, di, tri or poly haloalkanes depending upon the number of halogen atoms present in the molecule. Monohaloalkane Dihaloalkane Trihaloalkane Classification of Alkyl Halides Alkyl halides are classified into primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl halides. (i) Primary Alkyl Halides: Alkyl halide in which halogen atom is attached with a primary carbon are called primary alkyl halide. Primary carbon is the carbon to which one or no alkyl group is attached. Methyl chloride (Chloromethane) Ethyl chloride (Chloroethane) n-Propyl chloride (Chloropropane) (ii) Secondary Alkyl Halides: Alkyl halide in which halogen atom is attached with a secondary carbon atom is called secondary alkyl halide. Secondary carbon is carbon to which two alkyl groups are attached. Iso-Propyl chloride (2-Chloropropane) Sec-Butyl chloride (2-Chlorobutane) (iii) Tertiary Alkyl Halides: Alkyl halides, in which halogen atom is attached to a tertiary carbon is called tertiary alkyl halide. Tertiary carbon is carbon to which three alkyl groups are attached. t-Butyl chloride (2-Methyl-2-chloropropane) Nomenclature Alkyl halides are named according to the following systems: (i) Common System of naming. (ii) IUPAC System of naming. (i) Common System of Naming: This method consists in first writing the name of alkyl group to which halogen atom is attached and then writing the name of halide ion, e.g., Structural formula of Ethyl chloride is CH3CH2Cl. When all the carbons of alkyl group of primary alkyl halides are in a straight chain, the prefix n- is used before the name which indicates normal. e.g, n-butyl bromide (ii) IUPAC System of naming. According to this system alkyl halides are named as derivatives of alkanes. The following rules are observed for this purpose: (1) Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atom containing halogen atom. (ii) Prefix halo i.e., Chloro for Cl, Bromo for Br, etc, is used before the name of hydrocarbon. (iii) Positional numbers are used to indicate halogen and other substituent by the usual methods.

1-Bromobutane (Primary Alkyl halide) 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane (Secondary Alkyl halide) 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane (Tertiary Alkyl halide) The names given below are also accepted by the IUPAC: Ethyl Bromide Iso-propyl bromide tert-butyl bromide Physical Properties: Alkyl halides have high melting and boiling points as compared to alkanes. Reason: Due to bond polarity of C X bond (as halogen is more electronegative than carbon). The bond pair electron density is more concentrated on halogen, X. Structure: Alkyl halide (R-X) consists of a sp3 hybridized C atom which is bonded to a halogen, (X), via a sigma bond. The carbon halogen bonds (C-X) are typically quite polar due to the electronegativity difference of carbon and halogen. 4 Preparations of Alkyl Halides From Alcohol Alcohols may be converted to corresponding alkyl halides, when treated with HCl in the presence of anhydrous zinc chloride / thionyl chloride in the presence of pyridine as a solvent / phosphorous trihalides or phosphorous pentahalides. Ethanol HCl (Anhydrous ZnCl2) - Chloroethane H2O Ethanol SOCl2 (Pyridine as a solvent) - Chloroethane HCl SO2 Ethanol PBr3 - Bromoethane H3PO3 Ethanol PI3/PCl5 - Iodoethane/Chloroethane H3PO3/POCl3 HCl From Alkanes When alkanes are treated with chlorine or bromine in the presence of diffused sunlight, hydrogen of alkane is replaced by halogen and alkyl halide is formed. Ethane Cl2 (Sunlight) - Chloroethane HCl This method does not give pure alkyl halides. Halogen derivatives containing two or more halogen atoms are also formed along with alkyl halides. 5 Reactivity There are two main factors which control the reactivity of alkyl halides: (1) Bond polarity of C-X bond (2) Bond energy of C-X bond Bond Polarity The molecule of alkyl halide is polarized due to the greater electronegativity of halogens as compared to C. Hence carbon acquires partial positive charge whereas halogen acquires partial negative charge. Halogen becomes nucleophilic in character, which can be replaced by another nucleophile. On the basis of bond polarity, reactivity of alkyl halides decreases in the following order: RF RCl RBr RI Electronegativity: F 4.0, Cl 3.0, Br 2.8, I 2.5 Bond Energy Energy required to break the bond of the same type in one mole of bond is known as bond energy. The greater the bond energy, the more energy will be required to break the bond. Reactivity of alkyl halides depends upon the strength of C X bond. C F bond is the strongest while C I bond is the weakest. So, the overall order of reactivity of alkyl halides is: R-I R-Br R-Cl R-F In fact, the C-F bond is so strong that alkyl fluorides do not react under ordinary conditions. 6 Reactions of Alkyl Halides Alkyl halides undergo two types of reactions: Nucleophilic substitution reactions (SN Reaction) Elimination reaction Nucleophilic substitution (SN) reactions of Alkyl halides. Those reactions where halogen of alkyl halide is substituted or replaced by an attacking nucleophile are known as nucleophilic substitution reactions. Following represents the general SN reaction.

Attack of nucleophile RX - RNu Leaving nucleophile Substrate, nucleophile and Leaving Group Substrate Molecule The alkyl halide molecule on which nucleophile attacks is called a substrate molecule. Nucleophile It is a species having a lone pair of electrons and donates a pair of electrons to the electrophilic carbon of alkyl halide. (It may be neutral or negatively charged). Examples of Nucleophiles: HO- Hydroxide ion NH2- Amino group C2H5O- Ethoxide ion Cl- Chloride ion HS- Hydrogen sulphide ion Br- Bromide ion SCN- Thiocyanate ion NH3 Ammonia H2O Water Leaving Group (LG) Halogen of alkyl halide is called the leaving group. The leaving group is also a nucleophile. It departs with an unshared pair of electrons. The incoming nucleophile must be stronger than the departing one. Cl-, Br-, I-, HSO4- are good leaving groups. Poor leaving groups are OH-, OR- and NH2-. Iodide ion is a good nucleophile as well as a good leaving group. The more stable leaving group is a good leaving group. Some common leaving groups are: I-, Br-, Cl-, TsO- (Excellent), NH3. There are two fundamental events in a nucleophilic substitution reaction: formation of the new sigma bond between carbon and attacking nucleophile. breaking of the sigma bond between carbon and halogen. Two different mechanisms are possible in nucleophilic substitution reactions: Bond breaking to form a carbocation precedes the formation of the new bond: SN1 reaction. Simultaneous bond formation and bond breaking: SN2 reaction. Examples of Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions: RX I- - RI (alkyl iodide) RX OH- - ROH (alcohol) RX OR'- - ROR' (ether) RX SH- - RSH (thiol/mercaptan) RX CC-R'- - RCCR' (alkyne) RX CN- - RCN (nitrile) RX OC-R'- - RO-C-R' (ester) RX NH3 - RNH3 X- (Ammonium salt) Carbocations and their Stability Carbocation A carbon atom which is attached with three atoms or group of atoms and possesses a unit positive charge is known as a carbocation. Stability The general stability order of simple alkyl carbocations is: 3 2 1 methyl (most stable) (least stable) This is because alkyl groups are weak electron donors due to hyperconjugation and inductive effects. SN1 Mechanism It is a unimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction. It is a two-step reaction mechanism in which the substrate R-X first ionizes reversibly into a carbocation (R) and X- ions. This is the slow and rate-determining step. Then the carbocation combines with the attacking nucleophile to form the product. This is the fast step. Kinetic Evidence Experiments show that the rate of an SN1 reaction depends upon the concentration of alkyl halide only. The change in concentration of attacking nucleophile has no effect on the rate. It is a first order reaction. Rate kR-X Stereochemical Evidence SN1 reaction occurs with partial racemization. The extent of partial racemization depends upon several factors including stability of carbocation. The carbon atom of the carbocation is sp2 hybridized and carries one empty p orbital. The nucleophile can attach itself to the p-orbital either on the right or on the left side of the carbon with equal ease.

The expected product is a racemic mixture. However, the partial racemization suggests a different way of attachment, e.g., in case of an unstable carbocation, the attack of nucleophile is greater from the side opposite to that of the leaving group, leading to partial inversion of configuration. Thus, the side of the carbon atom to which the leaving group is attached is somewhat shielded from the attack of nucleophile. Therefore, the product has some optical activity. SN2 Mechanism It is a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution reaction. It occurs in one step. The attack of nucleophile on carbon and the departure of the halide ion take place simultaneously in a single step. This is the rate-determining step because the bond breaking and bond making processes occur simultaneously. Since two molecules are undergoing change in covalency in the rate-determining step, molecularity is two. Kinetic Evidence: The rate of an SN2 reaction depends both on the concentration of nucleophile and alkyl halide. The rate expression for the reaction can be written as: Rate KNuR-X It is a 2nd order reaction. Stereochemical Evidence: In SN2 reaction, back side attack with inversion of configuration takes place. The carbon atom in the transition state is sp2-hybridized and is planar. Comparison of SN1 and SN2 Mechanism (1) SN1 is a two-step mechanism. SN2 is a single step mechanism. (2) In SN1, the first step is slow and the second is fast. In SN2, it has only one step and that is slow. (3) SN1 is a unimolecular reaction. SN2 is a bimolecular reaction. (4) SN1 is favored in polar solvents. SN2 is favored in non-polar solvents. (5) Mostly tertiary alkyl halides give SN1 reaction. Mostly primary alkyl halides give SN2 reaction. (6) In SN1, 50 inversion and 50 retention of configuration takes place. In SN2, 100 inversion of configuration takes place. (7) Rate for SN1 K R-X. Rate for SN2 KNuR-X. 7 1,2 Elimination Reactions Definition The chemical reaction in which two groups (halogen and beta-hydrogen from alkyl halide) are eliminated from two adjacent carbon atoms to form a carbon-carbon double bond is called an elimination reaction. Since beta-hydrogen is necessary for eliminations, it is also called beta-elimination. There are two types of beta-elimination reactions. E1 mechanism It is a unimolecular two-step elimination reaction. Step 1: Ionization of Alkyl halide Alkyl halide ionizes reversibly into a carbocation and halide ion. Step 2: Removal of beta-hydrogen In this step the solvent or base attacks the beta-hydrogen to form an alkene. The first step is the slow step and is called the rate-determining step. Since only one molecule is undergoing a change in the rate-determining step, it is called an elimination reaction unimolecular and is symbolized as E1. It follows first order kinetics. Rate kRX Rearrangement of Carbocation: A relatively less stable carbocation rearranges to a more stable carbocation before giving the elimination product. For example: A secondary carbocation (less stable) can rearrange to a tertiary carbocation (more stable) before elimination.

E2 mechanism It is a bimolecular one-step elimination reaction in which the attack of base on beta-hydrogen, with formation of carbon-carbon double bond and removal of halogen takes place simultaneously. This is the rate-determining step because bond breaking and bond making processes are taking place simultaneously. Since two molecules are undergoing a change in the transition state, it is called an elimination reaction bimolecular and is symbolized as E2. Kinetic Evidence: Experiments show that the rate of reaction is directly proportional to the substrate and base. Rate K RXB It is second order kinetics and depends upon the concentrations of substrate and base. 8 Substitution versus Elimination Reactions Substitution and elimination reactions are very important for the formation of different products. Both types of reactions have close resemblance in their mechanism. Explanation: The beta-hydrogen atom in alkyl halides is slightly acidic due to the electron-withdrawing effect of halogen (inductive effect). The attacking nucleophile can either attack the alpha-carbon to give substitution product or the beta-hydrogen to give elimination product. Elimination occurs only in the presence of a beta-hydrogen, whereas substitution reactions do not require this condition. Factors The following factors help determine whether the reaction is elimination or substitution. (1) Structure of Substrate (Alkyl Halide): For tertiary alkyl halides, elimination is favored over substitution reaction because the approach of the nucleophile to the alpha-carbon is difficult for substitution. The reverse is the case for primary alkyl halides. (2) Nature of Base: Strong bases such as OH-, OR-, NH2- cause elimination in preference to substitution. Highly polarizable nucleophiles and weak bases such as I-, RS- etc. give substitution reactions. (3) The Nature of Leaving Group: The role of leaving groups in elimination reactions is similar to that in substitution reactions. In unimolecular reactions it does not affect the mechanism because both the elimination and substitution products are formed from the carbocation. However, in the bimolecular reactions the nature of the product greatly depends upon the nature of the leaving group. (4) Nature of Solvent Elimination is favored more than substitution by decreasing the solvent polarity. Thus, alcoholic KOH affects elimination while more polar aqueous KOH is used for substitution. E1 is favored by polar solvents like the SN1 reaction. In non-polar solvents, the reaction will follow the E2 mechanism. (5) Effect of Temperature An increase in temperature will favor elimination more than substitution, because substitution reaction involves less reorganization of bonds as compared to eliminations. (7) What are primary, secondary and tertiary carbon atoms? 2 ORGANOMETALLIC COMPOUNDS (GRIGNARDS REAGENTS) Preparation of Grignards Reagents When an alkyl halide reacts with magnesium in the presence of dry ether, a Grignard reagent is formed. RX Mg (dry ether) - R-Mg-X Alkyl halide - Alkylmagnesium halide Alkyl bromides are generally used in the preparation of Grignards reagent because of its intermediate reactivity.

Alkyl magnesium halide is used as an ethereal solution. Reactivity Organometallic compounds are nucleophiles because of the partial negative charge on the carbon of the alkyl group. The carbon atom being more electronegative than metals such as Mg, the alkyl group bears a partial negative charge. The following reaction with water supports the electrophilic character of organometallic compounds: CH3-Mg-Br H-OH - CH4 MgBr(OH) Reactions of Grignards Reagents A. Reaction of Grignard reagent With Aldehydes and Ketones When Grignard reagent reacts with aldehydes or ketones, primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols are formed. These reactions are carried out in the presence of ether followed by H3O. I. Reaction with Methanal (Formation of primary alcohol): Formaldehyde CH3-Mg-Br - (after H3O) Primary Alcohol II. Reaction with Ethanal (Formation of secondary alcohol): Acetaldehyde CH3-Mg-Br - (after H3O) Secondary Alcohol III. Reaction with Propanone (Formation of tertiary alcohol): Acetone CH3-Mg-Br - (after H3O) Tertiary Alcohol (tert-butyl alcohol) B. Reaction of Grignard reagent with an Ester When an excess of Grignard reagent reacts with an ester (other than alkyl formate) followed by acid hydrolysis, a tertiary alcohol is formed. Mechanism: Step 1: Nucleophilic attack on the ester carbonyl. Step 2: Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate to form a ketone. Step 3: Nucleophilic attack on the ketone carbonyl by another equivalent of Grignard reagent. Step 4: Protonation to form the tertiary alcohol. C. Reaction of Grignard reagent With CO2 (Formation of carboxylic acid) When a Grignard reagent reacts with carbon dioxide followed by acid hydrolysis, a carboxylic acid is formed. Step 1: Nucleophilic attack on carbon dioxide. Step 2: Protonation of the carboxylate ion gives the carboxylic acid. Quick Quiz 2 (1) What are organometallic compounds? (2) Define protonation. (3) How does RMgX react with CO2? (4) Write the formula of Grignard Reagent. 3 AMINES 1 Nomenclature: Common System of Naming The common names of amines are written by adding the suffix -amine to the name of alkyl or aryl radicals. Ethylamine (Primary amine) 2-Hexylamine (Primary amine) Dimethylamine (a secondary amine) Trimethylamine (a tertiary amine) Pyridine (a tertiary amine) Aniline, C6H5NH2, containing a methyl group on the ring is called Toluidine. If there is an alkyl group substituted on the -NH2, its name is represented by writing N-(alkyl group). It indicates that the alkyl group is located on the N-atom and not on the ring. If there are two substituents on N, it is repeated twice. p-Toluidine N-methylaniline N,N-dimethylaniline N,N-dimethyl-p-toluidine IUPAC System of Naming In this system, the amino group is indicated by the prefix amino- followed by the name of the hydrocarbon. The position of the amino group is indicated by a number obtained by numbering the chain of the hydrocarbon. Secondary and tertiary amines are named by using a compound prefix that includes the names of all but the largest alkyl group. Aminomethane (Methylamine) 2-Aminobutane (Methylamino)ethane (Dimethylamino)butane Physical Properties: The polar nature of the N-H bond (due to the electronegativity difference of the two atoms) results in the formation of hydrogen bonds with other amine molecules.

Because of hydrogen bonding, they have high melting and boiling points compared to analogous alkanes and high solubility in water. 3 Structure: In amines, the nitrogen atom is sp3-hybridized and has a nearly tetrahedral structure. It forms three sigma bonds with its three sp3-hybrid orbitals while the fourth non-bonding sp3 orbital carries a pair of electrons. An amine with three different groups is chiral and can be optically active. 4 Preparation of Amines I. Reaction of Alkyl Halides with ammonia When an alcoholic solution of ammonia is heated with an alkyl halide in a sealed tube at 100C, a mixture of primary, secondary, tertiary amines and a quaternary ammonium salt is obtained. Ethylamine Diethylamine Triethylamine Quaternary ethyl ammonium iodide At the end of the reaction, addition of strong alkali such as KOH liberates free amines from their salts, but the quaternary salt is unaffected. The three amines are separated by fractional distillation. Over-alkylation can be avoided by using excess ammonia but the yield is low. II. Reduction of nitrogen containing functional groups: (a) Reduction of Nitriles Reduction of alkyl or aryl nitriles gives primary amines. The reduction may be brought about by reducing agents i.e. LiAlH4, or sodium in ethanol. Catalytic Reduction: Nitriles on reaction with hydrogen gas in the presence of catalysts such as Rh-Al2O3, Pt or Raney nickel gives primary amines. (b) Reduction of Nitro Compounds Nitro compounds on catalytic or chemical reduction produce primary amines. Nitrobenzene can be reduced to Aniline (phenyl amine) by using reducing agents such as tin/iron in the presence of concentrated hydrochloric acid or by catalytic hydrogenation (e.g. H2/Pd). (c). Reduction of Amides When an amide is treated with the reducing agent LiAlH4, the -CO of amide is reduced to -CH2, and a primary amine is formed. (The carbon chain remains intact in this reaction). When an amide is treated with bromine in the presence of KOH, degradation of the amide takes place leading to the formation of a primary amine. This reaction is known as the Hoffmann degradation reaction. 5 Basicity of Ammonia and Methylamine Amines are basic and nucleophilic because of the non-bonding pair of electrons on nitrogen. The strength of a base is expressed in terms of pKb. For ammonia and methylamine, the pKb values are 4.76 and 3.38 respectively. Since pKb (CH3NH2) pKb (NH3), methylamine is a stronger base than ammonia. It can be explained as under: In ammonia, the pair of electrons is attracted by the s-orbitals of hydrogen atoms whereas in CH3NH2, the sp3 orbital of carbon pushes electrons towards nitrogen. Comparison of Basicity of primary, secondary and tertiary amines: The presence of electron-donating groups increases the basicity of amines. A secondary amine is a stronger base than a primary amine.

Although in a tertiary amine (trialkyl amine) the electron density is increased due to the electron-donating effect of three alkyl groups, due to the steric effect of three bulky alkyl groups, the approach of a proton to the electron pair on the nitrogen atom becomes relatively difficult. Order of basicity is: Secondary amine Primary amine Tertiary amine 7 Reactions of Amines Reaction of amine with acid halide: When an amine reacts with an acid halide, a secondary amide is formed. Reaction of amine with alkyl halide (Alkylation of Amine by Alkyl Halides) An amine reacts with an alkyl halide to form a secondary, tertiary amine and an ammonium salt. This reaction is called an alkylation reaction. Reactions of Primary Amines with Aldehydes and Ketones Aldehydes and ketones react with primary amines to form Schiffs bases. Reaction with nitrous acid. (Preparation of Diazonium Salts) When amines react with nitrous acid in the presence of hydrochloric acid, diazonium compounds are formed. The reaction mixture must be kept below 10C. Alkyl diazonium salts are generally too unstable for practical use. When the diazonium group is attached to a benzene ring, though, the ion is stabilized to some extent by the delocalized electrons of the ring. The benzene diazonium ion is therefore much more stable than its aliphatic counterparts. Nevertheless, it decomposes readily above 10C to form phenol and nitrogen gas. Quick Quiz 3 What are amines? How would you prepare a Diazonium salt? Society, Technology and Science ORGANOMETALLIC COMPOUNDS IN MEDICINES Cisplatin, (NH3)2PtCl2, displays anti-cancer activity in chemotherapy. Mercurochrome (Merbromin) is an over-the-counter topical antiseptic. Merthiolate (Thiomersal) has applications as an antifungal and antiseptic agent. This compound is also used as a vaccine preservative, in immunoglobulin preparations and nasal products. Titanocene dichloride, Cp2TiCl2, has shown significant anticancer attributes. Tamoxifen is an anticancer compound. Ferrocenyl derivative chloroquine is an antimalarial compound. Titanocene dichloride, (Cp)2V(NCSe)2, and carboplatin are anticancer drugs. Ferroquine, a combination of ferrocene and chloroquine, is an antimalarial drug. Comparison between hemoglobin and chlorophyll Hemoglobin and chlorophyll are both natural organometallic compounds. Both consist of a substituted porphyrin ring coordinated with a metal ion. Hemoglobin is a porphyrin ring with iron while chlorophyll is a porphyrin ring with magnesium. Hemoglobin is the red pigment in the blood while chlorophyll is the green pigment in green plants, algae, and certain organisms. Hemoglobin is involved in oxygen transport while chlorophyll functions as a receptor of light energy during photosynthesis. SUMMARY Mono halo derivatives of alkanes are called alkyl halides. The general formula of alkyl halides is CnH2n1X. The best method for the preparation of alkyl halides is by the reactions of alcohols with inorganic halides like SOCl2, PX3 and PX5. Alkyl halides are a very reactive class of organic compounds. They undergo nucleophilic substitution reactions and elimination reactions in the presence of a nucleophile or a base.

Nucleophilic substitution reactions can take place in two distinct ways. A one step mechanism is called SN2 while a two step mechanism is called SN1. SN1 reactions show first order kinetics whereas SN2 reactions show 2nd order kinetics. Nucleophilic substitution reactions take place simultaneously with elimination reactions and often compete with them. Elimination of two atoms or groups from adjacent carbon atoms in the presence of a nucleophile or a base is called an elimination reaction. Like nucleophilic substitution, beta-elimination reactions also take place in two distinct ways: E1 and E2. A nucleophile is an electron rich species that will react with an electron poor species. A substitution implies that one group replaces another. Grignard reagent can be prepared by adding alkyl halide to a stirred suspension of magnesium metal in diethyl ether. Grignard reagent has a reactive nucleophilic carbon atom, which can react with electrophilic centers to give products in high yields. Primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols can be best prepared by reacting Grignard reagent with formaldehyde, any other aldehydes and ketones, respectively. The polar nature of the N-H bond (due to the electronegativity difference of the two atoms) results in the formation of hydrogen bonds with other amine molecules. Primary amines, R-NH2 or ArNH2, undergo nucleophilic addition with aldehydes or ketones to give carbinolamines which then dehydrate to give substituted imines. Primary alkyl or aryl amines yield diazonium salts.

Introduction: Analytical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with separation and analysis of a sample to identify its components. The separation is carried out prior to qualitative and quantitative analysis. Qualitative analysis provides the identity of a substance (composition of chemical species). On the other hand, Quantitative analysis determines the amount of each component present in a sample. Hence, in this branch different techniques and instruments used for analysis are studied. The scope of this branch covers food, water, environmental and clinical analysis. 1 CLASSICAL METHOD OF ANALYSIS: Combustion analysis and determination of Molecular Formula: Combustion analysis is suitable for organic compounds. This analysis is used to calculate empirical and molecular formula of hydrocarbons or for compounds that contain carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen (CxHyOz). The combustion products will be CO2 and H2O and these two products of combustion are separately collected. Procedure: An accurately known mass of the given organic compound is completely burnt in excess oxygen. This oxidises carbon and hydrogen in the organic compound to carbon dioxide and water respectively. After completion of experiment, from the difference of initial and final masses of water and CO2 absorbers, masses of CO2 and H2O are measured.
