Quick Quiz 1 Give difference between qualitative and quantitative analysis. How mass of oxygen is calculated if it is present with carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound? Give general steps used to calculate empirical formula of an organic compound. Give drawback of combustion analysis. 2 MODERN METHODS OF ANALYSIS: Spectroscopy: The branch of science which describes the interactions of electromagnetic radiation with matter is known as spectroscopy. Spectroscopy involves instrumentation to examine the radiations emitted or absorbed by chemicals giving information about their molecular structure. Electromagnetic radiation is the form of energy commonly known as radiation energy such as light energy. According to quantum mechanics, electromagnetic radiation has the properties of both a wave and a particle. Electromagnetic radiation exists as discrete packets of energy, called quanta or photons. Electromagnetic spectrum: Electromagnetic spectrum covers a wide range of wavelengths. Radiations of different wavelengths have different characteristics. The whole spectrum can be conveniently divided into several regions, each region can be defined by the unit of any of the four parameters, i.e., wavelength, frequency, wave number or energy. Different kinds of radiations interact with chemicals in different ways. The effects are summarized. Principle of Spectroscopy: The compounds interact with electromagnetic radiation and absorb energy. Different molecules absorb different amounts of radiations. Lower energy radiation may cause: i) molecular rotation ii) a bond vibration. Higher energy radiation may cause: i) electronic excitation ii) bond cleavage. The absorption of radiation is selective for a particular transition which depends upon the structure of molecule. The wavelengths of absorption spectra of known compounds are correlated with the wavelengths of absorption spectra of unknown compounds. The information is then used to determine the structure of unknown compounds. Spectrophotometer: The instrument used to measure the amount of electromagnetic radiation absorbed by a compound is called spectrophotometer or spectrometer. Construction: It consists of: A light source of radiation. A monochromator (prism) to select the desired wavelength of radiations. A sample cuvette. A detector to detect the radiations absorbed by the sample. The result is recorded on a spectrograph against the wavelength or wave number. Infrared Spectroscopy (IR): The wavelength range in IR region is 2.5 - 16 µm (4000 to 625 cm-1). They have sufficient energy for bonds in the molecule to vibrate. A molecule is made up of large number of atoms. These atoms continuously undergo vibration and rotation. IR radiations have low energy and can affect the vibrational kinetic energy of the atoms in a molecule. During vibration small displacement of atoms from their mean position occurs and causes a change in dipole moment of a molecule. This changed dipole interacts with electric field of IR radiations and increases the rate of vibration and rotation. Different bonds absorb radiations of different frequencies. Polar molecules are IR active.

IR radiation absorption spectrum is used to identify the bonds and functional groups in an organic molecule. Types of vibrations: Stretching vibrations: Bond angle does not change, only the bond length changes. Bending vibrations: Bond angle changes but bond length remains same. Interpretation of IR Spectrum: IR spectrum shows downward peaks which correspond to absorbance (A) or percent transmittance (T) as ordinate against wavelength (λ) or wave number (ν) in cm-1 as abscissa. IR radiation absorption spectrum is used to identify the bonds and functional groups in an organic molecule. The strength of the peak is the characteristic of the bond itself, not of the number of bonds. Types of IR Regions: There are two important absorption regions in IR spectrum: Finger print region (600 to 1500 cm-1): The absorption in this region is a characteristic of a compound. Different compounds will give different absorption peaks in this region. Hence this region is called fingerprint region and is used to identify the structure of organic compounds. Functional group Region (1500 to 4000 cm-1): Different functional groups show absorption in this region. For example, figure shows IR spectrum of propanone (CH3COCH3). The characteristic absorption of some common bonds: In the spectrum of propanone the strong peak at about 1720 cm-1 corresponds to the CO bond. The weaker absorption at 3000 cm-1 corresponds to the C-H bond. This peak is weaker even though there are more H atoms in the molecule. Table: Characteristic IR absorptions of some common bonds. Compound: Alkanes, alkenes, arenes. Absorption/cm-1: 2840 to 3095, 1610 to 1680. Intensity: M, M. Compound: Aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters. Absorption/cm-1: 1680 to 1750. Intensity: S. Compound: Alcohols, ethers, esters. Absorption/cm-1: 1000 to 1300. Intensity: S. Compound: Chloro compound. Absorption/cm-1: 700 to 800. Intensity: S. Compound: O-H (free). Absorption/cm-1: 3580 to 3670. Intensity: S (sharp). Compound: O-H (Hydrogen-bonded in alcohols, phenols). Absorption/cm-1: 3230 to 3550. Intensity: M (broad). Compound: O-H (Hydrogen-bonded in acids). Absorption/cm-1: 2500 to 3300. Intensity: M (broad). Compound: N-H (Primary amines). Absorption/cm-1: 3100 to 3500. Intensity: M. Visible and Ultraviolet Spectroscopy (UV-VIS): It is also known as electronic spectroscopy. It involves the transition of electron(s) within the molecule or ion from lower to higher energy levels or vice versa by absorption or emission of radiation falling in UV/visible region of electromagnetic spectrum in the range of 200 to 800 nm. It determines the presence of unsaturation and the extent of conjugation in a molecule. Absorption of UV radiation causes the excitation of electrons from lower energy level to higher level (from HOMO to LUMO). There are three kinds of electrons in a molecule: (i) σ electrons, (ii) π electrons (iii) lone pair of electrons (non-bonding or unshared electrons which are denoted by the letter n). The higher energy levels are antibonding molecular orbitals i.e. σ and π. Types of electronic transition: σ - σ transition: The σ electron strongly holds and the radiations in UV region is not so energetic to excite e.g. σ to σ.

Such transition require energy in the range of 150 nm which is not available in UV-region. (occurs in the vacuum UV region). n - σ transition: Compounds which contain nonbonding electron pair show this type of transition. For example: compounds containing nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur and chlorine show this type of transition. π - π transition: This type of transition occurs in unsaturated organic compounds. For example: CC, CC, CN, NN, CO. n - π transition: This type of transition occurs in compounds containing nonbonding electron pair on heteroatoms. The electron gets excited to π antibonding orbitals. This type of transition requires least energy and occurs at longer wavelength. The relative energy for three electronic transitions detectable by UV spectrophotometer in order of increasing energy is: n - π π - π n - σ. Quick Quiz 2: How can we get information about a compound using UV/Visible spectroscopy? Give colour of following wavelength (i) 600-620 (ii) 490-520. Table: The approximate wavelengths of visible radiation of different colours. Colour: Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue-green, Green-blue, Violet, Ultraviolet. Approximate wavelength/nm: Above 700, 620-700, 600-620, 580-600, 520-580, 490-520, 440-490, 400-420, Below 400. Figure: The visible/UV spectrum of methylene blue. Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR): Like electrons, atomic nucleus also spins about an axis and behaves like a tiny magnet. Nuclei which contain odd number of protons or neutrons or both have a spin quantum number 1/2. Examples: C13, N15, F19 and P31. Nuclei having even number of protons and neutrons have zero spin and zero magnetic moment. Examples: C12, O16. These nuclei are magnetically inactive. Spin states of a nucleus have equal energies in the absence of magnetic field. When magnetic field is applied, the magnetic moments of different nuclei may either align with or oppose the applied magnetic field. As a result, the spin is split up into two energy levels having nuclear spin of 1/2 with low energy and -1/2 with high energy. The energy difference between the two spin states is very small and lies within the range of radiofrequency. In NMR spectrometer, the sample is placed in an external magnetic field and radio waves swept across it. At particular combination of magnetic field and frequency of radio waves, some protons change their spin state i.e. they "flip over". This is called spin flipping. Working of NMR Spectrometer: The sample is dissolved in a solvent having no protons, such as tetrachloromethane (CCl4). A small amount of tetramethyl silane, commonly known as TMS, is mixed with the sample to act as an internal reference (In TMS all the 12 protons are equivalent, and produce a peak at δ 0). The tube containing this mixture is suspended between the poles of the electromagnet. When no energy is absorbed by the sample, the detector does not pick up any energy from the oscillator. However, when the sample absorbs a definite amount of energy from the RF transmitter, the proton spins flip over.

This induces a signal in the detector which is indicated by an increase of current in the RF detector. This is recorded as a resonance signal. Only small amount of sample is enough to produce an NMR spectrum. Proton (1H) NMR spectra of organic compounds: When the protons in a molecule are similar, as in CH4 and C2H6, their spin states are equal and produce a single peak in NMR spectrum. Protons in different chemical environment require slightly different magnetic fields to come to resonance. That is why different types of protons produce peaks at different position in NMR spectrum. Area under a peak is proportional to the number of protons involved. Low-Resolution NMR spectrum of Ethanol: NMR spectrum of ethanol consists of three peaks at different absorption and of different areas. The areas under the peaks are in the ratio 1:2:3. The presence of three peaks is explained by the fact that one proton in the -OH group, the two protons in the -CH2 group and the three protons in the CH3 group are in different chemical environments. Hence, they require slightly different strength of magnetic field to bring them into resonance. Chemical Shift (δ): The separation of absorption position of particular proton from the absorption position of tetramethyl silane is called chemical shift. The symbol for chemical shift is δ (delta). Chemical shifts are quoted in parts per million of the applied field. Protons in most of the common organic molecules have chemical shift between values of 0.0-10 δ. Highly shielded protons require stronger field to resonate and have low chemical shifts. Quick Quiz 3 Write basic principle of NMR spectroscopy. What information are obtained from number of peaks and area under peaks in NMR spectrum? What is NMR reference? Atomic Emission Spectroscopy: Atomic emission spectroscopy pertains to electronic transitions in atoms which use an excitation source like flames sparks. Emission spectroscopy is related to atoms. Atoms emit radiations in the form of discrete wavelengths of light, called spectral lines while returning to the lower energy states. Principle: The source vaporizes the sample and causes electronic excitation of elementary particles in the gas. Excited molecules in the gas phase emit band spectra. Thus, a molecule in an excited state of energy, E2, undergoes a transition to a state of lower energy E1 and a photon of energy hν is emitted where E2 - E1 hν. In each electronic state a molecule may exist in a number of vibrational and rotational states of different energies. Types of Atomic or Line Spectrum: Spectrum may be classified as: Atomic or Line Emission Spectrum. Atomic Absorption Spectrum. Atomic or Line Emission Spectrum: When an element is vaporized in a flame, or in an electric arc or in a discharge tube, it emits a light of characteristic colour. The resolution of ray of this light produces coloured lines separated by dark spaces. This type of separation is called a line emission spectrum.

Each element has its own characteristic colour by which it can be identified i.e. Na gives yellow colour, Sr gives red colour and K gives violet colour in Bunsen flame. Similarly, in a discharged tube; Ne glows with orange red, He with orange pink, H2 with orange red or blue and Cl2 with orange green colour. The lines in the spectrum of an element are not haphazardly distributed but they occur in groups or series. In series the separation between them decreases regularly as their wavelength decreases. At a certain limiting value, the spectrum becomes continuous. Applications of emission spectroscopy: Emission spectroscopy has been used to detect 40 elements. The following materials have been analysed by emission spectroscopy: Trace major constituents in ceramics. Traces of Co, Ni, Mo and V in Graphite. Trace metal impurities in analytical reagents. Trace of Ca, Cu, Zn in blood. Zinc in pancreatic tissues. Atomic Absorption Spectrum: When white light is allowed to pass through a sample of a substance, it may absorb radiation of a particular wavelength. There will be a dark space in the continuous spectrum of white light for that particular wavelength. This spectrum is called a line or atomic absorption spectrum. Applications of Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy (AAS): The AAS technique has become the most powerful tool of analysis because in this method small concentration of sample is used. AAS methods are highly specific, hence analysis of a metal from a complex mixture is possible and a high energy sample is not required to be employed. The technique is used for the analysis of substance including ceramics mineralogy, biochemistry, metallurgy, water supplies and soil analysis. Quick Quiz 4: What is spectroscopy? Define atomic emission spectroscopy. List those elements which can be analyzed by emission spectroscopy. Give principle of atomic absorption spectroscopy. Give few applications of atomic absorption spectroscopy. Mass Spectrometry (MS): It involves the production of gaseous ions of different isotopes of elements or an organic molecule, their separation according to their m/e ratio and measurement of their intensity in the form of spectrum. Mass Spectrometer is a device used for the detection and identification of different isotopes of elements, and for determining their isotopic masses. Mass spectrometry is also used extensively to determine the structure of organic molecules. Working of Mass spectrometer: The action of a mass spectrometer involves the following basic processes: Vaporization: The sample is usually injected as gas but if liquid or solid sample is introduced then it may be evaporated in evaporation chamber. Ionization: Conversion of gaseous atoms and molecules into gaseous positive ions by bombardment with high speed electrons (70 eV). Acceleration: The cations are accelerated by the application of a suitable electric field of negative potential (500-2000 Volts). Deflection: Positive ions are deflected and separated according to their mass to charge ratio (m/e ratio) by the application of a variable magnetic field. The angle of deflection of positive ions is inversely proportional to their m/e ratio.

Detection: Ions with particular m/e ratio are detected and then amplified by an electron multiplier, which can record the number of ions striking it. The detector is in a fixed position while the magnetic field is changed so that ions of a particular m/e ratio are focused into the detector. The detector is essentially a counter, which generates an electric current proportional to the number of ions striking it. This electrical signal is amplified and fed into an oscilloscope. Determination of Relative Atomic Mass: The mass spectrum of an element can be used to obtain relative atomic mass and relative abundance of each isotope. Heights of peaks in the spectrum is proportional to the relative natural abundance of isotopes and number of peaks give number of possible isotopes. Relative atomic mass of an element is the average mass of different isotopes of that element. Example: Mass spectrum of chlorine shows that it consists of two isotopes in relative height of 3:1 which is 75 and 25 respectively. Relative atomic mass (Ar) of Chlorine (35 x 75 37 x 25) / 100 35.45.

INTRODUCTION TO BIOCHEMISTRY As the name indicates, biochemistry is a hybrid science. Biochemistry is the branch of science which deals with studying various biomolecules that occur in living cells and organisms and their chemical reactions. Living organisms should be able to transform matter and energy into different forms, show response to changes in their environment and show growth and reproduction. All living organisms undergo changes due to large organic compounds called macromolecules. Four major types of macromolecules control all activities in the body. They are carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. 1 CARBOHYDRATES Carbohydrates are called so because they contain carbon, oxygen and hydrogen in which hydrogen and oxygen are in the ratio 2:1 with the general formula Cx(H2O)y. Modern Definition: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy compounds of aldehydes or ketones. Carbohydrates or saccharides are the most abundant of the four types of macromolecules. These are sugars or starches. They have several roles in living organisms, including energy transportation, as well as being structural components of plants and arthropods. Carbohydrate derivatives are actively involved in fertilization, immune systems, development of disease, blood clotting and growth. Classification of Carbohydrates Carbohydrates are classified into three types. Monosaccharides: Definition: The carbohydrates which do not hydrolyze to simpler units are called monosaccharides. This is the smallest possible sugar unit. Examples are glucose, galactose and fructose. When we talk about blood sugar, we refer to glucose in the blood. Glucose is a major source of energy for a cell. Glucose is naturally in honey and corns. In human nutrition, galactose can be found most readily in milk and dairy products, while fructose is found mostly in vegetables and fruits (grapes). Disaccharides (Oligosaccharides): Disaccharides are carbohydrate molecules which upon hydrolysis form 2-10 units of simple sugars (monosaccharides). Examples of disaccharides include lactose, maltose, and sucrose. Sucrose H2O - Glucose Fructose. Lactose H2O - Galactose Glucose. Sucrose occurs in sugarcane, sugar beet, mango, pineapple, almond and apricot.

Polysaccharides: Definition: The carbohydrates producing large number of monosaccharides on hydrolysis are called polysaccharides. Starch and cellulose are the examples of polysaccharides. A brief summary is presented below: Monosaccharides: Glucose, Galactose, Fructose, Ribose, Glyceraldehyde. Disaccharides: Sucrose, Maltose, Lactose. Polysaccharides: Starch, Glycogen, Cellulose. Some common carbohydrates, with their structures are as follow: Glucose: Monosaccharide, aldose, hexose. Occurs abundantly in plants and animals. Fructose: Monosaccharide, ketose, hexose. In fruit and honey. Ribose: Monosaccharide, aldose, pentose. Component of nucleic acids and coenzymes. Sucrose: Disaccharide. In sugarcane, beetroot. Lactose: Disaccharide. In milk. Maltose: Disaccharide. In malt. Starch: Polysaccharide. In cereals, potatoes, corn, rice. Glycogen: Polysaccharide. In liver and muscle. Cellulose: Polysaccharide. In plant cell walls. 2 Functions of Carbohydrates The main functions of carbohydrates are given below: They spare protein so that protein can concentrate on building, repairing, and maintaining body tissues instead of being used up as an energy source. For fat to be metabolized properly, carbohydrates must be present. If there are not enough carbohydrates, then large amount of fats are used for energy. The body is not able to handle this large amount so quickly, so it accumulates ketone bodies, which make the body acidic. This causes a condition called ketosis. Carbohydrate is necessary for the regulation of nerve tissue and is the only source of energy for the brain. Certain types of carbohydrates support the growth of healthy bacteria in the intestines for digestion. Some carbohydrates are high in fibre, which help prevent constipation and lowers the risk for certain diseases such as cancer, heart disease and diabetes. 3 Nutritional Importance of Carbohydrates Main functions of carbohydrates are given below: Body Weight Regulation: People eating a diet high in carbohydrates are less likely to accumulate body fat compared with those who follow a low carbohydrate/high-fat diet. Studies show that carbohydrates, both in the form of starch and sugar, work quickly to aid satiety and that those consuming high carbohydrate diets are therefore less likely to overeat. It is evident that diets high in carbohydrate, as compared to those high in fat, reduce the likelihood of developing obesity. Diabetes: There is no evidence that sugar consumption is linked to the development of any type of diabetes. However, there is now good evidence that obesity and physical inactivity increase the likelihood of developing non-insulin dependent diabetes, which usually occurs in middle age. Weight reduction is usually necessary and is the primary dietary aim for people with non-insulin dependent (Type II) diabetes. Recent recommendations for the dietary management of diabetes allow a modest amount of ordinary sugar as the inclusion of sugar with a meal has little effect on either blood glucose or insulin concentrations in people with diabetes. Dental Health: Carbohydrate containing sugars or starches can be broken down by the enzymes and bacteria in the mouth to produce acid which attacks the enamel of the teeth. After an acid challenge, saliva provides a natural repair process which rebuilds the enamel.

When carbohydrate-containing foods are consumed too frequently, or nibbled over time, this natural repair process is overwhelmed and the risk of tooth decay is increased. 2 PROTEINS The molecules which yield amino acids on complete hydrolysis are called proteins. Proteins are the basis for the major structural components of animal and human tissue. Proteins are natural polymer molecules consisting of amino acid units. The number of amino acids in proteins may range from two to several thousand. These molecules contain nitrogen, carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. They act as biological catalysts (enzymes), form structural parts of organisms, participate in cell signal and recognition factors, and act as molecules of immunity. Proteins can also be a source of fuel. 1 Classification of Proteins Three classes of proteins are usually defined: Simple proteins 2) Compound or conjugated proteins 3) Derived proteins. a. Simple Proteins: These proteins on hydrolysis yield only amino acids or their derivatives. For example: Albumins, Globulins, Glutelins and Histones. b. Conjugated Proteins: Those proteins which are attached or conjugated to some non-protein group which are called prosthetic group. For example: Nucleoproteins, Mucoprotein, Glycoprotein and Phosphoprotein. c. Derived Proteins: Those proteins which are derived from simple and conjugated proteins. For example: Proteans, Proteoses, Peptones and Peptides. 2 Structure of Proteins The structure of a protein depends upon the spatial arrangement of polypeptide chains present in protein. Since three spatial arrangements are possible, proteins have the following four structures. a) The Primary Structure of Proteins: The sequence of amino acids in a peptide chain is called primary structure. Amino acids are linked one another through peptide bonds. The arrangement of these amino acids is called primary structure. b) The Secondary Structure of Proteins: Peptide chains may acquire spiral shape or may be present in a zig-zag manner. This coiling or zig-zagging of polypeptide is called secondary structure of protein. It is due to H-Bonding. c) The Tertiary Structure of Proteins: Twisting or folding of polypeptide chains represents tertiary structure of proteins. d) Quaternary Proteins: Quaternary means four. This is the fourth phase in the creation of a protein. Quaternary protein is the arrangement of multiple folded protein or coiling protein molecules in a multi-subunit complex. A variety of bonding interactions including hydrogen bonding, salt bridges, and disulfide bonds hold the various chains into a particular geometry. 3 Properties of Proteins Proteins are involved in such processes as food digestion, cell structure, catalysis, movement, energy manipulation and much more. There are about 20-22 common amino acids found in most proteins. All but one of these small molecules has the same common structure but varies in the nature of one chemical group - termed the "R-group". Amino acids are joined together in long chains called "polypeptides". 4 Importance of Proteins Following are the features of the protein which are very important: Proteins play an important role in the formation of protoplasm. Protoplasm is the essence of all form of life.

Nucleoproteins are complex proteins and act as the carrier of heredity from one generation to the other. Enzymes are the biological catalyst and they are also proteins. Without enzymes life is not possible. Hemoglobin is a protein. It acts as carrier of oxygen. Some of the proteins act as hormones. They carry out the regulatory function of the body. Proteins have great importance in industry. Tanning of hides is an industrial process. This process is the precipitation of protein by tannic acid. Gelatin is obtained by heating bones, skins and tendons in water. It is used in bakery goods. Casein protein is used in the manufacture of buttons and buckles. Proteins obtained from the soybean are used for the manufacture of plastics. Quick Quiz 2 What are proteins? What is their chemical composition? Differentiate primary, secondary and tertiary structure of proteins. What are polypeptides? Give example. 3 ENZYMES The word Enzyme means 'in yeast'. Enzymes are biocatalysts which alter the speed of metabolic activities in the living body. Enzymes are complex protein molecules which are quite specific in action and sensitive to temperature and pH. Role of Enzymes as a Biocatalyst: Metabolism is the set of biochemical reactions that occur in living organisms in order to maintain life. These processes allow an organism to grow and reproduce, maintain their structures, and respond to their environments. Metabolism consists of anabolism and catabolism. Anabolism includes the biochemical reactions in which larger molecules are synthesized while catabolism includes the biochemical reactions in which larger molecules are broken down. Usually, energy is released in catabolism and it is utilized in anabolism. In this way the biochemical reactions are actually energy transformations. During metabolism, chemicals are transformed from one form to the other by enzymes. Enzymes are crucial to metabolism because they act as biocatalysts and speed up and regulate metabolic pathways. Enzymes are proteins that catalyze (i.e. speed up) biochemical reactions and are not changed during the reaction. The molecules at which enzymes act are called substrates, and the enzyme converts them into different molecules, called products. How does Enzyme work? When enzyme attaches with substrate, a temporary enzyme-substrate (ES) complex is formed. Enzyme catalyzes the reaction and substrate is transformed into product. After it, the ES complex breaks into enzyme and product. E S - ES Complex - E P. In order to explain the mechanism of enzyme action a German chemist Emil Fischer in 1894, proposed lock and key model. According to this model, both enzyme and substrate possess specific shapes that fit exactly into one another. This model explains enzyme specificity. In 1958, an American biologist Daniel Koshland suggested a modification to lock and key model and proposed induced-fit model. According to this model: active site is not a rigid structure rather it is moulded into the required shape to perform its function. Induced fit model is more acceptable than lock and key model of enzyme action.

2 Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity Enzymes are very sensitive to the environment in which they work. Any factor that can change the chemistry or shape of enzyme molecule can affect its activity. Some of the factors that can affect the rate of enzyme action are being discussed here. Temperature: Increase in temperature speeds up the rate of enzyme catalyzed reactions, but only to a point. Every enzyme works at its maximum rate at a specific temperature, called as the optimum temperature for that enzyme. Example: Animal enzyme has optimum temperature 37C. Some plant enzymes have optimum temperature 60C. When temperature rises to a certain limit, heat adds in the activation energy and also provides kinetic energy for the reaction. So reactions are accelerated. But when temperature is raised well above the optimum temperature, heat energy increases the vibrations of atoms of enzyme and the globular structure of enzyme is lost. This is known as the denaturation of enzyme. It results in a rapid decrease in rate of enzyme action and it may be blocked completely. Substrate Concentration: In a reaction, if enzyme molecules are available in a concentration, increase in substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction. If enzyme concentration is kept constant and amount of substrate is increased, a point is reached after which any further increase in substrate does not increase the rate of reaction any more. This is because the active sites of all enzymes are occupied (at high substrate concentration), and any extra substrate molecules do not find free active site. This state is called saturation state and reaction rate does not increase. pH: All enzymes work at their maximum rate at a narrow range of pH, called as the optimum pH. A slight change in this pH causes retardation in enzyme activity or blocks it completely. Every enzyme has its specific optimum pH value. For example, pepsin (working in stomach) is active in acidic medium (pH 2) while trypsin (working in small intestine) shows its activity in alkaline medium (pH 8-9). 3 Inhibition of Enzyme A molecule that binds with an enzyme and decreases its activity is known as enzyme inhibitor. Inhibition can be reversible or irreversible according to the type of interaction formed between the inhibitor and the enzyme. There are two types of enzyme inhibition. Irreversible inhibition: When the inhibitors react and form strong covalent bonds with the active sites of the enzyme, it is called irreversible inhibition. It is stable and irreversible. Reversible inhibition: The inhibition in which the activity of an enzyme is restored is called reversible inhibition. There are two types of reversible inhibition. i) Competitive Inhibition: A competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate. It can bind to the enzyme in the same way that the substrate does. When present in the active site the inhibitor prevents the normal substrate from binding. The effect of inhibitor is overcome by decreasing the concentration of normal substrate. ii) Non-Competitive Inhibition: A non-competitive inhibitor also reduces enzyme activity.

The inhibitor usually binds at a separate binding site. It does not bind at the active site. When inhibitor binds at the second site (non-active site), it changes the shape of enzyme so that the shape of active-site is changed and substrate can no longer bind to the active site. 4 Industrial Application of Enzyme: Enzymes are extensively used in different industries for fast chemical reactions. For example: Food industry: Enzymes that break starch into simple sugars are used in the production of white bread, buns etc. Brewing industry: Enzymes break starch and proteins. The products are used by yeast for fermentation (to produce alcohol). Paper industry: Enzymes break starch to lower its viscosity that aids in making paper. Biological detergent: Protease enzymes are used for the removal of protein stains from clothes. Amylase enzymes are used in dish washing to remove resistant starch residues. Starch Industry: Amylase, Amyloglucosidase and Glucoamylase enzymes are used to convert starch into glucose and various syrups. Biofuel Industry: Cellulase enzymes are used to break down cellulose into sugars that can be fermented. Contact Lens Cleaners: Protease enzymes are used to remove proteins on contact lens to prevent infections. Rubber Industry: Catalase enzymes are used to generate oxygen from peroxide to convert latex into foam rubber. Photographic Industry: Protease (Ficin) enzymes are applied to dissolve gelatin off scrap film, allowing recovery of its silver content. Molecular Biology: Restriction enzymes, DNA Ligase and Polymerase enzymes are used to manipulate DNA in genetic engineering. More importantly in pharmacology, agriculture and medicine. It is also important in forensic science. Quick Quiz 3 What are enzymes? Why are they called biocatalysts? How does enzyme work? "Enzymes are extensively used in different industries". Comment on this statement. 4 LIPIDS (Greek, lipos means fat) Lipids are naturally occurring organic compounds of animals and plants origin, which are soluble in organic solvents and belong to a heterogeneous group of substances. These molecules consist of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. Lipids are the main constituents of all membranes in all cells (cell walls), food storage molecules, Vitamins A, D, E and K, cholesterol. All lipids are hydrophobic: that's the one property they have in common. Fats and oils are made from two kinds of molecules: glycerol (a type of alcohol with a hydroxyl group on each of its three carbons) and three fatty acids joined by dehydration synthesis. Since there are three fatty acids attached, so these are known as triglycerides. Classification of Lipids There are three broad classes of lipids: Simple Lipids: These are the ester of fatty acids with glycerol. For example: Triglycerides, Natural fats and Waxes. Compound Lipids: These contain in addition to fatty acids and alcohols, other groups also. For example: Phospholipids, Glycolipids, Sulpholipids, Lipositol and Sphingomyelin. Derived Lipids: These are hydrolytic product of compound lipids for example: Fatty acids. 2 Structure of Lipids Lipids are generally defined in terms of solubility, and not in terms of particular structures, as in the cases of proteins and nucleic acids.

Lipids associate with one another via van der Waals forces and the hydrophobic effect. In particular, we discuss the structure of Fatty Acids. The tail of a fatty acid is a long hydrocarbon chain, making it hydrophobic. The head of the molecule is a carboxyl group which is hydrophilic. Fatty acids are the main component of soap, where their tails are soluble in oily dirt and their heads are soluble in water to emulsify and wash away the oily dirt. However, when the head end is attached to glycerol to form a fat, that whole molecule is hydrophobic. 3 Properties of Lipids Physical Properties: Oils and fats may be either liquids or non-crystalline solids at room temperature. Fats and oils in the pure states are colorless, odorless and tasteless. The colored fats arise due to foreign substances, for example yellow color of the butter is due to the presence of keratin. They are lighter than water. They are insoluble in water. They are readily soluble in organic solvents like diethyl ether, carbon disulphide, acetone, benzene, chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. They form emulsions when they are agitated with water in the presence of soap or other emulsifier. Fats and oils are poor conductor of heat and electricity and serve as excellent insulator for the animal body. Chemical Properties: Fats and oils undergo various types of reactions but the most important are: Hydrolysis of fats and oils: Fats and oils are triglycerides. They are triesters. They are hydrolyzed by enzymes which act as catalyst. These enzymes are called lipases. This hydrolysis takes place in the digestive tract of human beings and animals. Fatty acids are produced in animal body which play an important role in the metabolic pathways. Saponification: Saponification is the hydrolysis of triglycerides (oils or fats) by alkalies. Glycerol is produced along with sodium or potassium salt of fatty acids. These Na and K salts are called soaps (salt of fatty acids). Hardening of Oils: We know that unsaturated triglycerides are liquids at room temperature. They are called oils. They can be saturated by passing hydrogen in them in the presence of metal catalysts. The result is the conversion of liquid triglycerides into a semisolid triglyceride. This process is called hardening of oils. This reaction is used commercially for the production of vegetable ghee or margarine. Hardened oils are also used extensively for making soaps and candles. 4 Nutritional and Biological Importance of Lipids Lipids play three major biochemical roles: As storage form for metabolic energy (triglycerides). As structural components of membranes. As messengers (prostaglandins, steroid hormones). A major role of lipids in nutrition is to provide energy, since unsaturated, saturated and trans fats all provide about 9 calories per gram compared to carbohydrates or protein with 4 calories per gram. Even though it is high in calories, fat does not necessarily cause weight gain if it fits into your total intake.

Our body also needs fat so that your body can absorb and use certain nutrients such as vitamin A, vitamin D and vitamin E. Essential Lipids: Those lipids which are not synthesized by our bodies and are supplied to our bodies through diet are called essential lipids. The essential lipids are polyunsaturated fats called omega-6 and omega-3 fats. We need these fats for hormone synthesis, cell membrane structure and healthy brain and vision, and they may help lower our blood cholesterol levels. We can get omega-6 fatty acids from vegetable oils and nuts. Omega-3 fatty acids are also in flaxseed, walnuts and fatty fish. Non-Essential Lipids: Monounsaturated fatty acids are not essential in the diet because our body can synthesize them, but they may help to reduce our risk for heart disease. They are in olive oil, peanuts and avocadoes. We do not need to get saturated fat, trans fat or cholesterol in our diet, and these lipids raise bad cholesterol levels in our blood. Saturated fat is in fatty meats and cheese, palm and coconut oil, and butter. Trans fat is in partially hydrogenated oils in processed and fried foods, while cholesterol is in fatty animal foods. Functions of Lipids: Tissues reconstruction. Nervous system organization. Increase and assure a normal function of the skin. Antibodies formation. Good function of endocrine glands (thyroid). Water metabolism. Quick Quiz 4 What are lipids? Briefly explain the only property that all the lipids have in common. What are triglycerides? Draw its structure. 5 NUCLEIC ACIDS Definition: The molecules that preserve hereditary information and that transcribe and translate that information in a way that allows the synthesis of all the varied enzymes of the cell are called nucleic acid. Types of Nucleic Acids: There are two types of nucleic acids: Deoxyribonucleic acids (DNA). Ribonucleic acid (RNA). 1 Structural Components of DNA and RNA DNA consists of very large polymeric molecules called nucleotides. Four types of nucleotides are involved in the formation of DNA. Each nucleotide consists of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate and a nitrogenous base attached to carbon number 1 of the pentose sugar. Components of Nucleotide: There are three components present in each nucleotide. Pentose sugar: Ribose in RNA and deoxyribose in DNA. In deoxyribose, the hydroxyl group at carbon number 2 of ribose is replaced by hydrogen. Nitrogenous base: Following are the four bases involved in the structures of the nucleotides of DNA. Two of these are pyrimidine bases and the other two are purine bases. The base is linked to carbon number 1 of deoxyribose. The pyrimidine bases: They consist of six membered rings composed of four carbon atoms and two nitrogen atoms. Pyrimidine bases involved in the structure of DNA are cytosine (C) and thymine (T). The purine bases: They are combination of one six membered ring and one five membered ring. Only two purine bases adenine (A) and guanine (G) are involved in the structure of DNA and RNA. Note: Uracil replaces thymine in RNA.

Phosphoric acid, H3PO4: It is linked to carbon number 5 of deoxyribose sugar. Difference between RNA and DNA: RNA contains ribose sugar while DNA contains deoxyribose sugar. Nitrogenous bases in DNA are cytosine, thymine, adenine and guanine while in RNA thymine is replaced by uracil. DNA is double stranded while RNA is single stranded, but the chain can fold back on itself forming a helical loop. The two strands in DNA are twisted into a double helix and held in position by hydrogen bonds between complementary pairs of bases. The two strands are antiparallel i.e. they run in opposite directions. 2 Storage of Genetic Information. It stores the genetic information that is passed on to the offspring. The genetic information or the genetic code is stored in DNA in the form of a sequence of base pairs between its two strands. It is a self-replicating molecule. It replicates the genetic information before the cell divides so that each daughter cell carries the correct genetic code. This code is passed on by the organism to their offspring. Each replication produces two identical daughter DNA molecules. But the daughter molecules consist of one original strand and one new strand. This type of replication is known as semi conservative replication (because only one original strand is conserved). DNA transcribes copies of the genetic code into messenger RNA. The mRNA carries these copies of the genetic code into cytoplasm for the synthesis of protein. The genetic information in mRNA is then translated with the help of transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) for the synthesis of protein. This chain of amino acids called a polypeptide will then be transported to Golgi Bodies where it is processed and will become part of a protein. Quick Quiz 5 Write the names of structural components of DNA and RNA. Differentiate Transcription and Translation. Which type of sugar is present in DNA? 6 MINERALS OF BIOLOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE Minerals are the nutrients that are present in the body, and are as essential as our need for oxygen to sustain life. Minerals are also found in organic and inorganic combinations in food. In the body only 5 of the human body weight is mineral matter, vital to all mental physical processes. They are most important factors in maintaining all physiological processes, constituents of the teeth, bones, tissues, blood, muscle, and nerve cells. Types of nutrients: Macronutrients: Nutrients which are required in large amount to the body are called macronutrients. Examples: Calcium, phosphorus, magnesium and sulphur. Micronutrients: Nutrients which are required in small amount to the body are called micronutrients. Examples: Iron, zinc, copper and iodine. 1 Sources and Biological Significance of important Minerals Iron: Sources of Iron: Red meat, egg yolk, whole wheat, fish, spinach and mustard etc. Importance / Significance of Iron: It is an important mineral because it is a part of haemoglobin which is a carrier of oxygen in the body.

Iron is needed by the body to make healthy red blood, which transports oxygen to the cells. It is also needed for adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production, which is for cellular energy and proper cell function. Iron is lost through sweat and through bleeding of the digestive tract due to harsh motion. Studies on iron indicate that 34 of female runners and 8 male runners are iron deficient. Iron is needed for proper placenta development and also for the prevention of pre-term and low birth weight babies. Studies estimate that up to 58 of pregnant women are iron deficient. Metabolic Processes: Iron plays an important part in the metabolic processes of the animals. It is present in some enzymes that catalyze reactions of cellular oxidation. In human body, the richest organs in iron are liver and spleen. In smaller amount, it is also present in bones, medulla, kidneys and intestines. Calcium: Sources of Calcium: Milk, cheese, egg yolk, beans, nuts, cabbage and green leafy vegetables. Importance / Significance of Calcium: Calcium is the most common mineral in the human body, where it is present in almost the same relative abundance as in the earth's crust. There are six stable isotopes of Calcium: calcium-40 is the most common (97), and calcium-46 the least abundant (0.003). The integrity of the system depends critically on vitamin D status: if there is a deficiency of vitamin D, the loss of its calcaemic action leads to a decrease in the ionised calcium and secondary hyperparathyroidism and hypophosphataemia. This is why experimental vitamin D deficiency results in rickets and osteomalacia whereas calcium deficiency gives rise to osteoporosis. Approximately 99 of total body calcium is in the skeleton and teeth and 1 in blood and soft tissues. Calcium has four major biological functions: Structural as stores in the skeleton, Electrophysiological - carries charge during an action potential across membranes, Intracellular regulator, and as a cofactor for extracellular enzymes and regulatory proteins. Phosphorus: Sources of phosphorous: Egg yolk, cheese, milk, cabbage etc. Importance / Significance of Phosphorus: Phosphorus is present in plants and animals. There is over 1 lb (454 grams) of phosphorus in the human body. It is a component of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), a fundamental energy source in living things. It is found in complex organic compounds in the blood, muscles, and nerves and in calcium phosphate, the principal material in bones and teeth. Phosphorus compounds are used as fertilizer. Organic phosphates, ferric phosphate, and tricalcium phosphate are added to foods. Calcium phosphate is added to animal feeds. The main function of Phosphorus is the formation of bones and teeth. It plays an important role in the body's utilization of carbohydrates and fats and in the synthesis of protein for the growth, maintenance, and repair of cells and tissues. It is essential for the production of ATP, a molecule the body uses to store energy. It also assists with the B vitamins.

It helps in the contraction of muscles, in the functioning of kidneys, in maintaining the regularity of the heartbeat, and in nerve conduction. Zinc: Sources of Zinc: Oyster, red meat, chicken, beans, nuts, dairy products and some sea foods. Importance / Significance of Zinc: Zinc is the most important of all trace elements involved in human metabolism. Human body contains about 2 gm of zinc. More than a hundred specific enzymes require zinc for their catalytic function. If zinc is removed from the catalytic site, activity is lost; replacement of zinc restores activity. Studies in individuals with acrodermatitis enteropathica, a genetic disorder with zinc malabsorption resulting in severe deficiency which causes impairments of dermal, gastrointestinal, neurologic and immunologic systems. Approximately half of the zinc is eliminated from the body through gastrointestinal tract. Considerable amount of zinc is secreted through the biliary and intestinal secretions, but most of it is reabsorbed and this process is important for regulation of zinc balance. Other routes of zinc excretion include the urine and surface losses (hair, sweat). Quick Quiz 6 What is biological significance of minerals? What problems are caused by deficiency of calcium and phosphorus? Give importance of zinc mineral. Society, Technology and Science Glycogen - A store house in the body: Glycogen is reserved food material which is stored in muscles and liver in animals and humans. When body requires energy due to lack of food or glucose, the glycogen is reconverted into glucose and provides energy to the body in the form of ATP. Hibernating Animals and Reserve Food: Large amount of fat is stored in the body of some animals that hibernate during winter. In winter the metabolic activities slow down. They use this fat as reserved food material that produces ATP during oxidation. Complex carbohydrates which Lubricate the Elbow and Knee: Glucosamine, glucosaminoglycans or Proteoglycan are the complex carbohydrates which provide lubrication to elbow and knee. Glucosamine (C6H13NO5) is an amino sugar that plays a role in building cartilage and in joints. It is produced naturally in the body. Glucosamine is a prominent precursor for glycosaminoglycans, which are a major component of joint cartilage. Glucosamine has been shown to help keep our joints resilient and healthy by lubrication that is retained. Glucosaminoglycans (GAGs) are the most abundant heteropolysaccharides in the body. They are long unbranched molecules containing a repeating disaccharide unit. GAGs are a component of joint cartilage. Fibrous Proteins from hair and Silk: Fibrous proteins consist of elongated molecules of one or more polypeptide chains in form of fibrils. They are insoluble in aqueous media. This property conferred by a high concentration of hydrophobic amino acid residues both in interior of the protein and on its surface. They play structural and supporting role in the body. Examples are silk fiber, keratin (of nails, and hair), myosin (in muscle) and fibrin (of blood clot).

Insulin - A protein hormone whose deficiency leads to diabetes mellitus: Insulin is a 51 amino acid peptide hormone that is produced by pancreatic beta cells, which consist of two chains, one alpha chain and one beta chain. The alpha chain contains 21 amino acids and the beta chain contains 30 amino acids. Both chains are held together by disulphide bridges. The molecular weight of insulin is 5808. Insulin hormone is central in regulating carbohydrate and fat metabolism in the body. It causes the cells in liver, muscles and fat tissue to take up glucose from the blood. In the liver and skeletal muscles, glucose is stored as glycogen, while in adipocytes, it is stored as triglycerides. It stops the use of fat as energy source. When blood glucose level fall below a certain limit, the body begins to use stored sugar as an energy source through glycogenolysis. As a central metabolic control mechanism its status is also used as a control signal to other body systems (such as amino acids uptake by body cells). In addition, it has several other anabolic effects throughout the body. Insulin is used medically to treat some forms of diabetes patients. Role of Minerals in the Body: Minerals act as cofactors for the enzyme reactions. Enzymes don't work without minerals. All cells require enzymes to work and function. They give us our vitality. Minerals maintain the pH balance within the body. Minerals actually facilitate the transfer of nutrients across cell membranes. They maintain proper nerve conduction. They help to contract and relax muscles. They help to regulate our bodies tissue growth. Minerals provide structural support for the body. Important Minerals in Human body: Dietary minerals are present in inorganic salts, or as part of carbon containing organic compounds. For example, magnesium is present in chlorophyll, the pigment that makes plants green. Major Minerals: Major minerals are required by people in gram amount: sodium (Na), potassium (K), calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg), phosphorus (P), and chlorine (Cl). Daily requirements range from 0.3 to 2.0 grams per day. Trace Minerals: Trace minerals are required by people in minute amounts: chromium (Cr), copper (Cu), iodine (I), iron (Fe), fluorine (F), manganese (Mn), molybdenum (Mo), selenium (Se), and zinc (Zn). There is no nutritional requirement for cobalt (Co) but these are generally expressed in terms of the cobalt containing vitamin B12. All trace minerals are toxic at high levels. SUMMARY: Carbohydrates are the most abundant macromolecules on earth. They are of three types: monosaccharides, disaccharides and polysaccharides. People eating a diet high in carbohydrates are less likely to accumulate body fat compared with those who follow a low carbohydrate/high-fat diet. Proteins are the most important class of biomolecules. They are major structural components of animals and human tissues. They are classified as simple proteins, conjugated proteins and derived proteins. They are actually the polymers of amino acids.

carboxylicandfunctderivatives2ndchemfed.txt After completing this lesson, you will be able to: Describe preparation of carboxylic acids by carbonation of Grignards Reagent, hydrolysis of nitriles, oxidation of primary alcohols, oxidation of aldehydes and oxidation of alkyl benzenes. Discuss reactivity of carboxylic acids. Describe the chemistry of carboxylic acids by conversion to carboxylic acid derivatives: acyl halides, acid anhydrides, esters, amides and reactions involving interconversion of these. Describe the reactions of carboxylic acid derivatives. Describe isomerism in carboxylic acids. Organic compounds which contain carboxyl group (-COOH) functional group in their molecule are called carboxylic acids. Aliphatic carboxylic acids have the carboxyl group attached with an open chain of carbon atoms. They may be represented by the general formula R-COOH where R H or any alkyl group. Aromatic carboxylic acids have the carboxylic group with phenyl or aryl group. 1 NOMENCLATURE (1) Common Names: Many carboxylic acids are known by their common names, which were given to them before the systematic names. The positions of other groups attached with the chain containing the carboxyl group are indicated by the Greek letters alpha, beta, gamma, etc. The carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group is called alpha carbon and the carbon atom in the carboxyl group is not the alpha carbon. (2) The IUPAC system: Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms containing carboxylic (COOH) group. Replace e of an alkane by oic acid. Number the chain but start from COOH group. If two COOH groups occur then write dioic acid. Examples: Formic acid or methanoic acid. Acetic acid or ethanoic acid. Propionic acid or Propanoic acid. n-Butyric acid or Butanoic acid. Isobutyric acid or 2-Methyl propanoic acid. Trimethylacetic acid or 2,2-Dimethylpropanoic acid. n-Valeric acid or Pentanoic acid. Oxalic acid or Ethanedioic acid. Malonic acid or Propanedioic acid. Succinic acid or Butanedioic acid. Glutaric acid or Pentanedioic acid. Adipic acid or Hexanedioic acid. Benzoic Acid (monocarboxylic acid). 1,2-Benzene dioic acid or phthalic acid (Dicarboxylic acid). 2 PHYSICAL PROPERTIES The polar nature of both the O-H and CO bonds in carboxyl group (due to the electronegativity difference of the atoms) results in: Higher melting and boiling points compared to analogous alcohols. High solubility in water because of hydrogen bonding. Existence in liquid state (Aliphatic acids) or in solid state (Aromatic acid). 3 STRUCTURE Carboxylic acid contains Carboxyl group -COOH. Carboxyl carbon exhibits sp2 hybridization, due to which it has trigonal structure with bond angle close to 120. The hydroxyl oxygen allows one of its lone pair electrons to conjugate with the pi system of the carbonyl group. This makes the carboxyl group planar and can be represented with the following resonance structures. 4 ACIDITY Carboxylic acids are the most acidic simple organic compounds (pKa 5). But they are only weak acids compared to acids like HCl or H2SO4. (Remember the lower the pKa, the stronger the acid). Examples: Ethanoic acid pKa 4.8. Propanoic acid pKa 4.9. Fluoroethanoic acid pKa 2.6. Chloroethanoic acid pKa 2.9. Dichloroethanoic acid pKa 1.3. Trichloroethanoic acid pKa 0.9. Nitroethanoic acid pKa 1.7.

Electron withdrawing group (Cl, F, NO2) bonded to the carbon atom next to the carboxyl group (COOH) make the acid stronger. Due to electron withdrawing group, electron will move away from oxygen. Hence decreases charge density on oxygen atom of carboxylate ion which stabilises the -COO- group and makes it less likely to bond with an H ion. For example, chloroacetic acid is 100 times stronger acid than acetic acid. Electron donating group (Alkyl) strengthens the O-H bond in the acids -COOH group. It donates negative charge towards the -COO- group of the carboxylate ion, making it more likely to accept an H ion, hence acidic strength decreases. For example, formic acid is more acidic than acetic acid. 5 PREPARATION OF CARBOXYLIC ACIDS 1 Reaction of Grignard Reagents (RMgX) with CO2 The reaction is carried out by passing carbon dioxide through the ethereal solution of corresponding Grignards reagent. The addition product on reaction with mineral acid produces carboxylic acid. RMgX CO2 - R-CO-OMgX - (H3O) R-COOH MgX2. 2 Hydrolysis of Nitriles Organic Compounds having a cyanide group are called nitriles. Hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrile on boiling with mineral acid or alkalis yields carboxylic acid. R-CN 2H2O - RCOOH NH3. Methyl nitrile - Acetic acid. The acid produced by this method contains one more carbon atom than the original alkyl halide. 3 Oxidation of Primary Alcohols Primary alcohol is readily oxidized to aldehyde, which further oxidizes to carboxylic acid in the presence of oxidizing agents such as potassium dichromate in an acidic medium. R-CH2OH - R-CHO - R-COOH. 4 Oxidation of Alkyl Benzenes Aromatic carboxylic acid can be prepared by the oxidation of alkyl benzene, when treated with alkaline KMnO4, acidic K2Cr2O7 or dil. HNO3. Toluene - Benzoic acid. 6 REACTIVITY The carboxyl group shows the chemistry of both the carbonyl (CO) and the hydroxyl (-OH) groups. In most reactions, the carbonyl group is retained. However, the reactivity of these molecules is due to the presence of carbonyl group. 7 REACTIONS OF CARBOXYLIC ACIDS Carboxylic acids undergo the following types of reactions: The reaction in which hydrogen atom of -OH group of carboxyl group is involved (salt formation). The reaction in which OH group is replaced by another group. The reactions involving carboxyl group as a whole. 1 Reaction involving H atom of the carboxyl group (Acidic properties of carboxylic acids) Carboxylic acids are weaker acids than mineral acids. They produce H ion when dissolved in water. RCOOH - RCOO- H. Reaction with bases: Carboxylic acids react with bases (NaOH, KOH) to form salts. CH3COOH NaOH - CH3COONa H2O. Reaction with carbonates and bicarbonates: Carboxylic acids decompose carbonate and bicarbonates evolving carbon dioxide gas with effervescence. 2CH3COOH Na2CO3 - 2CH3COONa H2O CO2. Reactions with metals: Carboxylic acids react with active metals such as Na, K, Ca, Mg etc to form their salts with the evolution of hydrogen gas. 2CH3COOH 2Na - 2CH3COONa H2.

2 Reaction involving the OH group of Carboxylic acid (Preparation of derivatives of Carboxylic acid) The addition of a nucleophile to the carboxyl group is always followed by the displacement of the -OH group by some other group producing a carboxylic acid derivative. The -OH group can thus be replaced by X, OR and NH2 to form halides, esters and amide respectively. Reaction with Thionyl Chloride (Preparation of Acyl Chlorides) Acyl chlorides are prepared by treating the carboxylic acid with thionyl chloride, (SOCl2), in the presence of a base (Pyridine). R-COOH SOCl2 - R-COCl SO2 HCl. Dehydration of Carboxylic acid (Preparation of Acid Anhydrides): Carboxylic acids are dehydrated on strong heating in the presence of phosphorous pentoxide (P2O5). 2 R-COOH - (R-CO)2O H2O. Reaction with Alcohol (Preparation of Esters): When carboxylic acids are heated with alcohols in the presence of conc. H2SO4, esters are formed. R-COOH R'-OH - R-COO-R' H2O. Acetic acid ethanol - Ethyl acetate water. This reaction is also known as the Fischer esterification. Esters can also be made from carboxylic acid derivatives, especially acyl halides and acid anhydrides, by reacting them with the appropriate alcohol in the presence of a weak base. Mechanism of reaction for Acid Catalyzed Esterification: Step 1: Protonation of the carbonyl makes it more electrophilic. Step 2: The alcohol OH functions as nucleophile attacking the electrophilic C of the CO group. Step 3: In this step, hydrogen ion transfers in the molecule. Step 4: In this step the elimination of water and a proton from the ion takes place. Reaction with Ammonia (Preparation of Amides): Carboxylic acids react with ammonia to form ammonium salt which on heating produces acid amide. CH3COOH NH3 - CH3COONH4 (Ammonium Acetate). CH3COONH4 - (heat) CH3CONH2 H2O. 3 Reactions involving Carboxyl group (-COOH) A. Reduction: Carboxylic acids are reduced to primary alcohols. As a result of their low reactivity, carboxylic acids can only be reduced by LiAlH4 to form primary alcohol. CH3COOH 4H - CH3CH2OH H2O. Carboxylic acids are less reactive to reduction by hydride than aldehydes, ketones or esters. B. Decarboxylation: The removal of carboxyl group or release of carbon dioxide from carboxylic acid is called decarboxylation. Simple carboxylic acids rarely undergo decarboxylation. (i) When sodium salt of carboxylic acid is strongly heated with soda lime (NaOH CaO), an alkane is formed. The alkane formed contains one carbon less than original carboxylic acid. CH3COONa NaOH - CH4 Na2CO3. (ii) Dry distillation of calcium salt of carboxylic acids gives aldehyde or ketone. Calcium acetate Calcium formate - (dry distillation) Acetaldehyde 2CaCO3. Calcium acetate - (dry distillation) Acetone CaCO3. 4 Reactions of Carboxylic Acid Derivatives A. Reactions of Acyl Halides. B. Reactions of Acid Anhydrides. C. Reactions of Esters: Hydrolysis, Reduction, and with Grignard reagents. D. Reactions of Amides: Hydrolysis and Reduction. E. Reactions of Nitriles: Hydrolysis, Reduction, and with Grignard reagents. A. Reactions of Acyl Halides (Acid Halides): Acid halides are derivatives of carboxylic acid in which (-OH) hydroxyl group has been replaced by a halogen atom.

Reactions: Reaction of Acid halide with water (Hydrolysis of Acid halide): Acid chlorides react with water, often violently, to give the corresponding carboxylic acids and hydrogen chloride. R-COCl H2O - R-COOH HCl. Reaction of Acid halide with carboxylic acid: When Acid halide reacts with carboxylic acid, acid anhydride is formed. R-COCl R'-COOH - R-CO-O-CO-R' HCl. Reaction of Acid halide with alcohol (Formation of ester): When Acid halide reacts with alcohol in presence of conc. H2SO4 as a catalyst, ester is formed. R-COCl R'-OH - R-COO-R' HCl. Reaction of acid halide with ammonia (Formation of amide): When acid halides are treated with ammonia, they form amides. R-COCl 2NH3 - R-CONH2 NH4Cl. B. Reactions of Acid Anhydrides: Hydrolysis (Reaction with water): Acid anhydrides are hydrolysed under acidic or basic conditions to form the parent acid. Acetic anhydride H2O - 2 Acetic acid. Alcoholysis: Acid Anhydrides react with alcohols to form esters. Acetic anhydride ROH - Ester Acetic acid. Formation of Amide: Acid Anhydrides react with Ammonia to form amide. Acetic anhydride NH3 - Acetamide Acetic acid. C. Reactions of Esters: Hydrolysis of Esters: Esters can be hydrolysed to acid and alcohol under acidic or basic conditions. Basic hydrolysis of esters is known as saponification because it leads to the formation of alkali salt of carboxylic acids which are soaps. Ethyl acetate H2O - Acetic acid Ethanol. Ethyl acetate NaOH - Sodium acetate Ethanol. Reduction of Esters: Esters can be reduced either catalytically or using chemical reducing agents, such as LiAlH4 into primary alcohols corresponding to the acid from which it was derived. Ethyl acetate LiAlH4 - 2 Ethanol. Reaction of Grignard reagent (RMgX) with Esters: Esters react with Grignard reagents to give tertiary alcohols. Esters (except formate) react with Grignard reagents to give tertiary alcohols. The tertiary alcohol that results contains 2 identical alkyl groups (from R in the scheme). The reaction proceeds via a ketone intermediate which then reacts with the second equivalent of the organometallic reagent. Ethylacetate CH3MgBr - (after hydrolysis) 2-methyl-2-propanol. D. Reactions of Amides: Hydrolysis of Amides: Amides are hydrolysed when heated with a strong acid or a base and yield carboxylic acids and ammonia (or amines). RCONH2 H2O - RCOOH NH3. Reduction of Amides: Amides can be reduced to primary amines on reduction with LiAlH4. RCONH2 LiAlH4 - R-CH2-NH2 H2O. E. Reaction of Nitriles: Nitriles are that class of organic compounds containing -CN group. Hydrolysis of Nitriles: Nitriles, R-CN, can be hydrolyzed to carboxylic acids, RCOOH via the amide, RCONH2 intermediate in the presence of strong acid (e.g. H2SO4) or strong base (e.g. NaOH) / heat. R-CN - RCONH2 - RCOOH. Reduction of Nitriles: Nitriles can be converted to primary amines by reaction with LiAlH4 (reducing agent). R-CN - (LiAlH4) R-CH2-NH2. Methyl nitrile - Amino ethane. Reactions of RMgX with Nitriles: Grignards reagents on reaction with alkyl nitriles give an addition product (imine salt) which on hydrolysis with dilute HCl yield ketones. Methylmagnesium bromide Methyl nitrile - (after hydrolysis) Acetone.

Society, Technology and Science Carboxylic acids occurrence: Caprylic acid is present in coconut. Lauric acid is also present in coconut. Myristic acid is present in nutmeg. Arachidic acid is present in peanut oil. Citric acid is present in citrus fruits e.g. lemon, limes, grapes, oranges. Tartaric acid is present in tamarind and wine. Lactic acid is present in apples, tomatoes, molasses and sour milk. Acetic acid is present in grapes and vinegar. Malic acid is present in green apples and plums. Benzoic acid is found in berries. Butyric acid is present in rancid butter. Caproic acid is present in goat fat. Caprylic acid is present in milk. Palmitic acid is present in palm oil. Stearic acid is present in waxes, animal fats and oils. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Acetoacetic acid and pyruvic acid are the acids of biochemical significance. Formic acid is used as preservative for silage (including fresh hay) and other livestock feed. Boric acid was used as a food preservative in caviar (a product made from salt-cured fish-eggs) but its use has been banned now. Benzoic acid is used as a preservative in jams, beer, preserved fruit, pickles, fruit juice, dessert sauces and syrups. Sorbic acid is used as a preservative in fish fingers, butter, margarine, processed cheese, curry powder and cooking oil. Acetic acid is used as a preservative in beer, tinned foods especially vegetables and fruit, fresh fruit and vegetables. Propionic acid is used as a preservative in dairy products, particularly in cheese and in baking products. Esters are derived from carboxylic acids by reaction of carboxylic acids and alcohols in the presence of hydrochloric acid or sulfuric acid, a process called esterification. This reaction can occur in nature as a result of a fermentation process. Fruits of ester flavors are acetic acid esters. Isoamyl acetate gives banana flavor. Ethyl butyrate gives pineapple flavor. Methyl anthranilate gives grape flavor. Methyl salicylate gives wintergreen flavor.

environmentchem2ndchemfed.txt After completing this lesson, you will be able to: Recognize various chemical reactions occurring in the atmosphere. Recognize that the release of CO2, SO2, NOx, VOCs is associated with the combustion of hydrocarbon based fuels. Outline problems associated with release of pollutants including acid rain and the formation by free radical reaction of hazardous inorganic and organic compounds e.g., PAN. Describe causes and impacts of urban smog. Explain greenhouse effect and global warming as resulting in climate change. Explain build-up of and recognize the adverse effects of ozone in the troposphere. Describe the role of CFCs in destroying ozone in the stratosphere. Describe the role of ozone in the stratosphere in reducing the intensity of harmful UV radiation reaching the earth. List possible alternatives to the use of CFCs. Recognize and describe various water pollutants. Explain various parameters of water analysis. List some major products of the petrochemical industry together with their uses. Environmental Chemistry is the branch of chemistry which deals with the chemicals and other pollutants in the environment resulting directly and indirectly from human activities. In this we study the sources, chemical reactions, transportation of the chemicals and their adverse effects on human beings. Components of the Environment: Atmosphere: We will study it in detail. Hydrosphere: Concerned with all water bodies i.e. ocean, rivers, streams, lakes, glaciers and ground water reservoirs. Lithosphere: Concerned with hard and rigid rocky earth crust. Biosphere: Area on earth which support life i.e. air, lakes, etc. Atmosphere: Our surrounding on earth is called atmosphere. It consists of gases i.e. N2, O2, CO2, He, Ne, Kr, Xe and water vapours. Its thickness is about 1000 km above the surface of earth. Importance of atmosphere: These gases absorb harmful radiations (cosmic rays and electromagnetic radiation) of Sun to protect life on earth. N2 is used by nitrogen fixing bacteria. O2 is necessary for breathing in animals. CO2 is necessary for photosynthesis in plants and water vapours are responsible for sustaining life on earth. Layers of atmosphere: Atmosphere is divided into four layers. We divide atmosphere into four layers: Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere. We are concerned here with only first two layers i.e. troposphere and stratosphere. CHEMISTRY OF TROPOSPHERE Troposphere is very close to earth in which we live. It extends up to 11 km. It contains all those gases which are present in our atmosphere. In this part of our atmosphere, we will discuss: Different pollutants (Their sources and effects and smog (development and chemistry)). Effects and chemical reactions which occur during acid rain, greenhouse effect and global warming. Role of automobile in air pollution. Smog: "It is a combination of smoke and fog i.e. 'sm' from smoke and 'og' from fog". Smog is of two types: Reducing Smog and Oxidizing Smog. Reducing smog: This smog contains high concentration of SO2. It is chemically reducing in nature and is known as reducing smog. For example, the smoke and SO2 produced from the burning of coal can combine with fog to create industrial smog.

Oxidizing smog: Photochemical smog consists of higher concentration of oxidants like Ozone. It is a yellowish, brownish, grey haze which is formed in the presence of water droplets and chemical reaction of pollutants in the air. It has unpleasant odor. It is oxidizing in nature and is called oxidizing smog. Ozone (O3) and peroxy acetyl nitrate (PAN) are primarily created from volatile organic compounds. Other oxidizing agents are H2O2, HNO3 etc. PAN is an eye irritant and is also toxic to plants. Reactions: 2NO O2 - 2NO2. NO2 - NO O. O O2 - O3. Conditions for Photochemical smog: Sunlight. The production of oxides of nitrogen (NOx). The production of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Temperatures greater than 18C. Major Chemical Pollutants in Photochemical Smog: (Sources and Environmental Effects) Toxic Chemical: Nitrogen Oxides (NO and NO2). Sources: Combustion of oil, coal, gas in both automobiles and industry, bacterial action in soil, forest fires, volcanic action, lightning. Environmental Effects: Decreased visibility due to yellowish color, NO2 causes heart and lung problems, NO2 can suppress plant growth, decreased resistance to infection, may cause cancer. Toxic Chemical: Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs). Sources: Evaporation of solvents, evaporation of fuels, incomplete combustion of fossil fuels. Environmental Effects: Eye irritation, respiratory irritation, some are carcinogenic, decreased visibility due to blue-brown haze. Toxic Chemical: Ozone (O3). Sources: Formed from photolysis of NO2, sometimes results from stratospheric ozone intrusions. Environmental Effects: Bronchial constriction, coughing, sneezing, eye irritation, decreased crop yields and plant growth. Toxic Chemical: Peroxyacetyl Nitrates (PAN). Sources: Formed by the reaction of NO2 with VOCs (can be formed naturally in some environments). Environmental Effects: Eye irritation, high toxicity to plants, respiratory irritation. Toxic Chemical: Carbon Oxide (CO and CO2). Sources: Incomplete combustion of carbon containing fuels (CO), incomplete combustion of agricultural or slush matter (CO2), eruption of volcanoes (CO2), respiration of living organism (CO2). Environmental Effects: CO causes respiratory irritation, CO2 causes greenhouse effect and global warming results climatic changes. Toxic Chemical: Oxides of Sulphur (SO2, SO3). Sources: Volcanic eruption, burning of oil coal, sulphide ores are roasted. Environmental Effects: Causes acid rain, respiratory irritation, loss of green color in plants. Acid Rain (pH less than 5.6): It was first observed by an English scientist R.A. Smith in 1853. Rain water is slightly acidic, having pH 5.6. Due to the absorption of CO2, SO2, NOx etc. The rain water becomes acidic and the pH decreases from 5.6 and is called acid rain. Burning of fuels produced gases SO2, NOx and CO2. These gases react with rainy water or moisture in the presence of oxygen from air to form acids. Reactions: SO2 H2O - H2SO3. 4NO2 2H2O O2 - 4HNO3. CO2 H2O - H2CO3. In some countries due to release of HCl by volcanic eruption, there is temporary acid rain.

H2SO3, HNO3 and H2CO3 formed as above come down the atmosphere as acid rain or acid snow. As far as H2CO3 is concerned, it has no severe effects on animals, plants or any other things. Adverse effects of acid rain: It makes the lakes so acidic that they can no longer support aquatic life. The yield of agricultural crops is reduced. HNO3 acid rain gradually damages lime stone and marble of the buildings and corrodes metals. It fades the colour of fabrics (e.g. cotton, nylon and rayon), leather and paper. It causes extensive leaf-drop in plants. It is very corrosive and attacks skin. Acidification of soil and rocks can leach metals like Al, Hg, Pb and Ca and discharge them into water bodies. Then these heavy metals are eaten by fish which proves very much dangerous for those animals and birds which eat these fish. It also damages steel, paint, plastic, cement and masonry work. Name the heavy metals which leach due to acidification of soil. 3 Green House Effect and Global Warming: Greenhouse Effect: Heat coming from sunlight have shorter wavelength and causes the atoms and molecules in the earth's surface to vibrate and radiate heat and infrared radiation of longer wavelength. Some substances in the atmosphere, especially CO2 and H2O, absorb infrared radiation. This absorption of radiations warms the atmosphere. The earth must lose heat in order to remain in equilibrium. But it is trapped in the atmosphere, and the temperature rises which produces a warming effect on the earth. Two gases CO2 and water vapours in the air, act as an insulating blanket to prevent heat from escaping. The trapping of heat (I.R. radiations of longer wavelength) on the surface of earth by CO2 and water vapour in the atmosphere is known as greenhouse effect. Global Warming: In the atmosphere, water vapours absorb more infrared radiation than CO2 due to its high concentration. The concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere which is 330 ppm increases up to 400 ppm and the temperature should rise as much as 5C. The main global temperature at Earth's surface is about 15C. This temperature is determined by a delicate balance between the energy which is absorbed by the earth and the energy emitted back into space by the Earth. Any change in the amount of energy absorbed or emitted by the Earth could upset this balance, which affect the climate. Due to global warming the rate of melting of glaciers is increasing and water level in sea is rising. Quick Quiz 3 Is CO2 responsible for greenhouse effect? If yes then how? Automobile (Pollutants and Converter): In automobiles during incomplete combustion of petrol, we get smoke of different gases which pollute our atmosphere.

The engine used in these motor vehicles are called internal combustion engines because the petrol which is used as a fuel is burnt inside the engine and contains CO, NO, NO2, un-burnt carbon particles, and lead oxide. All these substances are poisonous and hence pollute air. Production of Pollutants: The pollutants produced in the internal combustion engine by the use of petrol (which mainly contain hydrocarbon) are CO, NO, NO2. Due to incomplete combustion of petrol some CO, un-burnt carbon particles, CO2, water vapors, CO and carbon particles are emitted into the air, which causes air pollution. When petrol burns in a car engine, a very high temperature is produced. At this high temperature, N2 and O2 present in air of the engine combine together and form NO and NO2. These gases also pollute the air. Control Measures: By adding tetraethyl lead to the petrol: Tetraethyl lead improves the quality of petrol and hence enables it to burn more completely. Due to this air pollution is minimized. Drawbacks: Lead vapour pollutes the air. Lead oxide (PbO) deposits in the valves of the engine. Catalytic oxidation / Converter: The pollution of air caused by unburnt hydrocarbons and CO present in the exhaust gases of the vehicle engine can also be reduced by attaching a device with the vehicles engine, in which the exhaust gases can be mixed with more air and then burnt completely in the presence of platinum catalyst before they are discharged into the environment. Hydrocarbons and CO are oxidized by O2 of the air in presence of platinum catalyst. 2C8H18 25O2 - 16CO2 18H2O. 2CO O2 - 2CO2. 2NO 2CO - N2 2CO2. The overall result of passing exhaust gases through this kind of catalyst system is to convert CO, NOx, and CxHy to relatively harmless N2, CO2 and H2O. The catalytic reactions do not start working until the catalyst has reached a temperature of about 200C, so they are not effective until the engine has warmed up. Catalyst systems of this type cost several hundred pounds, mainly because of the high cost of the precious metal they contain. The catalyst is poisoned by lead, so unleaded fuel must always be used.
